explanation: The copy back is a blind overwrite, so it silently overwrites whatever your teammate changed in those same files. Nothing reports the loss, because as far as the tool is concerned you simply made those changes yourself.

prompt: An attempt to send is refused, with a message saying the shared copy holds work you do not have. What does that refusal protect against?
optionA: Sending a file that is too large to store
optionB: Recording a commit without a message
optionC: Two people editing the same line of the same file
optionD: Replacing your teammate's commits with a history that never contained them
correctAnswerText: Replacing your teammate's commits with a history that never contained them
explanation: Your history does not include their commits, so sending it as it stands would mean replacing your teammate's commits with a history that never contained them. The refusal is what forces you to bring their work down first.

prompt: A page has a title at the top of a section. Which element fits its meaning?
optionA: A paragraph with large text
optionB: A heading element
optionC: A list item, for the indentation
optionD: A quote element, which stands out
correctAnswerText: A heading element
explanation: A heading element says that the text titles what follows, which is what the content is. The other three would be chosen for how they look rather than for what they mean.

prompt: A page shows three product names, one after another, with no ordering between them. Which element fits?
optionA: Three paragraphs
optionB: An ordered list, since they appear in an order on screen
optionC: A table with one column
optionD: An unordered list
correctAnswerText: An unordered list
explanation: A group of related items with no meaningful order is exactly what an unordered list expresses. Appearing one after another on screen is not the same as being ordered.

prompt: A page reproduces a sentence taken from another source. Which element fits?
optionA: A quotation element
optionB: A paragraph in italics
optionC: A list item, which indents it
optionD: A heading, to set it apart
correctAnswerText: A quotation element
explanation: The content is a quotation, and one element says so. Italics and indentation are how quotations often look, which is a consequence rather than the meaning.

prompt: A developer uses a heading element because it makes the text large. What is wrong with that?
optionA: Nothing; the text is the right size
optionB: Headings should never be used
optionC: The element says the text is a heading, which will be untrue and will mislead anything reading the structure
optionD: The text will be the wrong size on some screens
correctAnswerText: The element says the text is a heading, which will be untrue and will mislead anything reading the structure
explanation: Choosing an element for its appearance puts a false claim into the document. Size can be set directly without changing what the markup says the content is.

prompt: Two developers produce pages that look identical. One used headings for its section titles and the other used styled paragraphs. What differs?
optionA: Nothing; the pages are identical
optionB: What the document says its structure is, which anything other than a sighted reader depends on
optionC: The file size
optionD: How quickly each page loads
correctAnswerText: What the document says its structure is, which anything other than a sighted reader depends on
explanation: Appearance is the same and meaning is not. A reader navigating by structure, or a tool building an outline, sees sections in one page and undifferentiated text in the other.

prompt: Which fragment is written correctly?
optionA: Hello
optionB: Hello
optionC: Hello
optionD: Hello
correctAnswerText: Hello
explanation: An element that holds content opens and closes once around it. Repeating the opening tag opens a second element, and a second closing tag closes something that is not open.

prompt: An image is being placed on a page. Which fragment is written correctly?
optionC: cat.png
explanation: An image element holds no content, so it takes no closing tag and its source is supplied as an attribute. Giving it content or a closing tag treats it like an element that wraps something.

prompt: Which fragment closes its tags in the right order?
optionA: text
optionB: text
optionC: text
optionD: text
correctAnswerText: text
explanation: Elements close in the reverse of the order they open, so the inner one closes first. Crossing them leaves each element half inside the other, which nothing can represent.

prompt: A paragraph element is opened and never closed, and the rest of the page follows. What happens to that later content?
optionA: It is discarded
optionB: It may be absorbed into the unclosed element, so it is treated as part of the paragraph
optionC: The page refuses to render
optionD: It renders exactly as though the tag had been closed
correctAnswerText: It may be absorbed into the unclosed element, so it is treated as part of the paragraph
explanation: An element that is never closed continues, so what follows falls inside it. The page still renders, which is why the fault shows up as misplaced content rather than as an error.

prompt: In Help, which part is an attribute?
optionA: a
optionB: Help
optionD: href="/help"
correctAnswerText: href="/help"
explanation: The attribute is href="/help", a name-and-value pair inside the opening tag. The letter at the front is the element name and the word between the tags is the content.

prompt: In , what does the alt attribute supply?
optionA: Text to use in place of the image
optionB: The file the image comes from
optionC: The name of the element
optionD: The width of the image
correctAnswerText: Text to use in place of the image
explanation: Each attribute supplies one thing, and this one supplies the alternative text. The file is supplied by a different attribute in the same tag.

prompt: Where do attributes belong?
optionA: In the closing tag
optionB: In either tag
optionC: In the opening tag
optionD: Between the opening and closing tags, with the content
correctAnswerText: In the opening tag
explanation: Attributes configure the element and are written where it opens. A closing tag carries the element name and nothing else.

prompt: A tag reads Help, with no quotation marks around the value. Is the value part of the attribute or content?
optionA: Content, because it is not quoted
optionB: Part of the attribute; it sits inside the opening tag whether or not it is quoted
optionC: Neither; the tag is invalid and is ignored
optionD: Part of the element name
correctAnswerText: Part of the attribute; it sits inside the opening tag whether or not it is quoted
explanation: What decides is position rather than punctuation: anything inside the opening tag after the element name is an attribute. Quoting is good practice and its absence does not move the value out of the tag.

prompt: Which fragment nests correctly?
optionA: • One
optionB: • One
optionC: • One
optionD: • One
correctAnswerText: • One
explanation: A list contains list items and an item may contain anything inline. Placing an emphasis element directly inside the list, or crossing the closing tags, breaks the containment.

prompt:
A fragment reads

Some bold

text. What is wrong, and what will happen?
optionA: The two elements overlap rather than nest, and the browser will guess at a structure
optionB: Nothing; the tags are all present
optionC: The strong element is missing a closing tag
optionD: The paragraph is missing an opening tag
correctAnswerText: The two elements overlap rather than nest, and the browser will guess at a structure
explanation: Every tag is present and they cross, which is what no tree can represent. Browsers recover by inventing a structure, and different ones may invent different structures.

prompt: Text is to be emphasised because it is genuinely important. Two elements render it in bold. Which fits?
optionA: The one that means the text should be bold
optionB: Either; they render the same
optionC: The one that means the text is important
optionD: A generic container with bold styling
correctAnswerText: The one that means the text is important
explanation: Both look the same and only one says why the text is different. That claim is what anything reading the structure rather than the pixels acts on.

prompt: A page has a block of navigation links. A generic container and a navigation element both produce the same appearance. Which fits, and why does it matter?
optionA: The generic container, because it is more flexible
optionB: The navigation element, because it lets a reader jump to or skip the navigation
optionC: Either; the appearance is what users see
optionD: The generic container, because it is shorter to type
correctAnswerText: The navigation element, because it lets a reader jump to or skip the navigation
explanation: A specific element exists for this content and carries information a generic one does not. Flexibility and brevity are real considerations and neither restores what the meaning would have supplied.

prompt:
A fragment reads

Hello world

, with five spaces between the words. What appears on the page?
optionA: Hello world, with five spaces
optionB: Helloworld, with no space
optionC: The text with the tags shown
optionD: Hello world, with a single space
correctAnswerText: Hello world, with a single space
explanation: Runs of whitespace collapse to one space when rendered. Tags are instructions rather than content and are not displayed.

prompt: A fragment has a paragraph whose text is written across three lines in the file, with no other markup. How does it appear?
optionA: As one continuous line of text, wrapped to fit the width
optionB: As three separate lines, as written
optionC: As three separate paragraphs
optionD: With the line breaks shown as blank lines
correctAnswerText: As one continuous line of text, wrapped to fit the width
explanation: A newline in the source is whitespace and collapses like any other. Breaking lines on the page requires markup that says so.

prompt: A developer formats their markup neatly across several lines and the rendered spacing between two words changes. The markup is valid and the elements are unchanged. What happened?
optionA: The formatting changed the elements
optionB: The browser reformatted the text
optionC: A newline was introduced where the two words previously touched, and it renders as a space
optionD: Nothing changed; the difference is imagined
correctAnswerText: A newline was introduced where the two words previously touched, and it renders as a space
explanation: Collapsing whitespace turns a newline into one space, so a line break inserted between two words adds a space that was not there. Reformatting markup is usually safe and is not always so.

prompt: A list fragment contains three list items and one line of text placed directly inside the list itself. How many list items does it have?
optionA: Four
optionB: Three
optionC: One
optionD: Three, plus a fourth once the text is wrapped
correctAnswerText: Three
explanation: Only content inside a list item counts as an item. The stray text is inside the list and inside no item, which is why it is not counted and is also not valid.

prompt: A table has a header row of 3 cells and 4 further rows of 3 cells each. How many cells does it contain in total?
explanation: Every row contributes its cells, header rows included, so five rows of three give fifteen. Omitting the header row is the commonest miscount.

prompt: A table is meant to have 4 columns. One row contains 3 cells and the rest contain 4. The markup is otherwise valid and the page renders. What is the effect?
optionA: That row is short by a cell, so its remaining cells may not line up with the columns above
optionB: The table refuses to render
optionC: The missing cell is created automatically and left blank
optionD: The whole table is reduced to three columns
correctAnswerText: That row is short by a cell, so its remaining cells may not line up with the columns above
explanation: A row supplies exactly the cells it contains, and nothing fills a gap. The table still renders, which is why the fault appears as misaligned data rather than as an error.

prompt: A site has /index.html and /about.html. A link in index.html reads href="about.html". Which file does it reach?
optionA: /index.html
optionB: A file called about.html inside a folder called about
optionC: /about.html
optionD: Nothing; the path is incomplete
correctAnswerText: /about.html
explanation: A path with no leading slash is resolved beside the page containing it, and both files sit at the top level. Nothing about it is incomplete.

prompt: The folder tree is: index.html at the top level, and a guides folder containing setup.html. A link written inside setup.html begins with a slash: href="/index.html". What does the leading slash change?
optionA: Nothing; a leading slash is optional
optionB: It resolves from the top of the site rather than from the folder the page is in
optionC: It resolves from the folder the page is in, as usual
optionD: It makes the link point outside the site
correctAnswerText: It resolves from the top of the site rather than from the folder the page is in
explanation: A leading slash starts the path at the root, so the same text means the same file wherever the page sits. Without it the link would be looked for inside the guides folder.

prompt: A site has /guides/setup.html and /images/logo.png. A link in setup.html reads href="../images/logo.png" and works. The same link is copied into /index.html and breaks. Neither file was moved. Why?
optionA: The image was moved
optionB: A leading slash is missing from both links
optionC: index.html cannot reach the images folder
optionD: The parent step goes up one level from wherever the page is, and from the top level there is nowhere to go up to
correctAnswerText: The parent step goes up one level from wherever the page is, and from the top level there is nowhere to go up to
explanation: A relative path is measured from the page containing it, so the same text means different things in different places. From the top level the parent step overshoots the site entirely.

prompt: A form contains a text input with no name attribute. Is its value submitted?
optionA: No; a control without a name has nothing to submit its value under
optionB: Yes; the value is submitted under its label
optionC: Yes; the value is submitted without a name
optionD: No; the form refuses to submit at all
correctAnswerText: No; a control without a name has nothing to submit its value under
explanation: The name is what the value is sent as, so a control without one is silently omitted. The form submits normally, which is what makes the omission hard to spot.

prompt: A form contains a disabled text input with a name and a value. Is its value submitted?
optionA: Yes; it has a name and a value
optionB: Yes; disabling only prevents editing
optionC: No; a disabled control is excluded from the submission
optionD: No; and the form refuses to submit
correctAnswerText: No; a disabled control is excluded from the submission
explanation: Disabling removes the control from the submission as well as from interaction. That is different from making it read-only, which prevents editing and still submits.

prompt: A form has a checkbox that the user leaves unchecked. The server receives no value for it and treats the field as missing rather than false. The checkbox has a name and the form submits correctly. What is happening?
optionA: The checkbox is disabled
optionB: An unchecked box submits nothing at all, so absence is the only signal that it was unchecked
optionC: The checkbox has no name
optionD: The form is submitting before the box is read
correctAnswerText: An unchecked box submits nothing at all, so absence is the only signal that it was unchecked
explanation: A checkbox submits its value only when checked, so unchecked and absent are indistinguishable on the server. The stem rules out the name and the submission, which leaves the behaviour itself.

prompt: An image is a company logo appearing in the page header. What alternative text fits?
optionA: logo.png
optionB: A rectangular blue image with white lettering
optionC: Image
optionD: The company name
correctAnswerText: The company name
explanation: Alternative text conveys what the image conveys, which here is the company's identity. A filename and a description of the appearance both leave the reader without the information the image carried.

prompt: An image is a chart showing sales rising over four quarters. What alternative text fits?
optionA: A statement of what the chart shows, such as that sales rose across the four quarters
optionB: chart.png
optionC: A line chart with four points
optionD: Chart
correctAnswerText: A statement of what the chart shows, such as that sales rose across the four quarters
explanation: The image carries a finding, so the alternative text has to carry that finding. Describing the shape of the chart gives the reader the picture without the point.

prompt: An image is a decorative flourish beside a heading and conveys nothing a reader needs. Every option below is a well-formed value. What alternative text fits?
optionA: A description of the flourish
optionB: The word "decoration"
optionC: Empty text, so that the image is passed over
optionD: The filename
correctAnswerText: Empty text, so that the image is passed over
explanation: An image carrying no information should not interrupt a reader, and empty alternative text is how that is expressed. Describing it, or announcing that it is decorative, makes the reader stop for something that does not matter.

prompt:
A fragment reads:

One two

Three

. What is the parent of the em element?
optionA: The div
optionB: The first paragraph
optionC: The second paragraph
optionD: The text "One"
correctAnswerText: The first paragraph
explanation: A parent is the element that directly contains another, and the em sits inside The first paragraph. The div is its grandparent rather than its parent.

prompt: In the same fragment, someone says the em element and the second paragraph are siblings. Both are contained within the div at some depth. Are they?
optionA: Yes; both are inside the div
optionB: Yes; they are at the same visual level
optionC: No; the em element has no siblings at all
optionD: No; siblings share the same direct parent, and these have different ones
correctAnswerText: No; siblings share the same direct parent, and these have different ones
explanation: Being inside the same ancestor is not the same as sharing a parent, which is what makes the claim tempting. The em element does have a sibling — the text beside it in the first paragraph.

prompt: A page shows its whole second half in bold. The markup contains an opening emphasis tag halfway down. Which line is at fault?
optionA: The line with the opening emphasis tag, which is never closed
optionB: The first line of the bold text
optionC: The last line of the page
optionD: The stylesheet, which must set bold
correctAnswerText: The line with the opening emphasis tag, which is never closed
explanation: The symptom starts where the element opens and continues because nothing closes it. The lines that appear bold are affected rather than responsible.

prompt: A page shows its navigation links inside the first article rather than above it. The stylesheet is unchanged and correct, and the navigation markup itself is well formed. Which kind of fault is it?
optionA: A styling fault in the navigation
optionB: A fault in the navigation markup
optionC: A structural one: something before the navigation was left unclosed, so it was absorbed
optionD: A fault in the article markup, which is too wide
correctAnswerText: A structural one: something before the navigation was left unclosed, so it was absorbed
explanation: Content appearing in the wrong place with correct styling and correct local markup points at an unclosed element earlier in the document. The cause sits before the symptom, which is what makes it awkward to find.

prompt: A form shows the word "Email" beside a text box, written as plain text with no association between them. What can a screen reader user not do?
optionA: See the text
optionB: Know what the box is for when they reach it
optionC: Type into the box
optionD: Submit the form
correctAnswerText: Know what the box is for when they reach it
explanation: The text is visible and unconnected, so a reader moving to the control is told nothing about it. Everything else on the page continues to work, which is why the fault is invisible on screen.

prompt: A page uses a top-level heading, then jumps to a third-level heading for its next section. The page looks correct and the headings are real heading elements. What is lost?
optionA: Nothing; the appearance is correct
optionB: The headings will not be announced at all
optionC: The second-level heading is created automatically
optionD: The outline implies a missing level, so a reader navigating by structure cannot tell how the sections relate
correctAnswerText: The outline implies a missing level, so a reader navigating by structure cannot tell how the sections relate
explanation: Heading levels describe nesting, and skipping one describes a nesting that does not exist. Everything is announced and the relationships between the sections are wrong.

prompt: A developer fixes an accessibility complaint by increasing the font size and the contrast. The complaint was that a form control had no label. Has the complaint been addressed?
optionA: No; the fix is visual and the fault is structural, so a reader who cannot see it is no better off
optionB: Yes; the page is now easier to read
optionC: Yes, provided the contrast is sufficient
optionD: No; the font size should have been left alone
correctAnswerText: No; the fix is visual and the fault is structural, so a reader who cannot see it is no better off
explanation: The change is a genuine improvement for some readers and touches nothing the complaint was about. Matching the kind of fix to the kind of fault is what makes accessibility work rather than gesture.

prompt: Two pages look identical. One uses heading elements and lists; the other uses styled generic containers throughout. What can a reader do on one and not the other?
optionA: Read the text, which only the first page allows
optionB: See the page, which only the first page allows
optionC: Navigate by structure — jump between sections, or move through a list — which only the marked-up page supports
optionD: Nothing differs; both pages carry the same information
correctAnswerText: Navigate by structure — jump between sections, or move through a list — which only the marked-up page supports
explanation: Both pages present the same words and only one says how they are organised. Structure is what navigation is built on, so its absence removes a way of moving through the page rather than the content.

prompt: Adding correct structure to a page costs a little time and changes nothing visible. Why is it worth doing?
optionA: Because it makes the page load faster
optionB: Because the structure is what every non-visual route through the page depends on, and nothing else supplies it
optionC: Because it makes the page look better
optionD: It is not worth doing if nothing changes visually
correctAnswerText: Because the structure is what every non-visual route through the page depends on, and nothing else supplies it
explanation: Nothing changing visually is exactly the point: the benefit accrues to readers who are not using the visual presentation at all. Judging the change by what it does to the picture measures the wrong thing.

prompt: A page is correct until its third section, after which everything is indented and misplaced. The third section's own markup is well formed. Where is the fault?
optionA: In the third section, where the symptom begins
optionB: In the last section, which is most affected
optionC: In the stylesheet, which indents the content
optionD: In an element opened before the third section and never closed
correctAnswerText: In an element opened before the third section and never closed
explanation: An unclosed element absorbs everything after it, so the symptom starts where the effect begins and the cause sits earlier. The section where trouble first appears is the one being affected.

prompt: Why is an unclosed tag harder to locate than a misspelled element name?
optionA: Its effect appears at a distance from its cause, and everything between them looks correct
optionB: Because browsers hide unclosed tags
optionC: Because a misspelled name is always reported as an error
optionD: It is not harder; both are equally visible
correctAnswerText: Its effect appears at a distance from its cause, and everything between them looks correct
explanation: The symptom of an unclosed tag is displaced from the line responsible, so reading around the symptom finds nothing wrong. A misspelling affects the element it appears on.

prompt: A page has one unclosed element near the top and renders as one enormous nested block. How many faults should be looked for?
optionA: One per misplaced section
optionB: At least two, since one tag cannot affect so much
optionC: One; a single unclosed element can misplace everything after it
optionD: None; the browser recovers automatically
correctAnswerText: One; a single unclosed element can misplace everything after it
explanation: The scale of a symptom says nothing about the number of causes, and containment cascades through everything that follows. Browsers do recover, and the structure they invent is what produces the symptom.

prompt: A developer proposes fixing misplaced content by adding closing tags at the end of the document. What is wrong with that?
optionA: Nothing; the tags are now balanced
optionB: It closes the elements in the wrong place, so the content is still inside them
optionC: Closing tags may not appear at the end of a document
optionD: It would make the page refuse to render
correctAnswerText: It closes the elements in the wrong place, so the content is still inside them
explanation: Balance is not the requirement; the element has to close where its content ends. Closing everything at the bottom produces a well-formed document with exactly the wrong structure.

prompt: Browsers recover from unclosed tags rather than refusing to render. What does that buy, and what does it cost?
optionA: It buys nothing; strictness would be better
optionB: It costs nothing; recovery is always correct
optionC: It buys speed, since no checking is needed
optionD: It keeps imperfect pages usable, and it lets a structural fault reach users without anything reporting it
correctAnswerText: It keeps imperfect pages usable, and it lets a structural fault reach users without anything reporting it
explanation: Recovery is why a small mistake does not take a page down, and it is also why the mistake is never announced. Different browsers may recover differently, so the same page can render differently for different people.

prompt: Two fragments render identically: one uses a heading element, the other a paragraph styled to match. Both look the same in every browser tested. Are they equivalent?
optionA: No; they look alike and say different things about what the content is
optionB: Yes; identical rendering is what equivalence means
optionC: No; they will render differently on some browsers
optionD: Yes, provided the styling is applied everywhere
correctAnswerText: No; they look alike and say different things about what the content is
explanation: Equivalence in markup covers structure and meaning as well as appearance. Identical rendering is what makes the difference invisible rather than absent.

prompt: Two fragments differ only in how their whitespace is laid out across lines, with no whitespace inserted between words. Are they equivalent?
optionA: No; the layout of the source affects the page
optionB: No; different line lengths render differently
optionC: Yes; whitespace between tags collapses and carries no meaning
optionD: Yes, but only if both are on one line
correctAnswerText: Yes; whitespace between tags collapses and carries no meaning
explanation: Formatting the source is one of the few changes that genuinely preserves both structure and appearance. The exception is whitespace between words, which the stem excludes.

prompt: Two fragments produce the same page: one wraps its content in three nested containers and one in a single container. Are they equivalent?
optionA: Yes, entirely
optionB: In appearance and in meaning yes; they differ in the tree, which styling and scripts may depend on
optionC: No; the extra containers change the meaning
optionD: No; extra containers always change the appearance
correctAnswerText: In appearance and in meaning yes; they differ in the tree, which styling and scripts may depend on
explanation: Containers carry no meaning of their own, so the document says the same thing either way. The shape of the tree is still real, and anything selecting by relationship can tell the two apart.

prompt: What does it take to say two fragments are truly equivalent?
optionA: That they render identically
optionB: That they contain the same text
optionC: That they use the same number of elements
optionD: That they agree in structure and meaning as well as in appearance
correctAnswerText: That they agree in structure and meaning as well as in appearance
explanation: Appearance is one of three things a fragment carries, and the other two are what markup exists to express. Two fragments can share their text and their picture while describing entirely different documents.

prompt: What kind of value is "42", written with the quotes shown?
optionA: A number
optionB: A string
optionC: A boolean
optionD: An empty value
correctAnswerText: A string
explanation: A string is what quotes produce, whatever is between them. Digits inside quotes are text and will not behave arithmetically until they are converted.

prompt: What kind of value is [1, 2, 3]?
optionA: A plain object with no particular kind
optionB: A string
optionC: Three separate numbers
optionD: An array
correctAnswerText: An array
explanation: An array is an ordered list written in square brackets and reached by position. It is one value, not three.

prompt: What kind of value is true, written without quotes?
optionA: A boolean
optionB: A string
optionC: A number
optionD: A name that has not been declared
correctAnswerText: A boolean
explanation: A boolean is one of the two truth values written bare. Putting quotes around it would make the word into text instead.

prompt: A name is declared with let and nothing is assigned to it. What value does it hold?
optionA: null
optionC: undefined
optionD: An empty string
correctAnswerText: undefined
explanation: undefined is what a declared name holds before anything is put in it. The other empty-looking values all have to be assigned deliberately.

prompt: One property is deliberately set to null and one name was declared without being assigned. Do the two hold the same value?
optionA: Yes; both simply mean empty
optionB: No; null was put there on purpose and undefined means nothing was ever put there
optionC: No; null means zero and undefined means empty text
optionD: Yes; null is only how undefined is printed
correctAnswerText: No; null was put there on purpose and undefined means nothing was ever put there
explanation: The two are separate values with separate meanings, which is the distinction the pair exists to draw: null was put there on purpose and undefined means nothing was ever put there. Treating them as interchangeable loses the information that somebody chose the emptiness.

prompt: A name is declared with let and given 5. A later line assigns 9 to the same name. Is that allowed?
optionA: No; a name can only be assigned once
optionB: Yes, but only inside the same line
optionC: No; the second assignment silently does nothing
optionD: Yes; a name declared with let can be assigned again
correctAnswerText: Yes; a name declared with let can be assigned again
explanation: Reassignment is exactly what let permits, so a name declared with let can be assigned again. Only a declaration that fixes the binding refuses it.

prompt: A name is declared with const and given 5. A later line assigns 9 to the same name. What happens?
optionA: It fails with an error
optionB: It succeeds and the name becomes 9
optionC: It silently does nothing and the name stays 5
optionD: It succeeds but only until the next line
correctAnswerText: It fails with an error
explanation: It fails with an error, because const fixes what the name refers to for as long as the name exists. Nothing is assigned and nothing is silently ignored.

prompt: Which declaration keyword prevents the name being pointed at a different value later?
optionA: let
optionB: var
optionC: const
optionD: No keyword does this
correctAnswerText: const
explanation: const is the declaration that fixes what a name refers to. The others allow the name to be reassigned freely.

prompt: An array is declared with const. A later line pushes a new item onto it. Does that work?
optionA: No; a const array cannot be changed at all
optionB: Yes; const fixes what the name points at, not the contents of what it points at
optionC: Yes, but the change is discarded at the end of the line
optionD: No; push replaces the array, which const forbids
correctAnswerText: Yes; const fixes what the name points at, not the contents of what it points at
explanation: The array itself is not frozen by the declaration, so pushing succeeds: const fixes what the name points at, not the contents of what it points at. Only assigning a different array to the name would fail.

prompt: let x = 5; console.log(x); What is printed?
optionA: x
optionB: let x = 5
optionC: undefined
explanation: The name is replaced by the value it holds before anything is printed, so 5 appears. Printing the name itself would need it in quotes.

prompt: let total = 3 + 4; console.log(total); What is printed?
optionC: total
explanation: The arithmetic is done at the moment of assignment, so the name holds 7 and 7 is printed. The expression itself is gone by then.

prompt: console.log("Score:", 8); What is printed?
optionA: Score:
optionC: Score: 8
optionD: Score:, 8
correctAnswerText: Score: 8
explanation: Score: 8 appears. Quoted text is shown exactly as written, and the comma separates a second thing to show rather than becoming part of what is shown.

prompt: let n = 1; console.log(n); n = 2; console.log(n); What is printed, in order?
optionA: 2 then 2
optionB: 1 then 2
optionC: 1 then 1
optionD: 2 then 1
correctAnswerText: 1 then 2
explanation: Each print shows the value held at the moment it runs, giving 1 then 2. A later assignment cannot reach back and change what was already printed.

prompt: What does 5 + "5" produce?
optionA: The number 10
optionB: The number 55
optionC: An error, because the types differ
optionD: The string 55
correctAnswerText: The string 55
explanation: The string 55 is produced, because plus joins as soon as either side is text. Nothing fails; the result is simply text rather than a number.

prompt: What does "3" + 4 - 1 produce?
optionA: The number 33
optionB: The number 6
optionC: The string 33
optionD: An error, because the first step gave text
correctAnswerText: The number 33
explanation: The number 33 is produced. Plus joins first, giving the text 34, and minus has no joining meaning at all, so it converts that text and subtracts, leaving a number.

prompt: Consider 5 == "5" and 5 === "5". What are the two results?
optionA: Both are true
optionB: Both are false
optionC: The first is true and the second is false
optionD: The first is false and the second is true
correctAnswerText: The first is true and the second is false
explanation: The converting form matches after making the types agree and the strict form refuses to convert at all, so the first is true and the second is false. That is the whole difference between them.

prompt: Consider null == undefined and null === undefined. Which of the two comparisons holds?
optionA: Neither holds
optionB: The first holds and the second does not
optionC: Both hold
optionD: The first does not hold and the second does
correctAnswerText: The first holds and the second does not
explanation: The converting form treats the two empty values as matching each other, while the strict form sees two different values, so the first holds and the second does not. Neither comparison fails or errors.

prompt: A condition is written as if ([]) with an empty array inside. Does the body run?
optionA: No; an empty array counts as false
optionB: It fails, because an array is not a condition
optionC: It runs only once the array has items
optionD: Yes; an empty array counts as true
correctAnswerText: Yes; an empty array counts as true
explanation: Every object, including an empty array, counts as true in a condition, so the body runs. Emptiness of a list is something that has to be checked by its length.

prompt: Two conditions are written: if (0) and if ("0"). Which bodies run?
optionA: The first is skipped and the second runs
optionB: Both run
optionC: Both are skipped
optionD: The first runs and the second is skipped
correctAnswerText: The first is skipped and the second runs
explanation: Zero counts as false, while a string containing a zero character is a non-empty string and counts as true, so the first is skipped and the second runs. The quotes are the whole difference.

prompt: A check written as if (count) is meant to run whenever a count was supplied. It runs for every supplied count except when the supplied count is 0. What is the cause?
optionA: count was never declared
optionB: The check should have used the strict form of equality
optionC: Zero counts as false, so a supplied 0 is treated the same as nothing supplied
optionD: A number cannot be used as a condition at all
correctAnswerText: Zero counts as false, so a supplied 0 is treated the same as nothing supplied
explanation: The stem rules out the check being broken in general, since every other supplied count works. Zero counts as false, so a supplied 0 is treated the same as nothing supplied, which is why this kind of check is written against undefined instead.

prompt: const a = [10, 20, 30]; What is a[1]?
optionD: An error, because positions start at 1
explanation: Positions are counted from zero, so a[1] is the second item, 20. Counting from one would give the first item instead.

prompt: const a = ["x", "y"]; a.push("z"); What are a.length and a[a.length - 1]?
optionA: 2 and y
optionB: 3 and undefined
optionC: 4 and z
optionD: 3 and z
correctAnswerText: 3 and z
explanation: Pushing adds one item, so the length becomes 3 and z is the last item. The length is one more than the last position, which is why one is subtracted to reach it.

prompt: const a = [1, 2]; console.log(a[5]); The program keeps running and prints one line. What is printed?
optionA: undefined
optionB: An error message
optionD: Nothing at all
correctAnswerText: undefined
explanation: Reading a position that does not exist gives undefined rather than failing, which is why the program keeps running. A language that raised an error here would have stopped instead.

prompt: function double(n) { return n * 2; } What does double(4) produce?
optionD: undefined
explanation: The argument is multiplied and handed back, giving 8. Nothing is printed unless the caller prints it.

prompt: function show(n) { console.log(n); } const r = show(3); What is printed, and what does r hold?
optionA: 3 is printed, and r holds 3
optionB: 3 is printed, and r holds undefined
optionC: Nothing is printed, and r holds 3
optionD: 3 is printed, and r holds 0
correctAnswerText: 3 is printed, and r holds undefined
explanation: Printing a value and returning it are separate acts, so 3 is printed, and r holds undefined. A function with no return hands back nothing.

prompt: function f() { return 1; console.log("here"); } The call hands back 1 and here is never printed. Why not?
optionA: Printing is not allowed after a return
optionB: The printing happened but was not shown
optionC: The function stopped because it had no arguments
optionD: The return ends the call, so the line after it never runs
correctAnswerText: The return ends the call, so the line after it never runs
explanation: Reaching a return leaves the function immediately, so the line after it never runs. Code placed after an unconditional return can never execute at all.

prompt: const u = { name: "Ana", age: 30 }; What is u.name?
optionA: Ana
optionB: name
optionD: undefined
correctAnswerText: Ana
explanation: The dot reaches the property of that name and gives what is stored there, Ana. The word before the dot names the object, not the property.

prompt: const u = { name: "Ana" }; What does u.email give, and does the program continue?
optionA: An error, and the program stops
optionB: An empty string, and the program continues
optionC: undefined, and the program continues
optionD: null, and the program continues
correctAnswerText: undefined, and the program continues
explanation: Reading a property that was never set gives undefined, and the program continues. Failing here would make optional properties impossible to test for.

prompt: const u = {}; console.log(u.address.city); The program stops at this line instead of printing anything. Why does this fail when reading a single missing property does not?
optionA: city is a reserved word
optionB: u.address is undefined, and reading a property of undefined is not allowed
optionC: An empty object cannot be read from at all
optionD: Two dots in one expression are not permitted
correctAnswerText: u.address is undefined, and reading a property of undefined is not allowed
explanation: The first step succeeds and gives undefined; the second step then tries to read from that, and reading a property of undefined is not allowed. One missing level is safe and two is not.

prompt: const a = [1, 2]; const b = a; b.push(3); What do a and b contain?
optionA: a contains 1, 2 and b contains 1, 2, 3
optionB: Both contain 1, 2
optionC: It fails, because a was declared with const
optionD: Both contain 1, 2, 3
correctAnswerText: Both contain 1, 2, 3
explanation: Assigning an array to a second name copies the reference and not the contents, so both contain 1, 2, 3. There is only one array here with two names for it.

prompt: let x = 1; let y = x; y = 5; What do x and y hold?
optionA: x holds 1 and y holds 5
optionB: Both hold 5
optionC: Both hold 1
optionD: x holds 5 and y holds 1
correctAnswerText: x holds 1 and y holds 5
explanation: A number is copied when it is assigned rather than shared, so x holds 1 and y holds 5. This is where numbers behave unlike arrays and objects.

prompt: const settings = { theme: "dark" }; settings.theme = "light"; The assignment succeeds and the theme becomes light. Why did const not prevent it?
optionA: const only restricts numbers and strings
optionB: The object was copied before the assignment
optionC: const fixes what the name points at, not the contents of what it points at
optionD: const is only enforced when the file first loads
correctAnswerText: const fixes what the name points at, not the contents of what it points at
explanation: The name still points at the same object afterwards, so nothing const guards has changed: it fixes what the name points at, not the contents of what it points at. Assigning a different object to settings would fail.

prompt: let total = 0; for (let i = 1; i <= 4; i++) { if (i % 2 === 0) total += i; } console.log(total); What is printed?
explanation: Only the even values 2 and 4 are added, giving 6. Adding every value would give ten and adding the odd ones would give four.

prompt: A loop builds text with s = s + i, starting from an empty s. It is meant to produce 123 and produces 012 instead. The loop header is for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++). Which single change fixes it?
optionA: Change s = s + i to s += i
optionB: Keep i starting at 0 and continue while i is not above 3
optionC: Move the printing inside the loop
optionD: Start i at 1 and continue while i is not above 3
correctAnswerText: Start i at 1 and continue while i is not above 3
explanation: The body is right and the range is wrong, so it has to start one later and end one later: start i at 1 and continue while i is not above 3. Changing only the end would give 0123.

prompt: function avg(nums) { let t = 0; for (const n of nums) t += n; return nums.length / t; } The call avg([2, 4]) gives about 0.33 rather than 3. What is wrong?
optionA: The division is the wrong way round; the total should be divided by the count
optionB: The loop never runs
optionC: The total should start at 1 rather than 0
optionD: The values were added as text
correctAnswerText: The division is the wrong way round; the total should be divided by the count
explanation: Six divided by two is three, and two divided by six is what was seen, so the division is the wrong way round; the total should be divided by the count. The loop itself is correct.

prompt: Three things happen while a program runs: one value prints as undefined, one line throws an error, and one total comes out quietly wrong. Which of them stops the program where it happens?
optionA: Only the value that prints as undefined
optionB: Only the total that is quietly wrong
optionC: Only the line that throws
optionD: All three of them
correctAnswerText: Only the line that throws
explanation: A value that prints as undefined and a total that is wrong both let the program continue, which is what makes them hard to notice. Only the line that throws halts it at that point.

prompt: Two values read from input fields are added. Entering 10 and 5 produces 105 rather than 15. Where does the fault lie?
optionA: The addition operator was written incorrectly
optionB: The values arrived as text, so plus joined them instead of adding
optionC: The values were too large to add
optionD: One of the fields was left empty
correctAnswerText: The values arrived as text, so plus joined them instead of adding
explanation: Joining is what plus does when either side is text, and the result is the two entries end to end: the values arrived as text, so plus joined them instead of adding. Converting each value before adding fixes it.

prompt: A loop adds each number in a list to a running total. Every value in the list is a number, and the final total is text. The running total was started as an empty string. What happened?
optionA: One of the values in the list was text after all
optionB: The values were never converted before being added
optionC: The loop ran one time too many
optionD: The total began as text, so every addition joined rather than added
correctAnswerText: The total began as text, so every addition joined rather than added
explanation: The stem says every value is a number, so the text can only have come from the starting value: the total began as text, so every addition joined rather than added. Starting it at 0 fixes it.

prompt: A total came out joined rather than added, because the running total began as text. Which single check would have caught it earliest?
optionA: Printing the type of the running total before the loop starts
optionB: Printing the final total
optionC: Comparing the final total against the expected number
optionD: Converting the final total to a number at the end
correctAnswerText: Printing the type of the running total before the loop starts
explanation: The fault exists before the first addition, so it is visible before the loop: printing the type of the running total before the loop starts finds it immediately. Every other check waits until the damage is complete and then only shows that something is wrong.

prompt: Every entry in a list is converted with Number() before being added. One entry is an empty string. What does that entry contribute to the total?
optionA: Nothing, because it is skipped
optionB: It makes the whole total not a number
optionC: 0, because an empty string converts to zero
optionD: It is joined onto the total as text
correctAnswerText: 0, because an empty string converts to zero
explanation: An empty string converts cleanly rather than failing, so it contributes 0, because an empty string converts to zero. A value such as "abc" is the one that would spoil the total instead.

prompt: Values can be converted to numbers as soon as they arrive, or only at the point where arithmetic happens. What does converting on arrival cost?
optionA: Nothing; it is better in every way
optionB: It forces a decision at the boundary about what an unconvertible value means
optionC: It makes the program noticeably slower
optionD: It makes the original text impossible to keep
correctAnswerText: It forces a decision at the boundary about what an unconvertible value means
explanation: Converting on arrival gains one place to check and one kind of value inside the program, and the price is paid at that boundary: it forces a decision about what an unconvertible value means, right where the program may not yet know what to do about it.

prompt: function sum(nums) { let t = 0; for (const n of nums) t += n; return t; } The call sum([]) finishes without an error. What does it return?
optionA: undefined
optionB: An empty array
optionC: Nothing at all
explanation: The loop body never runs, so the starting value is handed back untouched and the call returns 0. That is why a sum needs no special case for an empty list.

prompt: The same summing function is changed into an average by dividing by nums.length before returning. What does an empty list now produce?
optionA: Not a number, because zero is divided by zero
optionB: 0, exactly as the sum did
optionC: An error that stops the program
optionD: undefined
correctAnswerText: Not a number, because zero is divided by zero
explanation: Both the total and the count are zero for an empty list, so the result is not a number, because zero is divided by zero. The sum survived the empty list and the average does not, which is why the division is the line that needs guarding.

prompt: A greeting is built from user.name. It is called with an object that has no name property, and nothing crashes. What appears in the greeting?
optionA: The greeting is skipped entirely
optionB: An empty gap, with nothing where the name should be
optionC: The word undefined, where the name should be
optionD: An error message in place of the name
correctAnswerText: The word undefined, where the name should be
explanation: A missing property reads as undefined rather than failing, and joining that into text spells it out, so the word undefined appears where the name should be. This is why a missing value often reaches the user rather than the developer.

prompt: Two operations are applied to the same list: summing it, and finding its largest value. Which of the two needs a decision made about the empty case?
optionA: Summing, because there is nothing to start from
optionB: Finding the largest, because there is no value to hand back
optionC: Both, in exactly the same way
optionD: Neither; both are defined for an empty list
correctAnswerText: Finding the largest, because there is no value to hand back
explanation: A sum has a natural answer for an empty list, which is zero, and a largest value has none, so it is finding the largest, because there is no value to hand back, that needs the decision. The author has to choose between an error and a stand-in value.

prompt: An empty list can be handled by returning early at the top of the function, or by letting the ordinary code run and produce the right answer by itself. What does the early return cost?
optionA: Nothing; an early return is always the safer choice
optionB: Noticeably slower running on long lists
optionC: The ability to handle non-empty lists in the same function
optionD: A second path through the function that has to stay correct as the first one changes
correctAnswerText: A second path through the function that has to stay correct as the first one changes
explanation: Where the ordinary code already gives the right answer, the guard adds a second path through the function that has to stay correct as the first one changes. The guard earns its place only when the ordinary code would be wrong.

prompt: One fragment tests if (x) and another tests if (x !== undefined). They behaved identically on every value tried, all of which were non-empty strings. Are they equivalent?
optionA: No; they part company on 0, on the empty string and on null
optionB: Yes; both ask whether x has a value
optionC: No; the second one fails when x is a number
optionD: Yes; undefined is the only value that counts as false
correctAnswerText: No; they part company on 0, on the empty string and on null
explanation: Every value tried counts as true and is also not undefined, so the trials could not separate them. They part company on 0, on the empty string and on null, each of which is present but counts as false.

prompt: Two checks are written: x == null and x === null. Which input separates them?
optionA: null, which only the second matches
optionB: 0, which only the first matches
optionC: undefined, which the first matches and the second does not
optionD: No input separates them
correctAnswerText: undefined, which the first matches and the second does not
explanation: The converting form treats the two empty values as equal, so undefined, which the first matches and the second does not, is the separating input. Every other value is treated the same way by both.

prompt: Two fragments differ only in that one computes a + b and the other computes Number(a) + Number(b). They agreed on every pair of numbers tried. Are they equivalent?
optionA: Yes; converting a number changes nothing about it
optionB: No; they differ as soon as either value arrives as text
optionC: No; the second one fails when given numbers
optionD: Yes, since both give a number in every case
correctAnswerText: No; they differ as soon as either value arrives as text
explanation: Converting a number leaves it alone, which is why the trials agreed, but they differ as soon as either value arrives as text: one joins and the other adds. Numbers were the only inputs that could not tell them apart.

prompt: A colleague says two fragments are interchangeable because the tests pass. What would make the claim stronger?
optionA: Adding more tests of the same kind
optionB: Showing the two produce identical output for one typical input
optionC: Showing the two are the same length
optionD: Naming the inputs that could separate them and showing the two agree on those
correctAnswerText: Naming the inputs that could separate them and showing the two agree on those
explanation: Passing tests only shows the inputs tried did not separate them, and the interesting inputs are the ones nobody thought to try. Naming the inputs that could separate them and showing the two agree on those turns a hope into an argument.

prompt: What is the page tree that scripts work with?
optionA: The file that was delivered from the server
optionB: The browser's live in-memory representation of the page
optionC: A browser option that has to be switched on
optionD: Something supplied by a framework
correctAnswerText: The browser's live in-memory representation of the page
explanation: Scripts work on the browser's live in-memory representation of the page, which the browser keeps for as long as the page is open. The delivered file is only what it was built from.

prompt: Where does that tree come from?
optionA: It is downloaded from the server as a second file
optionB: The developer writes it alongside the markup
optionC: It is created only when a script first asks for it
optionD: The browser builds it from the delivered markup
correctAnswerText: The browser builds it from the delivered markup
explanation: The browser builds it from the delivered markup as the page is read, before any script runs. Nothing extra is fetched and nothing has to be requested.

prompt: Once a page has finished loading, can that tree still be changed?
optionA: Yes, for as long as the page stays open
optionB: No; it is fixed until the page is reloaded
optionC: No; it can be read but never changed
optionD: Only while the page is still loading
correctAnswerText: Yes, for as long as the page stays open
explanation: The tree stays available and changeable for as long as the page stays open, which is what makes interactive pages possible at all. Loading finishing is not a freeze.

prompt: Does a plain script on a page need a library before it can reach the page tree?
optionA: Yes; a library is required
optionB: Yes, unless a framework is used instead
optionC: No; reaching it is part of the browser itself
optionD: Only for changing it, not for reading it
correctAnswerText: No; reaching it is part of the browser itself
explanation: Reaching the tree is part of the browser itself, so a plain script can already read and change it. Libraries make the same work shorter to write rather than possible.

prompt: A script inserts a new paragraph into the page. The developer then asks the browser to show the page source. Is the new paragraph in what they see?
optionA: Yes; the source is kept in step with the page
optionB: No; the source shown is the delivered file, which the script never touched
optionC: Yes, but only after the page is reloaded
optionD: No; the paragraph was never really added
correctAnswerText: No; the source shown is the delivered file, which the script never touched
explanation: The paragraph is genuinely in the live page and not in the delivered file, so the source shown is the delivered file, which the script never touched. Inspecting the live tree shows the paragraph; viewing the source does not.

prompt: A lookup by identifier finds a matching element. What does the lookup produce?
optionA: A collection containing that one element
optionB: The text inside that element
optionC: True, to say it was found
optionD: That one element
correctAnswerText: That one element
explanation: A lookup by identifier produces that one element, ready to be read or changed directly. No collection is involved, so no position has to be taken from it.

prompt: A lookup for every element carrying a class matches three elements. What does the lookup produce?
optionA: A collection of the three elements
optionB: The first of the three elements
optionC: The three elements joined into one piece of text
optionD: The number of matches
correctAnswerText: A collection of the three elements
explanation: A lookup for every match produces a collection of the three elements, whatever the number of matches turns out to be. Reaching any one of them means taking it out of the collection first.

prompt: A lookup by identifier matches nothing. What happens?
optionA: It throws an error and the program stops
optionB: It produces an empty collection
optionC: It produces null and the program carries on
optionD: It produces the closest matching element instead
correctAnswerText: It produces null and the program carries on
explanation: A failed lookup produces null and the program carries on, which is why the failure is only noticed on the next line. Nothing is raised at the lookup itself.

prompt: One lookup asks for a single element and another asks for every match. Neither finds anything. How do the two results differ?
optionA: Both give null
optionB: The single lookup gives null and the every-match lookup gives an empty collection
optionC: Both give an empty collection
optionD: Both raise the same error
correctAnswerText: The single lookup gives null and the every-match lookup gives an empty collection
explanation: The two failures are shaped differently: the single lookup gives null and the every-match lookup gives an empty collection. That is why one crashes on the next line and the other quietly loops zero times.

prompt: A click handler is attached while the page is loading. Has the code inside it run at that point?
optionA: Yes; attaching runs it once
optionB: Yes, and it will also run on each click
optionC: Only once the page has been reloaded
optionD: No; it runs when a click happens
correctAnswerText: No; it runs when a click happens
explanation: Attaching only records what should happen later, so the code inside runs when a click happens and not before. Nothing about the attaching itself executes the body.

prompt: A button carrying one handler is clicked three times. How many times does the handler run?
optionA: Three times
optionB: Once, after which it stops listening
optionC: Once per page load, however many clicks occur
optionD: Never, unless it is attached again after each click
correctAnswerText: Three times
explanation: A handler stays attached and answers every click, so it runs three times. Nothing detaches it after the first.

prompt: A handler is attached and the user never clicks the element. What becomes of the code inside it?
optionA: It runs once when the page finishes loading
optionB: It runs when the user leaves the page
optionC: It never runs
optionD: It runs after a short delay
correctAnswerText: It never runs
explanation: Code inside a handler waits for its event and nothing else triggers it, so it never runs. There is no fallback moment at which it is executed anyway.

prompt: A script attaches a click handler and then prints a line. The user clicks a second later. In what order do the printing and the handler run?
optionA: The handler first, because handlers take priority
optionB: The printing first, because attaching does not wait for anything
optionC: They run at the same moment
optionD: The printing is held back until the click arrives
correctAnswerText: The printing first, because attaching does not wait for anything
explanation: Attaching finishes immediately and the script continues, so the printing happens first, because attaching does not wait for anything. The handler runs a second later when the click actually arrives.

prompt:
The page contains

A

B

. A lookup asks for a single element matching .note. Which is produced?
optionA: The paragraph containing B, as the last match
optionB: Both paragraphs, as a collection
optionC: null, because more than one element matches
optionD: The paragraph containing A
correctAnswerText: The paragraph containing A
explanation: A single-element lookup takes the first match in document order, which is the paragraph containing A. Extra matches are ignored rather than causing a failure.

prompt:
The page contains
X
followed by Y. A lookup asks for every element matching #box .tag. How many are found, and which?
optionA: One: the span containing X
optionB: Two: both spans
optionC: One: the span containing Y
optionD: None, because the span is not a direct child
correctAnswerText: One: the span containing X
explanation: The lookup is limited to what sits inside the identified element, so it finds one: the span containing X. The second span carries the same class but sits outside.

prompt:
The page contains

Hello there

. What does reading the paragraph's text produce?
optionA: Hello there
optionB: Hello
optionC: Hello there
optionD: there
correctAnswerText: Hello there
explanation: Reading the text gives the words with the tags stripped out and the nested words kept, which is Hello there. The nested element contributes its words but not its tags.

prompt:
The page contains
  • Price: 99
    • . What does reading the item's markup produce?
optionA: Price: 99
optionB: Price: 99
optionC: Price:
optionD: • Price: 99
correctAnswerText: Price: 99
explanation: Reading the markup gives everything between the opening and closing tags exactly as it stands, which is Price: 99. The element's own tags are not part of what is inside it.

prompt: A script sets a heading's text to Welcome. Who sees the change?
optionA: Everyone who loads the page from now on
optionB: Everyone, once the server has caught up
optionC: Nobody, until the change is saved
optionD: Only this visitor, in this browser, on this open page
correctAnswerText: Only this visitor, in this browser, on this open page
explanation: The change is made to the copy of the page held in one browser, so only this visitor, in this browser, on this open page sees it. Nothing was sent anywhere.

prompt: After a script has changed a heading, the visitor reloads the page. What heading appears?
optionA: The original one, because the page is built again from the delivered markup
optionB: The changed one, which survives reloads
optionC: No heading at all
optionD: The changed one, until the browser cache is cleared
correctAnswerText: The original one, because the page is built again from the delivered markup
explanation: A reload throws the live tree away and builds a new one, so the original one appears, because the page is built again from the delivered markup. The script would have to run again to change it again.

prompt: A student is sure their form saves data, because after clicking Save the entered values are still on the screen. Their Save handler only writes the values into the page. They reload and everything is gone. What does the reload demonstrate?
optionA: That the save worked but the server has not caught up
optionB: That reloading deleted what had been saved
optionC: That nothing ever left the browser; only the live page had been changed
optionD: That the browser cache was cleared at the wrong moment
correctAnswerText: That nothing ever left the browser; only the live page had been changed
explanation: Values staying on screen prove only that the live page holds them, and the reload rebuilds the page from the delivered markup: nothing ever left the browser; only the live page had been changed. Saving requires sending the values somewhere that outlives the page.

prompt: A stylesheet contains .hidden { display: none; }. A script adds the class hidden to a paragraph that is currently on screen. What happens to it?
optionA: It stays, because the sheet had already been applied when the script ran
optionB: It disappears from view
optionC: It disappears once the page is reloaded
optionD: It stays, because a script cannot bring a sheet rule into play
correctAnswerText: It disappears from view
explanation: Which rules match is worked out again every time the page changes, so the paragraph now matches and It disappears from view. Sheets are not applied once at the start and then forgotten.

prompt: A stylesheet contains #save { color: red; } and .btn { color: blue; }. A script adds the class btn to the element whose identifier is save. What colour is the element?
optionA: Blue, because the class was added most recently
optionB: Blue, because a change made by a script outranks the stylesheet
optionC: Neither; the two rules cancel each other
optionD: Red, because the identifier rule is the more specific of the two
correctAnswerText: Red, because the identifier rule is the more specific of the two
explanation: The element now matches both rules and the cascade settles it on specificity, so it stays red, because the identifier rule is the more specific of the two. When the class was added makes no difference.

prompt: A stylesheet sets an element's colour to red through its identifier. A script sets the colour to green on the element itself. The element shows green, even though an identifier rule is highly specific. Why?
optionA: A style set on the element itself is considered after every stylesheet rule
optionB: Because the script ran later in time than the stylesheet
optionC: Because a script always overrides a stylesheet
optionD: Because green is applied to the text and red to the background
correctAnswerText: A style set on the element itself is considered after every stylesheet rule
explanation: What the script produced is not another stylesheet rule but a style on the element, and a style set on the element itself is considered after every stylesheet rule. Running later is not the reason: a stylesheet loaded afterwards would still lose.

prompt: Three buttons each receive their own handler, and each handler hides the element that was clicked. The second button is clicked. What happens?
optionA: All three buttons are hidden
optionB: The first button is hidden
optionC: The second button is hidden
optionD: Nothing happens
correctAnswerText: The second button is hidden
explanation: Each handler acts on whatever was clicked, so the second button is hidden and the others are untouched. The click decides the target.

prompt: Three similar buttons exist, but a handler was attached to the first one only. The third button is clicked. What happens?
optionA: The first button is hidden
optionB: Nothing, because the third button has no handler
optionC: The third button is hidden
optionD: All three buttons are hidden
correctAnswerText: Nothing, because the third button has no handler
explanation: A handler only answers clicks on the element it was attached to, so nothing happens, because the third button has no handler. Attaching to one element does not cover its lookalikes.

prompt: Every button in a list has a handler attached, and clicking any of them always hides the first button. What is the fault?
optionA: Only the first button actually received a handler
optionB: The handlers were attached before the buttons existed
optionC: All the buttons share one identifier
optionD: The handler acts on a fixed element instead of the one that was clicked
correctAnswerText: The handler acts on a fixed element instead of the one that was clicked
explanation: Something happens on every click, so every button really is wired up and the attaching timing is fine; what is wrong is that the handler acts on a fixed element instead of the one that was clicked. The handler needs the clicked element rather than a name resolved once.

prompt: A script is placed above the markup it looks up and runs as soon as it is reached. Does the lookup find the element?
optionA: No; that part of the page has not been built yet
optionB: Yes; the browser waits for the whole page first
optionC: Yes; lookups search the delivered file rather than the page
optionD: Only when the lookup uses an identifier
correctAnswerText: No; that part of the page has not been built yet
explanation: The page is built from the top downwards and the script runs where it sits, so no, that part of the page has not been built yet. The lookup searches the live tree, which is still incomplete.

prompt: The same script is moved below the markup it looks up. Does the lookup find the element now?
optionA: No; where a script sits makes no difference
optionB: Only after the page is reloaded once
optionC: Yes; the element has been built by the time the script runs
optionD: Only if it also waits for the page to finish loading
correctAnswerText: Yes; the element has been built by the time the script runs
explanation: Everything above a script exists before the script runs, so yes, the element has been built by the time the script runs. Waiting for a load event is another way to get the same guarantee, not a further requirement.

prompt: A lookup gives null when the page loads. Typing exactly the same lookup into the console afterwards finds the element. What is the cause?
optionA: The selector does not match the element
optionB: The script ran before that element had been built
optionC: The element is hidden by a stylesheet rule
optionD: The browser does not support that kind of lookup
correctAnswerText: The script ran before that element had been built
explanation: The console result proves the selector matches and the element exists, so the only thing that differs between the two attempts is when they happened: the script ran before that element had been built.

prompt: A lookup returns the three elements carrying a class. The script then sets a style on the returned collection itself. What happens on the page?
optionA: All three elements change
optionB: The first element changes
optionC: An error stops the script
optionD: Nothing changes
correctAnswerText: Nothing changes
explanation: A collection is a list of elements and not an element, so setting a style on it changes nothing on the page. No error is raised either, which is what makes this hard to spot.

prompt: How is a style applied to every element in such a collection?
optionA: By going through the collection and setting the style on each element in turn
optionB: By setting the style on the collection once
optionC: By setting the style on the first element, which the rest follow
optionD: By running the lookup again for each element
correctAnswerText: By going through the collection and setting the style on each element in turn
explanation: The collection holds the elements but is not one of them, so the work is done by going through the collection and setting the style on each element in turn. There is no shortcut that reaches them all at once.

prompt: A script sets a style on a collection and nothing changes, with no error reported. A colleague says the selector must be wrong. What single check settles which of the two it is?
optionA: Reload the page and try again
optionB: Set the style on the first element instead
optionC: Print how many elements the collection holds
optionD: Try a different style property
correctAnswerText: Print how many elements the collection holds
explanation: A wrong selector and a style set on the collection look identical from outside, and they differ in exactly one observable: print how many elements the collection holds. Zero means the selector, three means the collection was styled instead of its members.

prompt: A control declared to accept numbers holds 20. A script reads its value and compares it with the number 20 using the strict form of equality. What is the result?
optionA: True, because both are 20
optionB: False, because the value read out is text
optionC: True, but only because the control accepts numbers
optionD: An error, because the two types cannot be compared
correctAnswerText: False, because the value read out is text
explanation: A control hands back what the user typed as text whatever the control is declared to accept, so the comparison is false, because the value read out is text. The strict form refuses to convert before comparing.

prompt: A script checks a text control against undefined to see whether the user typed nothing. The user types nothing and the check still never matches. Why?
optionA: The control was not found by the lookup
optionB: The value is null rather than undefined
optionC: The check has to use the converting form of equality
optionD: An untouched control gives an empty string, which is not undefined
correctAnswerText: An untouched control gives an empty string, which is not undefined
explanation: A control always has a value and it starts as text with no characters in it, so an untouched control gives an empty string, which is not undefined. Checking the length, or comparing against an empty string, is what detects it.

prompt:
The page contains

X

. Starting from the paragraph, which element is its parent?
optionA: The section
optionB: The div
optionC: The paragraph itself
optionD: The body
correctAnswerText: The section
explanation: The section is the parent, because a parent is the element that directly contains another. The div contains that section and is therefore one level further out.

prompt: The page contains a list written across several lines, with each item on its own line. Asking the first item for its next element sibling gives the second item. Asking it for its next node instead often gives something else. What?
optionA: The list itself
optionB: The second item again, by another route
optionC: The whitespace text sitting between the two items
optionD: Nothing, in every case
correctAnswerText: The whitespace text sitting between the two items
explanation: Line breaks and indentation between tags are themselves content in the tree, so the next node is the whitespace text sitting between the two items. Asking specifically for elements is what skips it.

prompt: A lookup written with the class name but without a leading dot finds nothing, although elements carrying that class exist and the script runs late enough. What is wrong?
optionA: The script still runs too early
optionB: The selector is being read as an element name rather than a class
optionC: The class is spelled differently in the markup
optionD: A class can only be found through a collection lookup
correctAnswerText: The selector is being read as an element name rather than a class
explanation: Without the dot the text names a kind of element, and no element is called that, so the selector is being read as an element name rather than a class. Adding the dot is the whole fix.

prompt: A lookup gives null. The script sits at the bottom of the page and runs after the markup, and the same selector typed into the console afterwards also finds nothing. What is the cause?
optionA: The script ran before the element existed
optionB: The element is hidden by a stylesheet rule
optionC: The page failed to finish loading
optionD: The selector matches nothing in the page
correctAnswerText: The selector matches nothing in the page
explanation: Timing is ruled out twice over, by the script's position and by the console attempt made after loading, so the selector matches nothing in the page. A hidden element would still be found.

prompt: Two causes give the same null lookup: the script ran too early, or the selector matches nothing. Which single check separates them?
optionA: Run the same lookup in the console once the page has finished loading
optionB: Reload the page and watch whether it happens again
optionC: Move the script to the bottom of the page
optionD: Add a short wait before the lookup
correctAnswerText: Run the same lookup in the console once the page has finished loading
explanation: The two causes differ only in whether the element exists at lookup time, so run the same lookup in the console once the page has finished loading and the answer is immediate. Moving the script or adding a wait would fix one cause without ever showing which it was.

prompt: Moving a script to the bottom of the page makes a failing lookup start working. What has that established?
optionA: That the selector was wrong and has now been corrected
optionB: Nothing; the change could have fixed anything
optionC: That timing was the cause, and the selector was correct all along
optionD: That the element was hidden and is now visible
correctAnswerText: That timing was the cause, and the selector was correct all along
explanation: Only when the script runs changed, and the outcome changed with it, so timing was the cause, and the selector was correct all along. A wrong selector would still find nothing from the bottom of the page.

prompt: A lookup works on the developer's page and gives null on another page built from the same template, where that element is only rendered when there is data to show. What is the likeliest cause?
optionA: The script runs earlier on that page
optionB: On that page the element genuinely is not there
optionC: The selector is wrong and only appeared to work
optionD: That page loads the script from a different place
correctAnswerText: On that page the element genuinely is not there
explanation: The stem gives a condition under which the element is left out entirely, and the failing page is the one meeting it, so on that page the element genuinely is not there. The code is the same on both pages; the data is not.

prompt: A handler was attached by writing the function name followed by parentheses. Its message appears once while the page is loading, and clicking afterwards does nothing. What happened?
optionA: The handler was attached to the wrong element
