optionB: Execute implies read and write
optionC: Each is granted separately and none implies another
optionD: They form a ladder, with each including the ones below
correctAnswerText: Each is granted separately and none implies another
explanation: Independence is the whole design. The ladder reading is intuitive and makes every real access question come out wrong.

prompt: A student cannot run a script and says it must be because they lack read permission on it. The read permission is granted and the execute permission is not. What is the actual obstacle?
optionA: The missing read permission, which running also requires
optionB: The missing execute permission, which is what running requires
optionC: Both permissions are needed and both are missing
optionD: Nothing; the script should run
correctAnswerText: The missing execute permission, which is what running requires
explanation: Running needs execute, and read is separately granted here. Assuming one permission covers another is what produces this diagnosis.

prompt: A file is owned by Asha. Asha opens it. Which set of permissions applies to her?
optionA: The group set
optionB: The everyone-else set
optionC: Whichever of the three is most generous
optionD: The owner set
correctAnswerText: The owner set
explanation: She is the owner, so the owner set governs. The other two describe other people.

prompt: A file is owned by Asha and belongs to the group "editors". Ravi is in that group and is not the owner. Which set applies to Ravi?
optionA: The group set
optionB: The owner set
optionC: The everyone-else set
optionD: The owner set and the group set together
correctAnswerText: The group set
explanation: Ravi falls into the group class, so that set governs him. He is judged by one set rather than a combination.

prompt: How many of the three sets apply to any one user?
optionA: All three
optionB: One or two, depending on the file
optionC: Exactly one
optionD: Whichever ones grant the action being attempted
correctAnswerText: Exactly one
explanation: A user falls into the first class that describes them and is judged by that set alone. Combining the sets is not how the decision is made.

prompt: A file is owned by Asha, whose owner set grants read only. It belongs to a group Asha is in, whose group set grants read and write. Can Asha write to the file?
optionA: Yes; the group set grants write and she is in the group
optionB: No; she is the owner, so the owner set governs and it grants no write
optionC: Yes; the most generous applicable set applies
optionD: It cannot be determined without the everyone-else set
correctAnswerText: No; she is the owner, so the owner set governs and it grants no write
explanation: Being the owner is what decides which set is consulted, and it is not the most generous one here. This surprises almost everyone the first time they meet it.

prompt: The current directory is /home/asha. A path is written as reports/june.txt. Which file does it reach?
optionA: /reports/june.txt
optionB: /home/reports/june.txt
optionC: /home/asha/june.txt
optionD: /home/asha/reports/june.txt
correctAnswerText: /home/asha/reports/june.txt
explanation: The relative path is joined to the current directory. Reading it from the top instead gives the first wrong answer.

prompt: The current directory is /var/www/site/public. A path is written as assets/img/logo.png. Which file does it reach?
optionA: /var/www/site/public/assets/img/logo.png
optionB: /assets/img/logo.png
optionC: /var/www/site/assets/img/logo.png
optionD: /var/www/site/public/img/logo.png
correctAnswerText: /var/www/site/public/assets/img/logo.png
explanation: Every segment of the relative path is appended to the current directory in order. Dropping one level or one segment produces the other answers.

prompt: A developer sitting in /home/asha/reports types a path made of two dots, a slash, and then notes.txt. Where does that land?
optionA: /home/asha/reports/notes.txt
optionB: /home/notes.txt
optionC: /home/asha/notes.txt
optionD: /notes.txt
correctAnswerText: /home/asha/notes.txt
explanation: Two dots mean the directory above, which from reports is asha, and notes.txt is taken from there. A second climb would have reached /home.

prompt: A build script runs from /a/b/c/d and refers to ../../x/y.txt. How many levels does it climb, and where does it end up?
optionA: One level, ending at /a/b/c/x/y.txt
optionB: Two levels, ending at /a/b/x/y.txt
optionC: Three levels, ending at /a/x/y.txt
optionD: Two levels, ending at /a/x/y.txt
correctAnswerText: Two levels, ending at /a/b/x/y.txt
explanation: Each pair of dots climbs once, so two pairs climb from d to b, giving Two levels, ending at /a/b/x/y.txt. Miscounting the climbs is what produces the other three.

prompt: A file grants its owner read and write, its group read only, and everyone else nothing. Ravi is in the group and wants to read it. Is he allowed?
optionA: No; only the owner may read it
optionB: Yes; he may read and write it
optionC: It cannot be determined without knowing the owner
optionD: Yes; the group set grants read
correctAnswerText: Yes; the group set grants read
explanation: Ravi falls in the group class and that set grants read. It does not grant write, so that is where his permissions stop.

prompt: Priya neither owns a document nor belongs to its group, and the everyone-else set on it permits reading and nothing more. She tries to save a change to it. What happens?
optionA: The save is refused, since the class she falls into grants no write
optionB: The save succeeds, because two of the three sets do permit writing
optionC: The save succeeds, because being able to read a file means being able to save it
optionD: The outcome depends on who else is in the group
correctAnswerText: The save is refused, since the class she falls into grants no write
explanation: She is judged by the everyone-else class alone, and it stops at reading. What the owner and group are permitted has no bearing on her.

prompt: A file grants its owner execute only, its group read and write, and everyone else read. Asha owns it and is also a member of the group. She wants to read it. A user is judged by the first class they fall into, and Asha is the owner. Is she allowed?
optionA: Yes; her group membership grants read
optionB: Yes; the everyone-else set grants read and she is a person like any other
optionC: No; the owner set grants execute only
optionD: Yes; owners may always read their own files
correctAnswerText: No; the owner set grants execute only
explanation: The owner class is consulted and it grants no read, so the more generous sets never come into it. Owning a file does not carry any permission of its own.

prompt: What does read permission on a directory allow?
optionA: Reading the contents of the files inside it
optionB: Seeing the names of what is inside it
optionC: Reaching a file inside it whose name you know
optionD: Adding a file to it
correctAnswerText: Seeing the names of what is inside it
explanation: A directory holds names, so reading it lists names. What those files contain is governed by their own permissions.

prompt: A directory grants execute and not read. A user knows the exact name of a file inside it. What can they do?
optionA: Nothing, since they cannot read the directory
optionB: List the contents but not reach any file
optionC: Both list the contents and reach the file
optionD: Reach that file by name, without being able to list what else is there
correctAnswerText: Reach that file by name, without being able to list what else is there
explanation: Execute on a directory permits passing through to something named. Read permits listing, and the two are separate.

prompt: A directory grants read and not execute. A user wants to open a file inside it. Reading the directory lists the names, and reaching anything inside requires execute, which is not granted. What happens?
optionA: They can see the file name and cannot open it
optionB: They can open the file, since they can see it
optionC: They can neither see nor open it
optionD: They can open it but not see it listed
correctAnswerText: They can see the file name and cannot open it
explanation: Being able to see a name is not being able to reach what it names. This combination produces the confusing result of a visible file that cannot be opened.

prompt: Removing a file changes which thing?
optionA: The file itself
optionB: Both the file and the directory equally
optionC: The directory that lists it
optionD: Neither; removal is handled separately
correctAnswerText: The directory that lists it
explanation: The name is an entry in the directory, and removing the file removes that entry. That is why the directory permissions are what govern it.

prompt: A file grants nobody write permission. Its directory grants write to everyone. Can an ordinary user remove the file?
optionA: No; the file grants no write permission
optionB: Yes; removal is governed by the directory, which grants write
optionC: No; both the file and the directory must grant write
optionD: Only the owner of the file may remove it
correctAnswerText: Yes; removal is governed by the directory, which grants write
explanation: The file own permissions govern changing its contents rather than its existence. A read-only file in a writable directory can be removed by anyone who can write to that directory.

prompt: A team protects an important file by removing every write permission from it. It sits in a directory that grants write to everyone. Removing a file changes the directory that lists it, and the directory grants write to everyone. Is the file protected from deletion?
optionA: Yes; a file with no write permission cannot be removed
optionB: Yes, unless the user owns the file
optionC: It depends on whether the file is currently open
optionD: No; anyone who can write to the directory can still remove it
correctAnswerText: No; anyone who can write to the directory can still remove it
explanation: The protection guards the contents and not the existence. Removing write from the directory is what would actually prevent deletion.

prompt: A summary reads rw-r--r--, in the order owner, group, everyone else, with each group of three in the order read, write, execute. What may the owner do?
optionA: Read and write, but not execute
optionB: Read only
optionC: Read, write and execute
optionD: Write only
correctAnswerText: Read and write, but not execute
explanation: The first group of three is rw-, which grants read and write with execute absent. The dash marks a permission that is not granted.

prompt: Two files are compared. One carries the summary r-xr-x--- and the other rwxr-x---. Groups of three run owner, then group, then everyone else; within each group the order is read, write, execute. What is the only difference between them?
optionA: The group may write on the second and not on the first
optionB: Everyone else gains read on the second
optionC: The owner may write on the second and not on the first
optionD: There is no difference between the two
correctAnswerText: The owner may write on the second and not on the first
explanation: Only the second character differs, and it sits in the owner group at the write position. The remaining six characters are identical.

prompt: A summary reads ---rwxrwx, in the order owner, group, everyone else, with each group in the order read, write, execute. The owner asks why they cannot open the file. The first group of three describes the owner and it grants nothing. What is the position?
optionA: The owner has full access, since owners always do
optionB: The owner is granted nothing, while everyone else has full access
optionC: The summary is invalid, since an owner cannot have fewer permissions than others
optionD: The owner may read but not write
correctAnswerText: The owner is granted nothing, while everyone else has full access
explanation: The arrangement is unusual and entirely legal, and the owner is judged by their own group of three. Owning the file carries no permission by itself.

prompt: The current directory is /home/asha. Do the paths notes.txt and /home/asha/notes.txt reach the same file?
optionA: No; they are written differently
optionB: No; one is relative and one is absolute
optionC: Only if the file exists
optionD: Yes; the relative one resolves to the absolute one from here
correctAnswerText: Yes; the relative one resolves to the absolute one from here
explanation: Resolving the relative path from the stated directory gives exactly the absolute one. Looking different is not being different.

prompt: The current directory is /a/b. Do the paths ../b/c.txt and c.txt reach the same file?
optionA: Yes; going up to /a and back into b returns to where you started
optionB: No; the first goes up a level and the second does not
optionC: No; the first names b explicitly
optionD: Only if /a/b contains a directory called b
correctAnswerText: Yes; going up to /a and back into b returns to where you started
explanation: Up one level and back down into the same directory is a round trip. Both paths resolve to /a/b/c.txt.

prompt: A script uses the path data/input.csv and works when run from /home/asha/project. A colleague runs the same script from /home/asha and it fails. The path is relative and is resolved from whichever directory the script is run from. Which file was it looking for the second time?
optionA: /home/asha/project/data/input.csv
optionB: /data/input.csv
optionC: /home/asha/data/input.csv
optionD: /home/asha/project/input.csv
correctAnswerText: /home/asha/data/input.csv
explanation: The relative path was joined to the second directory rather than the first. Nothing moved and nothing about the script changed.

prompt: A user cannot open /projects/secret/plan.txt. The file grants read to everyone. The directory /projects/secret grants the user nothing. What is blocking them?
optionA: The file, which must be misconfigured
optionB: The directory on the way, which they cannot pass through
optionC: The top of the tree, which is restricted
optionD: Nothing; the file should open
correctAnswerText: The directory on the way, which they cannot pass through
explanation: Reaching a file requires passing through every directory on the way to it. A perfectly readable file inside an unreachable directory cannot be opened.

prompt: A user cannot open /var/data/reports/q1.txt. Every directory on the path grants them execute, and the file grants read to its owner and to nobody else. The user is not the owner and is not in the group. Every directory on the path is passable and the file grants read only to its owner. What is blocking them?
optionA: A directory on the path, which they cannot pass through
optionB: The group, which they are not a member of
optionC: Nothing; the file should open
optionD: The file itself, since the class they fall into is granted no read
correctAnswerText: The file itself, since the class they fall into is granted no read
explanation: The path is clear all the way, which rules out the directories. Not being in the group is why they fall into the everyone-else class rather than being the obstacle itself.

prompt: A command using the path config/settings.json worked yesterday from one directory and fails today. The file is still present and still readable when reached by its full path from the top. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The command was run from a different directory, so the relative path resolved elsewhere
optionB: The file was moved
optionC: The file permissions were changed
optionD: The file was deleted and recreated
correctAnswerText: The command was run from a different directory, so the relative path resolved elsewhere
explanation: The file being reachable by its full path rules out both moving and permissions. What changed is where the relative path was resolved from.

prompt: A scheduled job using a relative path succeeds when a developer runs it by hand and fails when the scheduler runs it. The file is present and readable by the account the scheduler uses. The file is readable by the scheduler account and the path is relative. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The scheduler account lacks permission on the file
optionB: The scheduler runs the job at a time when the file is absent
optionC: The scheduler starts the job in a different directory from the one the developer runs it in
optionD: The relative path is malformed
correctAnswerText: The scheduler starts the job in a different directory from the one the developer runs it in
explanation: Permissions are stated to be in order, which leaves where the job starts. Schedulers commonly start jobs somewhere quite unlike a developer session.

prompt: A file grants read to its owner only. Read is added to the everyone-else set so that one colleague can see it. Who gains access?
optionA: Only that colleague
optionB: Everyone on the system, not only that colleague
optionC: Only members of the file group
optionD: Nobody, until the colleague is added to the group
correctAnswerText: Everyone on the system, not only that colleague
explanation: The everyone-else set describes everyone outside the owner and the group. Adding the colleague to the group and granting the group instead is the narrower change.

prompt: A directory is granted write for everyone so that a team can add files to it. The directory already contains files belonging to several people. Write on a directory permits adding and removing entries, and the directory holds other people files. What else does the change permit?
optionA: Nothing else; only adding files is permitted
optionB: Anyone can now change the contents of the files in it
optionC: Anyone can now read the files in it
optionD: Anyone can now remove the files already in it, whoever owns them
correctAnswerText: Anyone can now remove the files already in it, whoever owns them
explanation: Adding and removing are the same permission on a directory. The contents of the existing files are still governed by their own permissions, which is why removal rather than modification is the exposure.

prompt: A team grants read to everyone on a directory so that a listing works, and is satisfied that the files inside remain private because their own permissions were not changed. Reading a directory lists the names inside it, and the names themselves may be revealing. What has been exposed?
optionA: The file names, which may disclose more than the team intended
optionB: Nothing; the file contents are still protected
optionC: The file contents, since directory read implies file read
optionD: Nothing, since a listing is not access
correctAnswerText: The file names, which may disclose more than the team intended
explanation: The contents really are still protected and names are information in their own right. A directory of files named after clients or incidents discloses a great deal before anything is opened.

prompt: An administrator removes execute from a directory to stop people reaching a file inside it. A colleague points out that the file is also reachable through a second directory that still grants execute. Reaching a file requires passing through the directories on the route taken, and a second route is still open. What follows?
optionA: The file is now unreachable, since one route is blocked
optionB: The change has no effect at all on either route
optionC: The file is still reachable by the other route, so the change achieved little
optionD: The second route will stop working automatically
correctAnswerText: The file is still reachable by the other route, so the change achieved little
explanation: Permissions apply along the route actually taken rather than to the file globally. Every route has to be considered, which is why access questions get harder as trees get linked.

prompt: A team removes write permission from a configuration file so that a running service cannot change it. The service runs as an account that owns the file. An owner may restore write permission on a file they own, and the service account owns this one. Does the change prevent the service from writing?
optionA: Yes; without write permission the service cannot write
optionB: No; the owner can grant write back to itself before writing
optionC: Yes, unless the service runs with administrative rights
optionD: No, because permissions do not apply to running services
correctAnswerText: No; the owner can grant write back to itself before writing
explanation: Ownership carries the ability to change permissions, which makes removing one from an owner a speed bump rather than a barrier. Changing the owner is what would actually prevent it.

prompt: A log file must be readable by a monitoring account and by nobody else, and writable by the service that produces it. The service owns the file and the monitoring account can be placed in a group. Only two parties need access and one of them owns the file. What is the narrowest arrangement?
optionA: Read and write for everyone, since only two parties will use it
optionB: Read for everyone and write for the owner
optionC: Read and write for the owner and for the group
optionD: Write for the owner, read for a group containing the monitoring account, nothing for everyone else
correctAnswerText: Write for the owner, read for a group containing the monitoring account, nothing for everyone else
explanation: Each party gets exactly what it needs and nobody else gets anything. Granting the group write or everyone read both hand out access nobody asked for.

prompt: A shared directory must let team members add their own files and must stop them removing one another files. Write on a directory permits both adding and removing, and the two cannot be separated by the three ordinary permissions. What follows?
optionA: The ordinary three permissions cannot express this, so an additional mechanism is needed
optionB: Grant write to the group, which permits adding only
optionC: Grant write to the owner only, and let others add through the group
optionD: Remove write from the directory and grant it on each file
correctAnswerText: The ordinary three permissions cannot express this, so an additional mechanism is needed
explanation: Adding and removing are one permission, so no arrangement of the three achieves the split. Systems provide an extra directory setting for exactly this case, and recognising that the basic three cannot do it is the step that matters.

prompt: A script must be runnable by a group and must not be readable by them, so that the group cannot see how it works. Running a script requires the system to read its text, so execute without read does not work for a script. What follows?
optionA: Grant execute without read, which achieves exactly this
optionB: Grant read without execute, and run it another way
optionC: The requirement cannot be met for a script, since running it requires reading it
optionD: Grant both and rely on the group not to look
correctAnswerText: The requirement cannot be met for a script, since running it requires reading it
explanation: A compiled program can be executed without being readable, and a script cannot, because the interpreter has to read the text. The distinction is what makes this requirement impossible as stated.

prompt: A team can grant read to everyone on a directory of documentation, or maintain a group containing every person who needs it. The documentation is public information and the group would need updating every time somebody joins or leaves. The content is public and the group requires ongoing maintenance. Which fits?
optionA: Maintain the group, since narrow permissions are always preferable
optionB: Grant read to everyone, since the content is public and the group buys nothing
optionC: Maintain the group, since it records who has access
optionD: Grant read to everyone and also maintain the group
correctAnswerText: Grant read to everyone, since the content is public and the group buys nothing
explanation: Narrowing is worth paying for when there is something to protect, and here there is not. The group would be maintenance in exchange for restricting access to information that is not restricted.

prompt: An engineer is repeatedly blocked by permissions and proposes granting themselves full access to everything to save time. The permissions currently prevent a mistake in one area from affecting the others, and full access would remove that separation everywhere. What is the trade?
optionA: Nothing; full access is obviously correct for an engineer
optionB: Nothing; full access is obviously wrong in every case
optionC: Whether the engineer is trusted by their colleagues
optionD: Time saved against losing the containment that stops one mistake spreading
correctAnswerText: Time saved against losing the containment that stops one mistake spreading
explanation: The question is not about trust, since a trusted person makes mistakes too. What permissions buy here is that an error in one area stays there.

prompt: A document system records, for each document, an owner, a team, and a default for everyone else, with view and edit granted separately. A document grants its owner view only, its team view and edit, and everyone else view. The owner is also on the team. The owner class is consulted first and it grants view only. Can the owner edit it?
optionA: No; the owner class grants view only
optionB: Yes; their team membership grants edit
optionC: Yes; owners can always edit their own documents
optionD: It cannot be determined from the description
correctAnswerText: No; the owner class grants view only
explanation: The described system is the file permission model under other names, and the same conclusion follows. Being consulted first is what makes the owner class binding rather than a floor.

prompt: A storage service grants list and read as separate permissions on a container. A team grants read and not list, and a user complains they cannot find anything. Read permits fetching an item whose name is known, and list permits discovering the names. What can the user do?
optionA: Nothing, since they cannot see what is there
optionB: List the contents but not fetch anything
optionC: Fetch any item whose name they already know, without being able to discover names
optionD: Both list and fetch, since read implies list
correctAnswerText: Fetch any item whose name they already know, without being able to discover names
explanation: This is directory execute and directory read under other names. The combination is deliberate in storage services, where names are often known in advance.

prompt: A repository grants a user write on a folder of files. A colleague argues this means the user can also delete the folder itself. Write on the folder governs what happens inside it, while removing the folder changes the thing that contains it. Is the colleague right?
optionA: Yes; write on a folder includes removing it
optionB: No; removing the folder is governed by whatever contains the folder
optionC: Yes, if the user also owns the folder
optionD: It cannot be determined without knowing the repository
correctAnswerText: No; removing the folder is governed by whatever contains the folder
explanation: The same reasoning that puts file deletion under the directory puts folder deletion under the parent. Permission on a thing governs what happens inside it rather than its own existence.

prompt: A team must decide whether to grant access to a shared area by adding each person individually or by maintaining one group. People join and leave every month, and the same access is needed on forty separate areas. Individual grants would have to be made and removed on forty areas for every joiner and leaver. Which fits?
optionA: Individual grants, since they are more precise
optionB: Individual grants, since groups grant more than is needed
optionC: Either, since the resulting access is identical
optionD: The group, since membership is changed once rather than forty times per person
correctAnswerText: The group, since membership is changed once rather than forty times per person
explanation: The resulting access is identical, which is why correctness cannot decide it. What decides it is that one change to a group is forty changes avoided, and forty places to forget is forty places someone keeps access they should have lost.

prompt: A variable holding a running total is in use while a program runs. Where does it live?
optionA: On disk, since the program was loaded from disk
optionB: In working memory, and it is lost when the program ends
optionC: On disk, because totals are important
optionD: In both places at once
correctAnswerText: In working memory, and it is lost when the program ends
explanation: A value a program is using sits in working memory. Nothing puts it on disk unless the program deliberately writes it there.

prompt: A machine loses power while a program is running. What is lost?
optionA: Everything, including files already saved
optionB: Nothing, since the machine will restore its state
optionC: Only the program itself
optionD: Whatever was only in working memory
correctAnswerText: Whatever was only in working memory
explanation: Working memory does not survive without power and storage does. Files already written are unaffected.

prompt: A document is opened in an editor and changed but not saved. Where do the changes exist?
optionA: In working memory only
optionB: In storage, since the file was opened from there
optionC: In both, since editors save continuously
optionD: Nowhere until the editor is closed
correctAnswerText: In working memory only
explanation: The unsaved changes have not reached the file. Saving is what copies them from working memory into storage.

prompt: Why is working memory used at all, when storage is much larger?
optionA: Because storage cannot hold running programs
optionB: Because working memory is more reliable
optionC: Because it is far quicker to reach, which is what a running program needs
optionD: Because storage is only used for backups
correctAnswerText: Because it is far quicker to reach, which is what a running program needs
explanation: Speed is the whole reason for the arrangement. Storage could hold everything and would be far too slow to work from directly.

prompt: A student says a file of two gigabytes cannot be processed on a machine with one gigabyte of working memory. What is wrong with the claim?
optionA: Nothing; the file will not fit and cannot be processed
optionB: The file can be processed a piece at a time, so the whole of it need never be in memory at once
optionC: The file can be processed because memory expands as needed
optionD: The claim is right unless the file is compressed
correctAnswerText: The file can be processed a piece at a time, so the whole of it need never be in memory at once
explanation: Only what is held simultaneously has to fit. Reading a line, dealing with it and moving on keeps the requirement tiny however large the file is.

prompt: A value is needed only while one function call is in progress. Which region suits it?
optionA: The region for values outliving the call
optionB: Storage, since the value is temporary
optionC: Either; the choice makes no difference
optionD: The region tied to the call, released when the call returns
correctAnswerText: The region tied to the call, released when the call returns
explanation: Lifetime is what decides. A value needed only for the duration of a call belongs where it is released automatically at the end of it.

prompt: A value must still exist after the call that created it has returned. Which region suits it?
optionA: The region for values whose lifetime is not tied to a call
optionB: The region tied to the call
optionC: Storage, since it must survive
optionD: Either; the value survives regardless
correctAnswerText: The region for values whose lifetime is not tied to a call
explanation: The call-tied region is released when the call ends, which would take the value with it. Outliving a call means living somewhere the call does not control.

prompt: What decides which of the two regions a value belongs in?
optionA: How large it is
optionB: What type it has
optionC: How long it must last
optionD: How often it is used
correctAnswerText: How long it must last
explanation: Lifetime is the criterion. A small value that must outlive its call belongs in the longer-lived region, and a large one that need not can sit in the call-tied one.

prompt: A student says large values always belong in the longer-lived region and small ones in the call-tied region. What is wrong with the rule?
optionA: Nothing; size is the correct criterion
optionB: It uses size where lifetime is what matters, so it gets small long-lived values wrong
optionC: It is right except for values of exactly one byte
optionD: It is right for numbers and wrong for text
correctAnswerText: It uses size where lifetime is what matters, so it gets small long-lived values wrong
explanation: The rule happens to work often, because large things are frequently long-lived. It fails exactly where the two criteria disagree, and those are the cases that cause faults.

prompt: Two programs are running, and each holds a value at what it reports as the same address. Are they referring to the same memory?
optionA: Yes, since the addresses are identical
optionB: Yes, if the two programs were started together
optionC: It cannot be determined
optionD: No; each program has its own addresses
correctAnswerText: No; each program has its own addresses
explanation: The addresses a program sees are its own, and identical numbers in two programs point at different physical memory. This is what makes isolation possible rather than magical.

prompt: A program prints an address and a developer wants to inspect that location from another program. What is the difficulty?
optionA: The address means something only within the program that printed it
optionB: Addresses cannot be printed
optionC: The address will have changed by the time it is read
optionD: There is no difficulty; the address is universal
correctAnswerText: The address means something only within the program that printed it
explanation: Handing the number to another program hands it a number that means something else there. Inspecting it requires going through the first program.

prompt: What does a program address actually refer to?
optionA: A fixed location in the physical memory chips
optionB: A position on disk
optionC: A location within that program own view of memory
optionD: A position in the list of running programs
correctAnswerText: A location within that program own view of memory
explanation: The program view is translated to physical memory by the system, and the program never sees the physical location. That translation is what keeps programs apart.

prompt: A program is run twice and prints a different address for the same variable each time. Is something wrong?
optionA: Yes; the same variable should always have the same address
optionB: No; where the program view is placed can differ between runs
optionC: Yes; the program is corrupting its own memory
optionD: No, but only because the machine was restarted
correctAnswerText: No; where the program view is placed can differ between runs
explanation: Nothing guarantees the same placement from one run to the next, and some systems deliberately vary it. An address is meaningful within a run rather than across runs.

prompt: A value is placed in the call-tied region during a function call. When is that memory released?
optionA: When the value is last used
optionB: When the program ends
optionC: When the memory is needed by something else
optionD: When the call returns
correctAnswerText: When the call returns
explanation: The release happens at the end of the call regardless of whether the value was still wanted. That automatic release is what the region is for.

prompt: In a language that does not reclaim memory automatically, a value is obtained in the longer-lived region and the program stops referring to it. When is that memory released?
optionA: Only when the program explicitly releases it
optionB: When the last reference to it disappears
optionC: When the enclosing call returns
optionD: Immediately, since nothing refers to it
correctAnswerText: Only when the program explicitly releases it
explanation: Without automatic reclamation, no longer referring to memory does not free it. The memory stays held for as long as the program runs unless it is released deliberately.

prompt: A function calls a second, which calls a third. While the third is running, how many calls are holding space?
optionA: One, the innermost
optionB: One, the outermost
optionC: Three, since all three are still in progress
optionD: None, until they return
correctAnswerText: Three, since all three are still in progress
explanation: A call that has not returned still holds its own space. All three are in progress at once, so all three are holding.

prompt: A function calls itself a thousand times before any call returns. What does that do to the call-tied region?
optionA: Only one call holds space, since it is the same function
optionB: A thousand calls hold space simultaneously, which may exhaust it
optionC: Space is released as each call is entered
optionD: Nothing, since the region grows without limit
correctAnswerText: A thousand calls hold space simultaneously, which may exhaust it
explanation: Being the same function does not merge the calls; each has its own space. The region is considerably smaller than memory as a whole, which is why depth exhausts it first.

prompt: In a language that reclaims memory automatically, a program stops referring to a large structure. What happens to the memory?
optionA: It stays held until the program ends
optionB: It is released the instant the last reference disappears
optionC: It must be released explicitly by the program
optionD: It becomes available again once the system notices nothing refers to it
correctAnswerText: It becomes available again once the system notices nothing refers to it
explanation: Automatic reclamation notices unreachable memory and takes it back, though not necessarily at the moment the last reference goes. The timing is the system decision rather than the program.

prompt: In a language that reclaims automatically, a program keeps every structure it has ever created in a list it never empties. Is that memory reclaimed?
optionA: No; the list still refers to them, so nothing is unreachable
optionB: Yes, since the program has finished using them
optionC: Yes, once memory runs short
optionD: No, because automatic reclamation does not work on lists
correctAnswerText: No; the list still refers to them, so nothing is unreachable
explanation: Reclamation acts on what nothing refers to, and the list refers to everything. This is how a language that reclaims automatically still runs out of memory.

prompt: In a language that does not reclaim automatically, a function obtains memory each time it runs and never releases it. The function is called once per request. The language does not reclaim automatically and the function releases nothing it obtains. What happens over a day?
optionA: Memory is reclaimed when each call returns
optionB: Memory is reclaimed when the request finishes
optionC: Memory held rises with every request and is never given back
optionD: Nothing; memory obtained once is reused on later calls
correctAnswerText: Memory held rises with every request and is never given back
explanation: The call returning releases the call-tied region and not memory obtained for an indefinite lifetime. One request is unnoticeable and a day of requests is not.

prompt: Programs on a machine together want more memory than the machine physically has. What happens?
optionA: The newest program is refused and stopped
optionB: Some of it is kept in storage and fetched back when needed, which is much slower
optionC: Every program is given an equal share and none exceeds it
optionD: The machine stops immediately
correctAnswerText: Some of it is kept in storage and fetched back when needed, which is much slower
explanation: Borrowing space from storage lets the machine keep going and costs a great deal of speed. Refusal comes later, if at all.

prompt: A machine short of memory becomes very slow, and a team checks and finds the processor is busy. Does that rule out memory as the cause?
optionA: Yes; a busy processor means the processor is the bottleneck
optionB: Yes; memory problems leave the processor idle
optionC: No, but only if the machine has one processor
optionD: No; moving memory to and from storage keeps the processor busy
correctAnswerText: No; moving memory to and from storage keeps the processor busy
explanation: The processor being busy is consistent with memory pressure rather than evidence against it. What it is busy doing is the question worth asking.

prompt: A machine becomes slow at everything at once — unrelated programs, the interface, commands that normally return instantly. Every program on the machine is affected rather than one, and nothing was deployed. Which cause fits?
optionA: Memory pressure, since it degrades everything on the machine rather than one program
optionB: A fault in one program, which is consuming the processor
optionC: A slow disk affecting one program
optionD: A network problem
correctAnswerText: Memory pressure, since it degrades everything on the machine rather than one program
explanation: A single program consuming the processor leaves other work slower and not uniformly unresponsive. Everything degrading together points at a resource everything depends on.

prompt: Two separate programs each hold a counter and one increments its own. Does the other see the change?
optionA: Yes, since both run on the same machine
optionB: Yes, if the two counters have the same name
optionC: No; each has its own memory unless sharing was arranged
optionD: Only after both programs finish
correctAnswerText: No; each has its own memory unless sharing was arranged
explanation: Separate programs see separate memory by default. Sharing between them is something that has to be set up deliberately.

prompt: A program is started twice, and each run keeps a list. One run adds an item. Does the other run see it?
optionA: Yes, since both are running the same program
optionB: No; the two runs are separate and have separate memory
optionC: Yes, since the list has the same name in both
optionD: Only if the two were started at the same moment
correctAnswerText: No; the two runs are separate and have separate memory
explanation: Sharing a program does not mean sharing memory. Each run is its own process with its own view of memory.

prompt: A team runs four copies of a service to handle more load, and finds that a value cached by one copy is not seen by the other three. The four copies are separate programs and no sharing was arranged between them. Why?
optionA: The cache is expiring too quickly
optionB: The four copies are interfering with one another
optionC: The value was never cached at all
optionD: Each copy has its own memory, so a cache in one is invisible to the rest
correctAnswerText: Each copy has its own memory, so a cache in one is invisible to the rest
explanation: This is the ordinary consequence of running separate copies, and it surprises teams because the code is identical. A cache shared between them has to live somewhere all four can reach.

prompt: A program reads a large file one line at a time, dealing with each line and keeping nothing. What decides how much memory it needs?
optionA: The size of the largest single line
optionB: The size of the whole file
optionC: The number of lines in the file
optionD: The time the program takes to run
correctAnswerText: The size of the largest single line
explanation: Only one line is held at any moment, so that is what has to fit. The total processed can be far larger than the memory available.

prompt: A program reads the same large file by loading all of it into a list first. What decides how much memory it needs now?
optionA: The size of the largest single line
optionB: The number of lines only
optionC: The size of the whole file
optionD: Nothing; the requirement is the same either way
correctAnswerText: The size of the whole file
explanation: Holding everything at once means everything has to fit. The two approaches process identical data and have completely different requirements.

prompt: A program processes ten gigabytes of records and runs comfortably on a machine with two gigabytes of memory. A colleague says this is impossible. The program holds one record at a time and discards each before reading the next. Is it possible?
optionA: No; ten gigabytes cannot be processed with two
optionB: Yes; what must fit is what is held at once rather than what is processed in total
optionC: Yes, but only because the records are compressed
optionD: Yes, but only if the machine borrows from storage
correctAnswerText: Yes; what must fit is what is held at once rather than what is processed in total
explanation: The total processed and the amount held simultaneously are different quantities, and only the second has to fit. Borrowing from storage is not needed here and would be slow if it were.

prompt: A program disappears with no message while doing memory-intensive work. What is one plausible explanation?
optionA: The program finished successfully
optionB: The program is still running but hidden
optionC: The user must have stopped it
optionD: The system stopped it because memory ran out
correctAnswerText: The system stopped it because memory ran out
explanation: A process stopped from outside because memory ran short leaves no message of its own. The silence is what makes this hard to recognise.

prompt: A program reports that it could not obtain memory and continues running in a reduced way. What has happened?
optionA: A request for memory was refused, and the program handled the refusal
optionB: The program was stopped by the system and restarted
optionC: The machine has no memory left at all
optionD: The program is about to be stopped
correctAnswerText: A request for memory was refused, and the program handled the refusal
explanation: A refused request is a different symptom from being stopped, and it is one the program can respond to. Being stopped from outside gives it no such opportunity.

prompt: A service disappears every few days with no message in its own log, and the machine log records that the system stopped it. The service own log ends mid-operation and the system log records the system stopping it. What does this indicate?
optionA: The service crashed and failed to log the crash
optionB: The service stopped itself deliberately
optionC: The system stopped it from outside, most likely because memory ran short
optionD: The machine restarted
correctAnswerText: The system stopped it from outside, most likely because memory ran short
explanation: A service that crashed would usually record something, and one stopped from outside cannot. The two logs together distinguish the cases.

prompt: A service memory use rises steadily over a week under constant load and never falls. What does that indicate?
optionA: Normal behaviour under sustained load
optionB: Something is being obtained repeatedly and never released
optionC: A cache filling up
optionD: Increasing traffic
correctAnswerText: Something is being obtained repeatedly and never released
explanation: Load is constant, so rising demand does not explain it. Growth that never levels off is the signature of memory that is never given back.

prompt: A service memory use rises quickly for two hours after each restart and then stays flat for days. A team plans to spend a week hunting a leak. Memory rises and then levels off rather than continuing to rise. What does the pattern indicate?
optionA: A leak that pauses when the machine is busy
optionB: A leak that is being partly reclaimed
optionC: Memory pressure from other programs
optionD: A cache filling to its limit, which is not a leak
correctAnswerText: A cache filling to its limit, which is not a leak
explanation: A leak does not stop. Levelling off is what a bounded cache does, and the week would have been spent looking for something that is not there.

prompt: A program fails within a second of starting, on an input of five items, on a machine with plenty of free memory. It uses a function that calls itself. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The function is calling itself without ever stopping, exhausting the call-tied region
optionB: The machine is short of memory
optionC: The input is too large
optionD: Memory is leaking over time
correctAnswerText: The function is calling itself without ever stopping, exhausting the call-tied region
explanation: Failing at once on five items rules out both a shortage and a leak, since neither would act that fast on that little. A call chain with no end exhausts a small region very quickly.

prompt: A program processing a list of three items fails immediately, while the machine reports fifteen gigabytes free. A colleague proposes adding memory. The input is three items and fifteen gigabytes are free, so the machine is not short of memory. What is the fault?
optionA: A memory leak that has consumed the available memory
optionB: The machine is short of memory despite what it reports
optionC: A call chain with no end, which exhausts the small call-tied region regardless of free memory
optionD: The three items are unusually large
correctAnswerText: A call chain with no end, which exhausts the small call-tied region regardless of free memory
explanation: Adding memory would not touch the region that is actually full, which is sized separately and is far smaller. The failure being instant on three items is what points at depth.

prompt: One program on a machine is slow and everything else is normal. Does memory pressure explain it?
optionA: Yes; the program must be the one short of memory
optionB: No; memory pressure would slow the whole machine rather than one program
optionC: Yes; other programs may have enough memory
optionD: It cannot be decided
correctAnswerText: No; memory pressure would slow the whole machine rather than one program
explanation: Borrowing from storage affects everything competing for memory. A single slow program points somewhere within that program.

prompt: A machine becomes slow at the same time each night. A team suspects memory pressure. Every program on the machine slows together at that time and a large report job runs then. What would confirm it?
optionA: Checking whether the report job has grown longer
optionB: Checking whether the processor is busy at that time
optionC: Restarting the machine before the report job runs
optionD: Checking whether memory in use rises at that time and storage activity rises with it
correctAnswerText: Checking whether memory in use rises at that time and storage activity rises with it
explanation: The processor being busy is consistent with memory pressure and does not confirm it. Memory in use rising together with storage activity is what distinguishes it from anything else.

prompt: A team doubles the memory on a machine that was slow, and it becomes fast. They conclude the cause was memory pressure. Doubling the memory removed the need to borrow from storage, and nothing else about the machine changed. Is the conclusion sound?
optionA: Yes; the change addressed one thing and the symptom went with it
optionB: No; correlation is not causation and nothing has been shown
optionC: No; the machine may have been restarted at the same time
optionD: Yes, but only if the load was measured before and after
correctAnswerText: Yes; the change addressed one thing and the symptom went with it
explanation: A single change followed by the symptom disappearing is genuine evidence, and this is what a controlled change looks like. Refusing to conclude anything from it is as unreasoning as concluding without it.

prompt: A service is slow and using far more memory than expected. A team adds memory and it stays slow, while the memory in use rises to fill the new space as well. Memory in use expands to fill whatever is provided, which is what a leak does and a genuine requirement does not. What does that indicate?
optionA: The service genuinely needs even more memory
optionB: The added memory was not configured correctly
optionC: Something is holding memory it does not need, so more memory is consumed rather than helping
optionD: The slowness has a cause unrelated to memory
correctAnswerText: Something is holding memory it does not need, so more memory is consumed rather than helping
explanation: A real requirement would have been satisfied and levelled off. Expanding to fill whatever is available is what unbounded retention does, and adding memory postpones it rather than fixing it.

prompt: A program is slow and a team finds it is using only a small fraction of the available memory. A colleague concludes memory cannot be involved. The program holds very little at once and repeatedly reads data that no longer fits in the fastest layers of memory. Is the conclusion sound?
optionA: Yes; low memory use rules memory out entirely
optionB: No; how memory is accessed can matter even when the amount used is small
optionC: Yes, unless the machine is also running other programs
optionD: No; the program must actually be using more than reported
correctAnswerText: No; how memory is accessed can matter even when the amount used is small
explanation: Running out is one memory problem and access patterns are another. A program touching a large range unpredictably is slow while using very little.

prompt: A value is expensive to compute and is needed on every request. The machine has ample free memory and the value never changes. The value never changes and memory is not constrained. Should it be held or recomputed?
optionA: Recomputed, since holding values risks running out of memory
optionB: Recomputed, since held values become stale
optionC: Held, but only for a few minutes at a time
optionD: Held, since it never changes and memory is not the scarce resource here
correctAnswerText: Held, since it never changes and memory is not the scarce resource here
explanation: Both conditions that argue against holding are absent: it cannot go stale and memory is plentiful. Recomputing would pay the cost on every request for nothing.

prompt: A team caches every result the service has ever computed, with no limit. The machine has ample memory today. A cache with no limit grows with every distinct request and there is no point at which it stops. What follows?
optionA: It will eventually exhaust memory, however much there is, because nothing bounds it
optionB: It is safe while the machine has ample memory
optionC: It is safe, since caches are reclaimed automatically
optionD: It will level off once the common requests are cached
correctAnswerText: It will eventually exhaust memory, however much there is, because nothing bounds it
explanation: Levelling off requires the set of distinct requests to be bounded, which nothing has established. A limit on size or age is what turns this from a leak into a cache.

prompt: A program can hold an entire dataset in memory and answer instantly, or read from storage each time and answer slowly. The dataset is four gigabytes, the machine has three, and holding it would force the machine to borrow from storage continuously. Holding four gigabytes on a three-gigabyte machine means borrowing from storage for every access. What follows?
optionA: Holding it is faster, since memory is faster than storage
optionB: Holding it is faster, since the system manages the borrowing efficiently
optionC: Holding it would be slower than reading from storage deliberately, since the borrowing happens anyway and unpredictably
optionD: The two approaches perform identically
correctAnswerText: Holding it would be slower than reading from storage deliberately, since the borrowing happens anyway and unpredictably
explanation: The intended benefit disappears once the data does not fit, and the borrowing is less efficient than reading deliberately would be. Reading a working subset into memory is the arrangement that gets the benefit.

prompt: A team must choose between holding a value that becomes stale after a minute, and recomputing it each time at a cost of fifty milliseconds. Requests arrive a thousand times a second and a stale value would show a customer an out-of-date balance. A stale balance is shown to a customer, while recomputing costs fifty milliseconds per request. What should decide?
optionA: The request rate, since a thousand a second makes recomputing impossible
optionB: Whether showing a balance up to a minute out of date is acceptable, since that is the cost of holding it
optionC: The recomputation cost, since fifty milliseconds is small
optionD: Neither; the value should be held and refreshed every second
correctAnswerText: Whether showing a balance up to a minute out of date is acceptable, since that is the cost of holding it
explanation: The rate makes holding attractive and does not settle whether staleness is tolerable, which is a question about what the customer is being shown. Refreshing every second is a reasonable compromise that the stem gives no grounds to prefer.

prompt: A service holds a large structure for the whole of its run because releasing and rebuilding it is complicated. It is used for one minute in every hour. The structure occupies memory for fifty-nine minutes in every hour during which nothing uses it. What is the trade?
optionA: Nothing; holding it is obviously correct
optionB: Nothing; rebuilding it is obviously correct
optionC: Whether the structure can be made smaller
optionD: Memory held almost all the time against the complexity of building it when needed
correctAnswerText: Memory held almost all the time against the complexity of building it when needed
explanation: Both sides are real: the memory is genuinely wasted and the rebuilding is genuinely complicated. Which wins depends on whether that memory is needed for anything else.

prompt: A system provides a pool of twenty connections. Code takes one for each request and returns it when finished. One path through the code takes a connection and returns early without returning it. Connections are taken from a fixed pool and this path never returns the one it took. What happens over time?
optionA: The pool empties and later requests wait for a connection that never comes
optionB: Nothing; unreturned connections are reclaimed automatically
optionC: The pool grows to meet demand
optionD: Only the affected path fails, and other requests are unaffected
correctAnswerText: The pool empties and later requests wait for a connection that never comes
explanation: This is a leak in a different resource and behaves exactly the same way. Every request eventually suffers, not only the ones taking the faulty path.

prompt: A program opens files and relies on them being closed when it ends. It runs for months and opens thousands of files a day. The limit on open files applies while the program runs and the program does not end for months. What is the difficulty?
optionA: Nothing; files are always closed when a program ends
optionB: The files will be closed automatically when memory runs short
optionC: The limit is reached long before the program ends, so relying on that cleanup fails
optionD: The program will slow down but continue
correctAnswerText: The limit is reached long before the program ends, so relying on that cleanup fails
explanation: Cleanup at exit is real and arrives far too late for a program that does not exit. This is the same shape as memory obtained and never released.

prompt: A team is told that a resource is released automatically when the code holding it goes out of scope. They wrap every use in that construct and one path exits by throwing an error before reaching it. The construct releases the resource when scope is left, and an error leaves scope in the same way a normal return does. What happens on that path?
optionA: The resource leaks, since the error skipped the release
optionB: The resource is still released, since leaving scope by an error is still leaving scope
optionC: The resource leaks, since errors bypass automatic cleanup
optionD: The behaviour depends on the type of error
correctAnswerText: The resource is still released, since leaving scope by an error is still leaving scope
explanation: This is why the construct exists rather than a manual release at the end of a block. The path that would leak under a manual release is exactly the one it protects.

prompt: A team must decide whether to give each request its own connection or share one across all requests. Connections are limited and a shared one would serialise every request behind a single point. Connections are a bounded resource and sharing one forces requests to queue. What follows?
optionA: One per request, since that is simplest
optionB: One shared, since connections are limited
optionC: One per request, with the limit raised as needed
optionD: Neither extreme fits; a bounded pool shared among requests is what the constraint implies
correctAnswerText: Neither extreme fits; a bounded pool shared among requests is what the constraint implies
explanation: One per request exhausts the bound and one shared destroys concurrency, and the constraint rules out both. A pool sized to the bound is the arrangement the two facts point at.

prompt: A running process is given a number by the system. What does that number identify?
optionA: The program on disk
optionB: This particular run of the program
optionC: The user who started it
optionD: The position of the program in a menu
correctAnswerText: This particular run of the program
explanation: The number belongs to one run and not to the program. Starting the same program again produces a different number.

prompt: A program is stopped and started again. What happens to the number it was given?
optionA: The same number is reused for the new run
optionB: The number is kept because the program is the same
optionC: The program has no number until it finishes
optionD: The new run receives a different number
correctAnswerText: The new run receives a different number
explanation: Each run is a separate process and gets its own number. Expecting the number to follow the program is what makes stale numbers dangerous later.

prompt: The same program is started three times at once. How many numbers are in play?
optionA: Three, one for each run
optionB: One, since it is the same program
optionC: One, with the three runs sharing it
optionD: None, since only one program is involved
correctAnswerText: Three, one for each run
explanation: Three separate runs mean three separate processes, each with its own number. What they have in common is the program they were started from.

prompt: Why does anything wanting to act on a running process need its number?
optionA: Because the number records how long it has been running
optionB: Because the number states how much memory it may use
optionC: Because the number is how a particular run is named
optionD: Because the number gives its position in the start order
correctAnswerText: Because the number is how a particular run is named
explanation: The number is an address for one run. Without it there would be no way to say which of several runs an instruction applies to.

prompt: A script records the number of a process it started, so that it can stop it later. A colleague says it should record the program name instead. What is the weakness of using the name?
optionA: Program names change too often to rely on
optionB: Several runs of the same program may exist, and the name does not say which is meant
optionC: Program names cannot be recorded in a script
optionD: There is no weakness; the name is more reliable
correctAnswerText: Several runs of the same program may exist, and the name does not say which is meant
explanation: The name identifies the program and the number identifies the run. When only one run exists the two agree, which is why the weakness stays hidden until it does not.

prompt: A process has asked to read from a file and is waiting for the data to arrive. What condition is it in?
optionA: Using the processor
optionB: Ready and waiting for the processor
optionC: Finished
optionD: Blocked, waiting on something outside itself
correctAnswerText: Blocked, waiting on something outside itself
explanation: It cannot proceed until the data arrives, so giving it the processor would achieve nothing. That is what distinguishes this from waiting for a turn.

prompt: A process has everything it needs and is simply waiting for its turn on the processor. What condition is it in?
optionA: Ready, waiting only for the processor
optionB: Blocked, waiting on something outside itself
optionC: Using the processor
optionD: Finished
correctAnswerText: Ready, waiting only for the processor
explanation: Nothing is missing except a turn, so it could run the instant one is available. A blocked process could not.

prompt: Two processes are both described as "not running". What distinguishes them?
optionA: How long each has existed
optionB: How much memory each is using
optionC: Whether each is waiting only for a turn or waiting for something else entirely
optionD: Nothing; not running is a single condition
correctAnswerText: Whether each is waiting only for a turn or waiting for something else entirely
explanation: Adding processors would help one and not the other, which is why the two are kept apart. Lumping them together makes every performance question unanswerable.

prompt: A machine has many processes that are not running, and adding a faster processor makes no difference. What does that suggest about them?
optionA: They were waiting for the processor and the new one is too slow
optionB: They were waiting on something other than the processor
optionC: They have all finished
optionD: The measurement must have been taken incorrectly
correctAnswerText: They were waiting on something other than the processor
explanation: Processes waiting for a turn would have benefited from a faster processor. That nothing changed points at waits the processor cannot end.

prompt: A terminal session is used to start a long-running task. What is the relationship between the two processes?
optionA: The task started the terminal session
optionB: The task runs inside the terminal session as part of it
optionC: The two are unrelated once both are running
optionD: The terminal session started the task
correctAnswerText: The terminal session started the task
explanation: One started the other, and that relationship is recorded. It is a relationship between two separate processes rather than one containing the other.

prompt: When one process starts another, what is recorded about the pair?
optionA: Which one started the other
optionB: Which one will finish first
optionC: That the two must finish together
optionD: That the two share their memory
correctAnswerText: Which one started the other
explanation: The starting relationship is kept and is what lets a process be told how its children fared. Nothing about it forces them to end together.

prompt: A process starts three others. How is it related to them?
optionA: The three are copies of it
optionB: The three run inside it
optionC: It is the starter of all three, and they are unrelated to one another
optionD: The three are related to each other as well as to it
correctAnswerText: It is the starter of all three, and they are unrelated to one another
explanation: Each has the same starter and no relationship to its siblings. Nothing connects them except where they came from.

prompt: A student says that stopping a process automatically stops everything it started, because the children run inside it. What is wrong with the reasoning?
optionA: Nothing; children always stop with their starter
optionB: The children are separate processes; the relationship records who started whom and does not contain them
optionC: The children stop only if they were started recently
optionD: The reasoning is right for programs and wrong for scripts
correctAnswerText: The children are separate processes; the relationship records who started whom and does not contain them
explanation: Containment is the wrong picture. Each child is a process in its own right with its own number and its own life.

prompt: A process that was using the processor asks to read from a slow device. What happens to its condition?
optionA: It moves from using the processor to waiting for a turn
optionB: It keeps the processor until the data arrives
optionC: It finishes
optionD: It moves from using the processor to waiting for the device
correctAnswerText: It moves from using the processor to waiting for the device
explanation: The request cannot be satisfied at once, so holding the processor would waste it. The move is made so that something else can run.

prompt: A process was waiting for data, and the data has now arrived. What condition is it in immediately afterwards?
optionA: Ready, waiting for a turn on the processor
optionB: Using the processor straight away
optionC: Still waiting for the data
optionD: Finished, since its request has been satisfied
correctAnswerText: Ready, waiting for a turn on the processor
explanation: Its obstacle has gone and a free processor has not appeared. It joins the queue for a turn rather than resuming instantly.

prompt: A task is started so that the terminal prompt returns immediately and the task keeps running. How was it started?
optionA: In the foreground, so it holds the terminal
optionB: In the foreground, with the prompt shown early
optionC: In the background, so it does not hold the terminal
optionD: It was not started at all, which is why the prompt returned
correctAnswerText: In the background, so it does not hold the terminal
explanation: Holding the terminal is exactly what a foreground task does. The prompt returning is the observable sign that this one is not.

prompt: A task running in the background prints a message. Where does the message appear?
optionA: Nowhere, since background tasks produce no output
optionB: On the terminal, interleaved with whatever else is there
optionC: In a file, since background output is always redirected
optionD: On the terminal only after the task finishes
correctAnswerText: On the terminal, interleaved with whatever else is there
explanation: Not holding the terminal is not the same as being disconnected from it. The message arrives in the middle of whatever the user is doing, which is why background output is usually sent elsewhere deliberately.

prompt: A process finishes. What does it report about how it went?
optionA: Everything it printed while running
optionB: How long it ran for
optionC: Nothing; a finished process reports nothing
optionD: A value saying whether it succeeded
correctAnswerText: A value saying whether it succeeded
explanation: The reported value is a small signal about success, separate from anything printed. Whatever started it can read that value.

prompt: A task prints several pages of output and then reports failure. What follows?
optionA: It failed, whatever it printed along the way
optionB: It succeeded, since it produced output
optionC: It partly succeeded, in proportion to the output
optionD: The two reports contradict each other and one must be wrong
correctAnswerText: It failed, whatever it printed along the way
explanation: Printing and reporting are different channels and do not contradict each other. A task can do a great deal of work and still not achieve what it was asked to.

prompt: A script runs a task and decides what to do next by reading what the task printed, searching the output for the word "error". The task reports failure through its result value and prints nothing containing that word. The script inspects the printed text and never reads the reported result value. What happens?
optionA: The script detects the failure from the reported value
optionB: The script fails to run, since the task failed
optionC: The script treats the failure as a success, because it never looked at the result
optionD: The script detects the failure from the absence of output
correctAnswerText: The script treats the failure as a success, because it never looked at the result
explanation: The signal was there and the script was reading the wrong channel. Searching output for words is fragile in exactly this way, since the wording is not guaranteed.

prompt: A process is politely asked to stop. What can it do about the request?
optionA: Nothing; it ends immediately
optionB: Notice it and tidy up before ending
optionC: Refuse it permanently and continue as though nothing happened
optionD: Pass the request to whatever started it
correctAnswerText: Notice it and tidy up before ending
explanation: The polite request is deliverable and the process decides how to respond. That opportunity is the whole difference between the two ways of stopping something.

prompt: A process is stopped outright rather than asked. What can it do about it?
optionA: Tidy up first, then end
optionB: Save its work and then end
optionC: Refuse if it is holding a file open
optionD: Nothing; it ends without any opportunity to prepare
correctAnswerText: Nothing; it ends without any opportunity to prepare
explanation: The forced stop is not delivered to the process to be handled. Anything it was part-way through is left as it was.

prompt: A process writing a large file is stopped outright. A colleague expects the file to be either complete or absent. Being stopped outright gives the process no opportunity to finish or to remove what it had already written. What is the likely state of the file?
optionA: Partly written, being neither complete nor absent
optionB: Complete, since the write had started
optionC: Absent, since the process did not finish
optionD: Complete but marked as incomplete
correctAnswerText: Partly written, being neither complete nor absent
explanation: Nothing arranges for a half-written file to be cleaned up unless the process does it, and it was given no chance. Asking politely would have let it either finish or remove the file.

prompt: A process that started another finishes first. What happens to the one it started?
optionA: It stops immediately
optionB: It is suspended until a new starter appears
optionC: It keeps running
optionD: It restarts from the beginning
correctAnswerText: It keeps running
explanation: The relationship records who started whom and does not tie their lives together. The child continues and is adopted by something else.

prompt: A user starts a long task from a terminal and then closes the terminal window. The task is still running afterwards. Is that surprising?
optionA: Yes; closing the terminal should have stopped the task
optionB: No; the task is a separate process and does not end because its starter did
optionC: Yes; the task should have been suspended
optionD: No, but only because the task was started in the background
correctAnswerText: No; the task is a separate process and does not end because its starter did
explanation: Whether it was started in the background affects the terminal rather than survival. Some setups do arrange for tasks to be stopped when a session ends, and that is an arrangement rather than the default behaviour.

prompt: A deployment script starts a server process and then exits. Hours later the server is still running and nobody knows how to stop it, because the script that started it is gone. The server survived its starter and the number it was given was never recorded anywhere. What is the difficulty?
optionA: The server should have stopped when the script exited
optionB: The server cannot be stopped once its starter has gone
optionC: The script must still be running somewhere
optionD: The server is running with no record of its number, so it has to be found before it can be stopped
correctAnswerText: The server is running with no record of its number, so it has to be found before it can be stopped
explanation: Survival is the expected behaviour and the missing record is the problem. A listing of running processes will find it; recording the number at start time would have avoided the search.

prompt: A process ends. What happens to the number it was using?
optionA: It becomes available for a later process
optionB: It is retired and never used again
optionC: It is kept in case the process restarts
optionD: It is transferred to whatever started the process
correctAnswerText: It becomes available for a later process
explanation: Numbers are a finite supply and are reissued once free. That is why one recorded some time ago may now name something entirely different.

prompt: A number was written into a file yesterday when a process was started. What can be concluded from it today?
optionA: That the same process still has it
optionB: That no process has it now
optionC: That some process had that number yesterday; nothing certain about today
optionD: That the process finished, since the number was recorded
correctAnswerText: That some process had that number yesterday; nothing certain about today
explanation: The number may name the original process, a completely different one, or nothing at all. Checking what is actually running is what distinguishes the three.

prompt: A monitoring script records a number at start time and checks each hour whether a process with that number is running, reporting the service as healthy if one is. A number becomes available when its process ends and may then be given to something unrelated. What is wrong with the check?
optionA: The check is sound, since the number is unique
optionB: A different process may now hold that number, so the check can report health when the service has died
optionC: The check will report failure even when the service is running
optionD: The check should be run more often than hourly
correctAnswerText: A different process may now hold that number, so the check can report health when the service has died
explanation: Presence of the number is not presence of the service. Comparing the program name as well, or asking the service itself, is what makes the check mean something.

prompt: A listing of running processes is produced. What does it describe?
optionA: The situation continuously as it changes
optionB: Every process that has run since the machine started
optionC: Every process that will run today
optionD: The situation at the moment it was taken
correctAnswerText: The situation at the moment it was taken
explanation: The listing is a snapshot. Anything that started or ended after it was taken is not reflected in it.

prompt: A process a user expected to find does not appear in a listing. What follows?
optionA: It was not running at that moment; whether it ran earlier is a separate question
optionB: It has never run
optionC: It is running but hidden
optionD: It has finished successfully
correctAnswerText: It was not running at that moment; whether it ran earlier is a separate question
explanation: Absence from a snapshot says only that it was not there then. It may have ended a second earlier, successfully or otherwise.

prompt: A listing shows one process using a very high share of the processor. A team concludes it has been overloading the machine all morning. The listing describes the instant it was taken and says nothing about the hours before it. What does the listing support?
optionA: That the process has been busy all morning
optionB: That the process is faulty
optionC: That the process was busy at that instant, and nothing about the morning
optionD: That the machine is short of processors
correctAnswerText: That the process was busy at that instant, and nothing about the morning
