explanation: One instant is one instant. Sampling repeatedly, or consulting a record kept over time, is what would support a claim about the morning.

prompt: A process is politely asked to stop and does not. It is waiting for a reply from a machine that is not responding. Why has the request had no effect?
optionA: The request was not delivered
optionB: It cannot act on the request while it is blocked waiting
optionC: The process has crashed and can no longer receive anything
optionD: The process is refusing the request deliberately
correctAnswerText: It cannot act on the request while it is blocked waiting
explanation: A blocked process is not running any instructions, so it cannot notice the request. When the wait ends it would act on it, and the wait may not end.

prompt: A process ignores a polite stop request. It is mid-way through writing a file. Forcing it would end it at once and would leave the file part-written, while waiting risks waiting indefinitely. What is the trade being made?
optionA: Nothing; forcing it is always correct here
optionB: Nothing; waiting is always correct here
optionC: Whether the process is important enough to keep
optionD: Ending it now at the cost of a part-written file, against waiting for a wait that may not end
correctAnswerText: Ending it now at the cost of a part-written file, against waiting for a wait that may not end
explanation: Both options have a real cost and the stem states both. Which is right depends on whether the part-written file can be recovered from, which is a question about this file.

prompt: An administrator stops a process using a number from a note made last week. The command reports success, and an unrelated service goes down. What most likely happened?
optionA: The number now belonged to the unrelated service
optionB: The command was mistyped
optionC: The original process had a dependency on the service
optionD: The command failed silently and something else caused the outage
correctAnswerText: The number now belonged to the unrelated service
explanation: The command reporting success means it found and stopped a process with that number. The number was reissued between last week and today.

prompt: A cleanup job stops every process whose number appears in a list built at midnight. It runs at six, reports every stop as successful, and two unrelated services are found stopped. The job reported success for every number, and success means a process with that number was found and stopped. What happened?
optionA: The job failed and the outage has another cause
optionB: The original processes had been restarted with the same numbers
optionC: Some of those numbers had been reissued to other processes in the six hours since the list was built
optionD: The list was built incorrectly at midnight
correctAnswerText: Some of those numbers had been reissued to other processes in the six hours since the list was built
explanation: Every stop succeeding is the evidence: each number named a live process. The list was correct when it was built and had six hours to go stale.

prompt: A process created a temporary file at the start of its run and removes it just before finishing. It is stopped outright halfway through. What is left behind?
optionA: Nothing; temporary files are always cleaned up
optionB: The temporary file, since the removal never happened
optionC: The temporary file, but it will be removed automatically later
optionD: Nothing, since the process did not finish
correctAnswerText: The temporary file, since the removal never happened
explanation: Cleaning up was something the process was going to do and it was not given the chance. Nothing else knows the file was temporary.

prompt: A process holds a lock while it works and releases it when it finishes. It is stopped outright. Releasing the lock was something the process did on finishing, and it was given no opportunity to do anything. What is the state of the lock?
optionA: Released, since the process is gone
optionB: Released after a short delay
optionC: Held by whatever started the process
optionD: Still held, with no process holding it, so anything waiting for it waits indefinitely
correctAnswerText: Still held, with no process holding it, so anything waiting for it waits indefinitely
explanation: A lock that outlives its holder is the classic consequence of forcing a stop. Locks that are released automatically when the holder disappears exist and have to be built that way deliberately.

prompt: A service is restarted every night by stopping it outright and starting it again. It has worked for months. It writes to a file continuously, and the stop can land at any point in a write. What is the position?
optionA: It has been fortunate; a stop landing mid-write will eventually corrupt the file
optionB: It is safe, since months of success is strong evidence
optionC: It is safe, since restarts are a normal operation
optionD: It is unsafe, and the corruption has certainly already happened
correctAnswerText: It has been fortunate; a stop landing mid-write will eventually corrupt the file
explanation: Months without incident is evidence that the window is narrow rather than that it is absent. Asking politely first, and forcing only if the request is ignored, closes it.

prompt: A process starts a child and finishes immediately. The child runs for an hour and then fails. The starter has already finished, so there is nothing left to receive a report of how the child fared. What happens to the information that it failed?
optionA: It is reported to whatever adopted the child
optionB: It is reported to the user who started the original process
optionC: It has nowhere to go, so the failure is unreported unless the child recorded it itself
optionD: It is kept until the starter is restarted
correctAnswerText: It has nowhere to go, so the failure is unreported unless the child recorded it itself
explanation: The reported value goes to whatever is waiting for it and nothing is. This is why long-running work started this way has to write its own record of what happened.

prompt: A process finishes successfully in one second, every time it is run, and a monitoring system that checks once a minute never sees it running. The process exists for one second in every sixty and the check samples one instant per minute. What does the monitoring establish?
optionA: That the process is never running
optionB: Almost nothing; a process this short is unlikely to be caught by a check this infrequent
optionC: That the process fails to start
optionD: That the process finishes too quickly to be useful
correctAnswerText: Almost nothing; a process this short is unlikely to be caught by a check this infrequent
explanation: The absence is what sampling predicts rather than evidence of anything. Recording each run as it happens is what would answer the question the monitoring was trying to answer.

prompt: A process is consuming a great deal of processor time and is part-way through writing a report file. It is not blocked and it responds to requests. It is responsive and mid-write, so it can be asked and can tidy up. How should it be stopped?
optionA: Force it, since it is consuming resources now
optionB: Force it, since polite requests are unreliable
optionC: Leave it, since stopping it risks the file
optionD: Ask it politely, so that it can finish or remove the part-written file
correctAnswerText: Ask it politely, so that it can finish or remove the part-written file
explanation: Both conditions for the polite route are present. Forcing would end it faster and leave the file in the state this family exists to warn about.

prompt: A process is blocked waiting on a machine that will not respond, holding no files open, and is preventing a deployment. It has been asked politely and has not reacted. It holds no files open and cannot act on a polite request while it is blocked. What should be done?
optionA: Force it, since nothing is at risk and the polite route cannot work while it is blocked
optionB: Keep waiting, since the polite request may still be acted on
optionC: Restart the machine, since the process cannot be stopped
optionD: Ask politely again, in case the first request was lost
correctAnswerText: Force it, since nothing is at risk and the polite route cannot work while it is blocked
explanation: The two facts together settle it: the polite route is unavailable and forcing costs nothing here. Repeating a request that cannot be noticed changes nothing.

prompt: A team wants a script to stop a service reliably. A colleague proposes forcing it immediately, because polite requests sometimes go unanswered. The service tidies up when asked politely, and forcing gives it no opportunity to do so. What is the better arrangement?
optionA: Force immediately, since it is reliable
optionB: Ask politely and never force, since forcing risks the tidy-up
optionC: Ask politely, wait a stated period, and force only if it has not ended
optionD: Ask politely twice before forcing
correctAnswerText: Ask politely, wait a stated period, and force only if it has not ended
explanation: Forcing immediately gives up the tidy-up in every case to handle the case where it is needed. Never forcing leaves the script unable to finish when a process is stuck.

prompt: A process must be stopped, and a colleague proposes stopping everything started by the same session to be thorough. That session also started an unrelated long-running job that has been running for hours. Stopping everything from the session would also stop the unrelated job, which nobody asked to stop. What follows?
optionA: Stop everything from the session, since thoroughness is safer
optionB: Only the intended process should be stopped, since the broader action reaches something unrelated
optionC: Stop everything from the session, since the jobs are related by their starter
optionD: Stop nothing, since the two cannot be separated
correctAnswerText: Only the intended process should be stopped, since the broader action reaches something unrelated
explanation: Sharing a starter is not sharing a purpose. The two jobs are separate processes and can be addressed separately by their own numbers.

prompt: A team can stop a stuck process now, losing the state that would explain why it stuck, or leave it and investigate while it is still stuck. The service is degraded but working, and the stuck state is the only evidence of why this keeps happening. What should decide?
optionA: Stopping it, since service always comes first
optionB: Investigating, since understanding always comes first
optionC: Neither; the process should be left indefinitely
optionD: Whether the recurring cause is worth more than restoring full service immediately
correctAnswerText: Whether the recurring cause is worth more than restoring full service immediately
explanation: Both have a real cost and the stem supplies what makes it a genuine choice: the service is degraded rather than down, and this is the only chance to see the cause. Capturing the state and then stopping it is often the way to have both.

prompt: A container platform gives each running container an identifier, records which one launched which, and reports a result value when one ends. A container is launched by another that then exits. The platform records the launching relationship and nothing in the description says a launched container ends with its launcher. What happens to the launched container?
optionA: It keeps running, since nothing described ties its life to its launcher
optionB: It stops, since its launcher has gone
optionC: It is suspended until the launcher returns
optionD: It cannot be determined without knowing the platform
correctAnswerText: It keeps running, since nothing described ties its life to its launcher
explanation: The described model is the process model under another name, and the same conclusion follows from it. A platform could arrange otherwise and this description does not.

prompt: A job scheduler gives each run an identifier and reuses identifiers once a run has completed. A dashboard stores identifiers and displays the status of whatever currently holds each one. Identifiers are reused after completion and the dashboard looks up whatever holds one now. What will the dashboard eventually show?
optionA: Nothing, once the original run has completed
optionB: The status of the original run, retained after completion
optionC: The status of an unrelated later run, presented as though it were the original
optionD: An error, since the identifier no longer exists
correctAnswerText: The status of an unrelated later run, presented as though it were the original
explanation: This is identifier reuse in a different setting and produces the same fault. Recording the start time alongside the identifier is what lets the dashboard tell the two apart.

prompt: A platform sends a shutdown request to a running task and stops it outright if it has not ended within thirty seconds. A team writes a task that takes two minutes to save its state on shutdown. The task needs two minutes to tidy up and will be stopped outright after thirty seconds. What will happen?
optionA: It will be allowed to finish saving, since it responded to the request
optionB: It will be stopped part-way through saving, every time
optionC: It will be stopped only if the platform is under load
optionD: It will never receive the shutdown request
correctAnswerText: It will be stopped part-way through saving, every time
explanation: Responding to the request is not the same as finishing within the window. Saving faster, or saving continuously so that shutdown has little to do, is what fits the platform.

prompt: A team must decide whether a background worker should record its own outcome to a log or rely on the system that started it to capture the result value. The starter exits immediately after launching the worker, so nothing is waiting to receive a result value. Which should they choose?
optionA: Rely on the starter, since result values are the standard mechanism
optionB: Rely on the starter, since logs can be lost
optionC: Neither is needed, since failures are always visible
optionD: The worker should record its own outcome, since nothing will be there to receive a reported result
correctAnswerText: The worker should record its own outcome, since nothing will be there to receive a reported result
explanation: The reported value goes to whatever is waiting, and the stem states that nothing will be. Where the starter waits, relying on the result value would be the simpler choice.

prompt: A command line names a command, then a setting that changes how it behaves, then a file. Which part is the thing being acted on?
optionA: The command name
optionB: The file
optionC: The setting
optionD: All three equally
correctAnswerText: The file
explanation: The command says what to do and the setting adjusts how, leaving the file as what it is done to. The three parts have distinct roles.

prompt: What is the purpose of a setting given on a command line?
optionA: To name what the command acts on
optionB: To say where the output should go
optionC: To name the user running the command
optionD: To change how the command behaves
correctAnswerText: To change how the command behaves
explanation: A setting adjusts behaviour and does not supply the target. Confusing the two is what makes a command act on nothing or on the wrong thing.

prompt: A command line lists three file names after the command. What does that usually mean?
optionA: The command acts on all three
optionB: The command acts on the first and ignores the rest
optionC: The command acts on the last only
optionD: The command will refuse, since it expects one file
correctAnswerText: The command acts on all three
explanation: Most commands accept several targets and act on each. That is what makes a pattern expanding to many names work at all.

prompt: Why does the order of the parts on a command line matter?
optionA: Because commands run their parts left to right as separate steps
optionB: Because the last part is always ignored
optionC: Because the command has to be named first and its targets identified as targets
optionD: It does not matter; the parts can be given in any order
correctAnswerText: Because the command has to be named first and its targets identified as targets
explanation: The command name comes first because it decides how everything after it is read. Settings and targets are then distinguished by their form.

prompt: A user means to act on a file named in a certain way and the command reports that it cannot find a file with that name, while also behaving unusually. The name resembles the form a setting takes. What has most likely happened?
optionA: The file has been deleted
optionB: The name was read as a setting rather than as a target
optionC: The command does not accept targets
optionD: The command was misspelled
correctAnswerText: The name was read as a setting rather than as a target
explanation: A target that looks like a setting is read as one, so the command adjusts its behaviour and finds no target at all. Files whose names begin like settings need marking as targets explicitly.

prompt: A command is given a file name with no path. Where does it look for the file?
optionA: In the user home directory always
optionB: In the directory where the command itself is installed
optionC: Everywhere on the machine
optionD: In the directory the session is currently in
correctAnswerText: In the directory the session is currently in
explanation: A bare name is read from wherever the session happens to be. That location is a property of the session rather than of the command.

prompt: Is the current directory a property of the session or of the command being run?
optionA: Of the session
optionB: Of the command
optionC: Of the user account
optionD: Of the machine
correctAnswerText: Of the session
explanation: The session carries a current directory and every command run from it inherits that. Two sessions on the same machine can be in different places.

prompt: Two terminal sessions are open on one machine. Must they be in the same directory?
optionA: Yes; the machine has one current directory
optionB: Yes, if the same user opened both
optionC: No; each keeps its own current directory
optionD: Only if both are running commands
correctAnswerText: No; each keeps its own current directory
explanation: Each session tracks its own location independently. Moving around in one has no effect on the other.

prompt: A user runs a command that works, moves to a different directory, and runs the identical command line, which now fails. Nothing on disk has changed. What explains it?
optionA: The command was corrupted by the move
optionB: The bare names in the command resolved to different places from the two directories
optionC: The command can only be run once per session
optionD: The second directory has different permissions on the command
correctAnswerText: The bare names in the command resolved to different places from the two directories
explanation: The command line is identical and what it names is not, because bare names depend on where they are read from. Using paths that begin at the top removes the dependence.

prompt: A user wants a second copy of a file, keeping the original. Which kind of command does that?
optionA: One that moves
optionB: One that removes
optionC: One that lists
optionD: One that copies
correctAnswerText: One that copies
explanation: Copying leaves the original where it was and creates a second. Moving would relocate the one file rather than producing two.

prompt: A user wants to give a file a different name in the same directory. Which kind of command does that?
optionA: One that moves
optionB: One that copies
optionC: One that removes
optionD: One that inspects
correctAnswerText: One that moves
explanation: Renaming and relocating are the same operation: the entry changes and no second copy appears. Copying would leave the old name in place as well.

prompt: A user wants to see what a text file contains without changing it. Which kind of command does that?
optionA: One that lists names in a directory
optionB: One that copies the file
optionC: One that displays contents
optionD: One that changes the file permissions
correctAnswerText: One that displays contents
explanation: Displaying contents and listing names answer different questions. A listing tells you the file is there and nothing about what is in it.

prompt: A user wants to know which files in a directory were changed most recently. Which kind of command answers that?
optionA: One that displays the contents of each file
optionB: One that lists names together with their details
optionC: One that copies the directory somewhere else
optionD: One that searches inside the files for text
correctAnswerText: One that lists names together with their details
explanation: The question is about the entries rather than the contents, so a detailed listing answers it. Opening every file would answer a different question slowly.

prompt: A session starts in /home/asha, moves into reports, and then moves up one level. Where is it?
optionA: /home/asha/reports
optionB: /home
optionD: /home/asha
correctAnswerText: /home/asha
explanation: Moving in and then back up returns to the starting point, which is /home/asha. One further move up would have reached the directory above it.

prompt: A session starts in /var/log, moves up two levels, and then moves into tmp. Where is it?
optionA: /tmp
optionB: /var/tmp
optionC: /var/log/tmp
optionD: /tmp/log
correctAnswerText: /tmp
explanation: Two levels up from /var/log reaches the top of the tree, and entering tmp from there gives /tmp. Climbing only one level would have left the session inside /var.

prompt: A plain listing of a directory produces no output. What follows?
optionA: The directory is definitely empty
optionB: The directory does not exist
optionC: Nothing was shown, which does not establish that the directory is empty
optionD: The user lacks permission to read it
correctAnswerText: Nothing was shown, which does not establish that the directory is empty
explanation: Entries whose names mark them as hidden are left out of a plain listing. An empty result and an empty directory are different things.

prompt: A directory contains a subdirectory holding four files. A plain listing of the directory shows one entry. Why?
optionA: The listing failed to read the subdirectory
optionB: A listing shows what is in the directory, and the subdirectory is one entry
optionC: The four files are hidden
optionD: The listing shows only the first entry
correctAnswerText: A listing shows what is in the directory, and the subdirectory is one entry
explanation: The subdirectory is a single entry however much is inside it. Reaching inside is a separate request.

prompt: A file is moved from one directory to another. What exists afterwards?
optionA: Two files, one in each directory
optionB: One file, in the old directory
optionC: Two files, both in the new directory
optionD: One file, in the new directory
correctAnswerText: One file, in the new directory
explanation: Moving relocates the single file rather than duplicating it. Copying is what would leave two.

prompt: A file called report.txt is copied into a directory that already contains a different file called report.txt. What is the likely result?
optionA: The existing file is replaced by the copy, and its previous contents are gone
optionB: The copy is refused because the name is taken
optionC: The copy is renamed automatically to avoid the clash
optionD: Both files exist afterwards under the same name
correctAnswerText: The existing file is replaced by the copy, and its previous contents are gone
explanation: Most such commands overwrite without asking. Two entries cannot share one name in a directory, so one of them has to go.

prompt: A user copies notes.txt into a backup directory each evening. Tonight the backup directory already holds a notes.txt from last night, which they wanted to keep. The copy replaces any file of the same name in the destination, and both files are called notes.txt. What happens to last night version?
optionA: It is kept, since the two came from different days
optionB: It is renamed automatically before the copy arrives
optionC: It is replaced and its contents are lost
optionD: The copy is refused, leaving last night version intact
correctAnswerText: It is replaced and its contents are lost
explanation: Nothing about the file records which day it came from, so the name is all the command sees. Including a date in the destination name is what would keep both.

prompt: A directory contains a.txt, b.txt, c.log and notes.txt. A pattern matching anything ending in .txt is used. Which entries are selected?
optionA: a.txt and b.txt only
optionB: a.txt, b.txt and notes.txt
optionC: Every entry in the directory
optionD: c.log only
correctAnswerText: a.txt, b.txt and notes.txt
explanation: The pattern selects by name and every name ending in .txt qualifies, including the longer one. The log file does not.

prompt: A directory contains report.txt, report1.txt, report2.txt and a subdirectory called reports holding three more .txt files. A pattern matching anything ending in .txt is used. Which entries are selected?
optionA: All six .txt files, including those in the subdirectory
optionB: Only report.txt, since the others have digits
optionC: The subdirectory as well, since its name begins with report
optionD: The three .txt files in this directory, and none of those inside the subdirectory
correctAnswerText: The three .txt files in this directory, and none of those inside the subdirectory
explanation: A pattern of this kind selects entries in the directory it is applied to and does not descend. The subdirectory name does not end in .txt.

prompt: A directory contains data.csv, data_old.csv, .data_hidden.csv and archive.csv. A user applies a pattern matching anything beginning with data. A general pattern does not match names beginning with a dot, and one of the four begins with one. Which entries are selected?
optionA: data.csv and data_old.csv
optionB: data.csv, data_old.csv and .data_hidden.csv
optionC: data.csv only
optionD: All four entries
correctAnswerText: data.csv and data_old.csv
explanation: Names beginning with a dot are excluded from ordinary patterns deliberately, so the hidden file is left out. Archive.csv does not begin with data.

prompt: A file is removed with a command that deletes it. Where does it go?
optionA: To a recycle bin, from which it can be restored
optionB: To a temporary directory for a period
optionC: Nowhere; it is gone and there is no bin to recover it from
optionD: To the directory above, renamed
correctAnswerText: Nowhere; it is gone and there is no bin to recover it from
explanation: A command-line removal does not pass through a bin. Recovery afterwards depends on a backup having been taken.

prompt: A directory contains four files. A removal command is applied with a pattern matching anything ending in .tmp, and three of the four end in .tmp. What is lost?
optionA: All four files
optionB: The three .tmp files, without any confirmation being asked
optionC: Nothing, until the user confirms
optionD: The three .tmp files, after a confirmation prompt
correctAnswerText: The three .tmp files, without any confirmation being asked
explanation: The pattern selects three names and the command acts on each. Nothing asks first unless it has been set up to.

prompt: A user means to remove files ending in .bak and types a pattern that matches everything instead. The directory holds twelve files, three of them .bak. The pattern selects all twelve names and the command acts on each without asking. What is lost?
optionA: The three .bak files only
optionB: Nothing, since the pattern was clearly a mistake
optionC: The three .bak files, with the rest reported as errors
optionD: All twelve files
correctAnswerText: All twelve files
explanation: The command has no way to know which of the twelve were intended. Listing what a pattern matches before removing is the habit this exists to justify.

prompt: A command is told to work throughout a tree, starting at a directory. How far does it reach?
optionA: Everything below that directory, at every depth
optionB: Only the immediate contents
optionC: Only the directories, not the files
optionD: Only two levels down
correctAnswerText: Everything below that directory, at every depth
explanation: Working throughout a tree means every level below the starting point. Depth is not limited unless something limits it.

prompt: A directory holds two files and one subdirectory. That subdirectory holds three files and another subdirectory holding one file. A command working throughout the tree is applied to the top directory. How many files does it reach?
optionA: Two
optionB: Five
optionC: Six
optionD: Three
correctAnswerText: Six
explanation: Two at the top, three in the first subdirectory and one deeper: Six in all. Counting only the entries directly inside the starting directory would give a much smaller answer.

prompt: A user applies a removal command throughout a tree, meaning to clear one subdirectory, and gives the parent directory by mistake. The parent holds nine files of its own and four subdirectories. Working throughout a tree reaches every level below the directory given, and the directory given was the parent. What is lost?
optionA: Only the one subdirectory that was intended
optionB: The nine files, all four subdirectories and everything inside them
optionC: The nine files only, with the subdirectories left alone
optionD: The four subdirectories only, with the nine files left alone
correctAnswerText: The nine files, all four subdirectories and everything inside them
explanation: Naming the parent hands the command the whole tree beneath it. This single mistake is the reason for listing what a command would reach before running it.

prompt: A file is named "my report.txt", with a space in the middle. It is given to a command unquoted. What does the command receive?
optionA: One target, "my report.txt"
optionB: One target, "myreport.txt"
optionC: Nothing, since the name is invalid
optionD: Two separate targets, "my" and "report.txt"
correctAnswerText: Two separate targets, "my" and "report.txt"
explanation: A space separates one part of a command line from the next, so the name arrives as two. Quoting is what keeps it together.

prompt: A removal command is given the unquoted name "old notes.txt" in a directory that happens to contain a file called old and a file called notes.txt. What is removed?
optionA: Both old and notes.txt
optionB: Nothing, since no file is called old notes.txt
optionC: Only the file called old
optionD: A file called oldnotes.txt, if one exists
correctAnswerText: Both old and notes.txt
explanation: The command receives two names, both of which exist, and removes both. It succeeds completely and does entirely the wrong thing.

prompt: A script builds a file name from a value that sometimes contains a space, and passes it unquoted to a command. Most of the time the value has no space and the script works. An unquoted value containing a space arrives as two separate targets rather than one. What happens on the day it does?
optionA: The command fails and the script stops
optionB: The command acts on the first part and ignores the second
optionC: The command acts on two things instead of one, and reports success
optionD: The script refuses to build the name
correctAnswerText: The command acts on two things instead of one, and reports success
explanation: Nothing detects the split, so the failure is silent and intermittent. That the script has worked for months is exactly what makes the day it does not so confusing.

prompt: A command reports that a file does not exist. The user can see the file listed in a window on the same machine. What is the most likely explanation?
optionA: The file was deleted a moment ago
optionB: The session is in a different directory from the one being viewed
optionC: The command lacks permission to see it
optionD: The file name contains an invisible character
correctAnswerText: The session is in a different directory from the one being viewed
explanation: The command looked where the session is and the window is showing somewhere else. Both reports are accurate about different places.

prompt: A command reports that a file does not exist. A listing of the current directory shows a file whose name looks identical. The listing shows the name and the command searched the same directory, so the two names must differ in something not visible. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The session is in a different directory
optionB: The user lacks permission on the file
optionC: The command was misspelled
optionD: The two names differ in something that does not show, such as a trailing space or a differing character
correctAnswerText: The two names differ in something that does not show, such as a trailing space or a differing character
explanation: Being in the wrong directory is ruled out by the stem, which leaves the names themselves. Names that look identical and differ invisibly are a genuine and maddening case.

prompt: A user intends to act on files beginning with log and finds that a directory called logs was affected too. Why?
optionA: The pattern matched the directory name as well, since it also begins with log
optionB: Directories are always included regardless of the pattern
optionC: The command treats directories as files
optionD: The directory was affected by a different command
correctAnswerText: The pattern matched the directory name as well, since it also begins with log
explanation: A pattern matches names, and a directory has a name like anything else. Nothing about being a directory exempts it.

prompt: A user applies a pattern intending to select three files and twelve entries are affected. The directory contains twelve entries in total. The pattern matched every entry in the directory rather than the three intended. What does that indicate about the pattern?
optionA: It matched only files and there were twelve files
optionB: It matched the three intended files three times each
optionC: It was general enough to match every name present
optionD: The command ignored the pattern entirely
correctAnswerText: It was general enough to match every name present
explanation: Twelve of twelve is the signature of a pattern that constrains nothing. Listing what a pattern expands to before acting is what turns this into a non-event.

prompt: A user is about to remove files matching a pattern and wants to know first what would go. What should they do?
optionA: Run the removal and watch what happens
optionB: Apply the same pattern to a command that only lists
optionC: Take a backup of the directory
optionD: Remove the files one at a time
correctAnswerText: Apply the same pattern to a command that only lists
explanation: Listing with the identical pattern shows exactly the set the removal would act on. A backup is a good habit and answers a different question.

prompt: A user plans a destructive command and takes a full backup first. A colleague says they should still list what the command would affect. A backup allows recovery afterwards and does not show what the command would act on beforehand. Is the colleague right?
optionA: No; the backup makes the listing unnecessary
optionB: No; listing and backing up achieve the same thing
optionC: Yes, but only if the backup might be incomplete
optionD: Yes; the backup allows recovery and does not tell them what is about to happen
correctAnswerText: Yes; the backup allows recovery and does not tell them what is about to happen
explanation: Recovering from a mistake and avoiding one are different goods, and the backup only offers the first. Noticing that a pattern matches twelve things rather than three costs nothing.

prompt: A user lists what a pattern matches, sees the expected three files, and then runs the removal ten minutes later. In the intervening ten minutes another process created four more files matching the same pattern. What happens?
optionA: Seven files are removed, since the pattern is evaluated again when the removal runs
optionB: Three files are removed, as listed
optionC: Three files are removed and the four new ones are reported as errors
optionD: The removal is refused because the directory changed
correctAnswerText: Seven files are removed, since the pattern is evaluated again when the removal runs
explanation: The listing described the directory at the moment it ran, and the pattern is expanded afresh. On a directory something else writes to, the gap between checking and acting is the risk.

prompt: A team wants a script to remove old files safely. A colleague proposes having it print what it would remove and do nothing, until somebody has read the output. Printing without acting lets the set be checked before anything is destroyed. What does the proposal buy?
optionA: Nothing; the script will remove the same files either way
optionB: A guarantee that the right files are removed
optionC: The chance to see the set before anything is destroyed, at the cost of a second run
optionD: Protection against the directory changing between the two runs
correctAnswerText: The chance to see the set before anything is destroyed, at the cost of a second run
explanation: It buys review and guarantees nothing, since the set can change between the two runs. That remaining gap is why this is a safeguard rather than a proof.

prompt: A user is about to run a destructive command and cannot decide whether the risk justifies the time spent checking. The command would act on a directory holding work that exists nowhere else. The material exists in no other copy, so a mistake could not be undone. What follows?
optionA: The check is unnecessary, since the command is simple
optionB: The check is worth its cost, since a mistake here cannot be undone
optionC: The check is unnecessary if the user is experienced
optionD: The command should not be run at all
correctAnswerText: The check is worth its cost, since a mistake here cannot be undone
explanation: Irreversibility is what makes checking worth the time rather than the complexity of the command. The same command against a directory with a backup would be a different decision.

prompt: A user must place a file in a second directory while keeping it available in the first. The file must remain in the original directory and must also be present in the second. Which command fits?
optionA: One that moves
optionB: One that removes and recreates
optionC: One that renames
optionD: One that copies
correctAnswerText: One that copies
explanation: Keeping both requires a duplicate, which is what copying produces. Moving satisfies the second requirement and breaks the first.

prompt: A user must clear temporary files from a directory that also holds work in progress. The temporary files all end in .tmp and no file of value ends in .tmp. Only .tmp files are to go and no valuable file carries that ending. Which approach fits?
optionA: A removal restricted to a pattern matching .tmp, applied to that directory only
optionB: A removal applied throughout the tree, to be thorough
optionC: A removal of everything, followed by restoring the work in progress
optionD: Removing the files one by one after inspecting each
correctAnswerText: A removal restricted to a pattern matching .tmp, applied to that directory only
explanation: The pattern is exactly as wide as the requirement. Working throughout the tree reaches directories nobody mentioned, and inspecting each by hand is unnecessary given the stated rule.

prompt: A user must remove a directory and everything in it. A colleague suggests removing the files first and then the directory, to be careful. Working throughout the tree does both in one step and reaches the same set of things. What is the difference between the two approaches?
optionA: The careful route destroys less
optionB: The careful route is safer because it can be stopped partway
optionC: None in what is destroyed; the careful route only makes the set visible along the way
optionD: The single command destroys more than the careful route
correctAnswerText: None in what is destroyed; the careful route only makes the set visible along the way
explanation: Both end with the same directory gone. What the slower route offers is the chance to notice something unexpected before it is too late, and it can indeed be stopped partway — which is a reason to prefer it and not a difference in reach.

prompt: A user must rename two hundred files according to a rule. They can do it by hand or write a short loop. The rule is mechanical and applies to every one of the two hundred files in the same way. Which fits?
optionA: By hand, since a loop might affect the wrong files
optionB: The loop, since the rule is uniform and two hundred repetitions invite mistakes
optionC: By hand, since two hundred is not many
optionD: The loop, but only after renaming ten by hand first
correctAnswerText: The loop, since the rule is uniform and two hundred repetitions invite mistakes
explanation: Uniformity is what makes the work automatable and repetition is what makes doing it by hand error-prone. Testing the loop on a copy first is a sensible refinement rather than a reason to avoid it.

prompt: A user must free space and can either remove old files or move them to slower storage. The files are needed a few times a year and cannot be regenerated. The files cannot be regenerated and are still wanted occasionally. Which fits?
optionA: Removing them, since they are used only a few times a year
optionB: Removing them, since space is the stated problem
optionC: Leaving them where they are
optionD: Moving them to slower storage, since they are still wanted and cannot be recreated
correctAnswerText: Moving them to slower storage, since they are still wanted and cannot be recreated
explanation: Both facts point the same way: still wanted rules out removal and irreproducible makes removal irreversible. Rarity of use is an argument about where they live rather than whether they should exist.

prompt: A command is documented as acting on every entry below the directory it is given, following the tree to any depth, and as asking for no confirmation. A user gives it their home directory. It follows the tree to any depth from the directory given and asks for no confirmation. What would it act on?
optionA: Everything anywhere below their home directory
optionB: Only the entries directly inside their home directory
optionC: Only the files, leaving the directories alone
optionD: Nothing, until the user confirms
correctAnswerText: Everything anywhere below their home directory
explanation: The documented behaviour settles it without any need to recognise the command. Reading what a command says it does is what makes an unfamiliar one safe to reason about.

prompt: A command is documented as taking a source and a destination, and as replacing the destination if it exists. A user gives it two file names by mistake in the wrong order. The command replaces whatever is at the destination, and the two names were supplied the wrong way round. What happens?
optionA: The command refuses, since the order is wrong
optionB: The command detects the mistake and swaps them
optionC: The file they meant to keep is replaced by the one they meant to overwrite
optionD: Both files are left unchanged
correctAnswerText: The file they meant to keep is replaced by the one they meant to overwrite
explanation: The command cannot know which order was intended, and both names are valid in either position. The documented replacement behaviour is what makes the mistake destructive rather than harmless.

prompt: A command is documented as expanding any pattern it is given before acting, and as acting on every resulting name. A user gives it a pattern in a directory they have not looked at. The pattern is expanded against a directory whose contents the user has not seen. What is the safest next step?
optionA: Run the command, since the pattern was written carefully
optionB: List what the pattern expands to in that directory before running the command
optionC: Run the command from a different directory
optionD: Give the command a single file name instead of the pattern
correctAnswerText: List what the pattern expands to in that directory before running the command
explanation: The pattern is precise and the directory is unknown, so what it selects is unknown. Listing first converts an unknown set into a visible one.

prompt: A command is documented as reporting success whether or not it found anything to act on. A script uses it and treats success as meaning the work was done. Success is reported even when nothing was found, so a successful result does not establish that anything happened. What is wrong with the script?
optionA: Nothing; success means the command ran correctly
optionB: The command should be replaced, since reporting success is misleading
optionC: The script should run the command twice to be certain
optionD: It cannot distinguish work done from nothing found, since both report success
correctAnswerText: It cannot distinguish work done from nothing found, since both report success
explanation: The command is behaving exactly as documented, which is why reading the documentation matters here. Checking that the expected change actually occurred is what the script has to do instead.

prompt: A command produces results and also produces a warning. Do the two travel on the same channel?
optionA: Yes; everything a command produces travels together
optionB: No; results go on the ordinary output channel and warnings on the error channel
optionC: Yes, unless the command is told otherwise
optionD: No; warnings are not produced by commands at all
correctAnswerText: No; results go on the ordinary output channel and warnings on the error channel
explanation: Two separate outgoing channels exist and both are shown on the screen by default. Sharing a screen is what makes them look like one.

prompt: How many channels does a command typically have?
optionA: One, used for everything
optionB: Two, one in and one out
optionC: Four, one for each kind of message
optionD: Three: one incoming and two outgoing
correctAnswerText: Three: one incoming and two outgoing
explanation: Input arrives on one channel and output leaves on two, separated into ordinary results and errors. The separation is what makes the two independently routable.

prompt: A command reports that a file could not be opened. Which channel carries that message?
optionA: The error channel
optionB: The ordinary output channel
optionC: The incoming channel
optionD: Neither; failures are not written to a channel
correctAnswerText: The error channel
explanation: Anything reporting that something went wrong belongs on the error channel. Keeping it apart is what lets results be captured cleanly.

prompt: Why are results and errors kept on separate channels?
optionA: So that errors can be displayed in a different colour
optionB: So that errors are produced faster
optionC: So that results can be sent somewhere without the errors going with them
optionD: So that a command can produce only one of the two
correctAnswerText: So that results can be sent somewhere without the errors going with them
explanation: Separation exists to make the two routable independently. Capturing results into a file while still seeing problems on the screen is the everyday consequence.

prompt: A user watching a terminal sees results and an error message appear together and concludes they are on one channel. What is wrong with the conclusion?
optionA: Nothing; appearing together means one channel
optionB: Both channels point at the screen by default, which is why they appear together
optionC: The error must have been written to the output channel by mistake
optionD: The two appeared together by coincidence
correctAnswerText: Both channels point at the screen by default, which is why they appear together
explanation: The screen is the default destination for both, so the evidence is consistent with either account. Sending one of them elsewhere is what makes the separation visible.

prompt: A command output is sent to a file instead of the screen. What appears on the screen?
optionA: The output, as well as going to the file
optionB: A summary of the output
optionC: The output, delayed until the command finishes
optionD: Nothing from the ordinary output channel
correctAnswerText: Nothing from the ordinary output channel
explanation: Redirecting moves the output rather than copying it. The screen sees none of what went to the file.

prompt: A command that produces no output at all has its output redirected to a new file. Is the file created?
optionA: Yes, and it is empty
optionB: No, since there was nothing to write
optionC: No, and the command fails
optionD: Yes, containing a message saying there was no output
correctAnswerText: Yes, and it is empty
explanation: The file is prepared before the command runs, so it exists whether or not anything is written. That preparation is what makes the emptying behaviour matter.

prompt: What does redirecting a command output achieve?
optionA: It saves a copy while still showing it
optionB: It changes what the command produces
optionC: It sends that channel to a file rather than to the screen
optionD: It makes the command run faster
correctAnswerText: It sends that channel to a file rather than to the screen
explanation: The destination changes and the content does not. The command behaves identically and its output ends up somewhere else.

prompt: A user redirects a command output to a file and is surprised to see a message still appear on the screen. What is the explanation?
optionA: The redirection failed
optionB: The message was on the error channel, which was not redirected
optionC: The file was full
optionD: The command wrote the message twice
correctAnswerText: The message was on the error channel, which was not redirected
explanation: Only the ordinary output channel was sent to the file. Errors continue to the screen unless they are redirected as well.

prompt: Two commands are joined by a pipe. What does the second receive?
optionA: The name of the first command as an argument
optionB: The errors produced by the first
optionC: Nothing; the two simply run one after the other
optionD: The ordinary output of the first, as its incoming channel
correctAnswerText: The ordinary output of the first, as its incoming channel
explanation: The pipe connects one outgoing channel to the next incoming one. The second command reads it as though it were typed in.

prompt: Do errors from the first command travel down a pipe to the second?
optionA: No; a pipe carries the ordinary output channel only
optionB: Yes; everything the first produces is passed on
optionC: Yes, but only if the first command fails
optionD: No; errors stop the pipeline entirely
correctAnswerText: No; a pipe carries the ordinary output channel only
explanation: The error channel is not what the pipe connects, so errors go to the screen as usual. This is why an error can appear while the pipeline continues.

prompt: Three commands are joined by two pipes. What does the third receive?
optionA: The output of the first
optionB: The outputs of the first and second combined
optionC: The output of the second
optionD: The original input to the first
correctAnswerText: The output of the second
explanation: Each pipe connects one stage to the next, so each stage sees only what its immediate predecessor produced.

prompt: A user pipes a command output into a second command and finds the second acting on nothing. The first produced only errors and no ordinary output. Why did the second receive nothing?
optionA: The pipe was written incorrectly
optionB: Errors do not travel down a pipe, and there was no ordinary output to send
optionC: The second command cannot read from a pipe
optionD: The first command finished too quickly
correctAnswerText: Errors do not travel down a pipe, and there was no ordinary output to send
explanation: The first command did produce something and put it on the channel the pipe does not carry. The second correctly received an empty input.

prompt: A file of ten lines is fed into a stage that keeps only lines containing the word error, and three lines contain it. That stage output goes to a stage that counts lines. What does the counting stage receive?
optionA: Ten lines
optionB: Seven lines
optionC: One line
optionD: Three lines
correctAnswerText: Three lines
explanation: The counting stage sees what reached it, which is what the filter let through. The original ten are no longer available to it.

prompt: Twenty lines are fed through a stage keeping only lines containing "warn", which passes eight, and then through a stage keeping only lines containing "disk", which passes two of those eight. What does a fourth stage receive?
optionA: Two lines
optionB: Twenty lines
optionC: Eight lines
optionD: Ten lines
correctAnswerText: Two lines
explanation: Each stage narrows what the next one sees, so the fourth receives what survived both filters. The counts at earlier points are not recoverable later in the chain.

prompt: A file already contains fifty lines. A command producing three lines has its output redirected into that file in the replacing form. What does the file contain afterwards?
optionA: Fifty-three lines
optionB: The fifty original lines only
optionC: The three new lines only
optionD: The three new lines followed by the fifty original ones
correctAnswerText: The three new lines only
explanation: The replacing form empties the file first. Adding to the end is a different form that would have given fifty-three.

prompt: A file contains a week of records. A command that turns out to produce no output at all has its output redirected into that file in the replacing form. What does the file contain afterwards?
optionA: The week of records, since the command wrote nothing
optionB: Nothing; it was emptied before the command ran and nothing replaced the contents
optionC: The week of records, plus an empty line
optionD: Nothing, and the file no longer exists
correctAnswerText: Nothing; it was emptied before the command ran and nothing replaced the contents
explanation: Emptying happens as the redirection is set up rather than as output arrives. A command that produces nothing still destroys what was there.

prompt: A command output is redirected to a log file. The command produces an error. Where does the error appear?
optionA: In the log file, with the output
optionB: Nowhere; it is discarded
optionC: In a separate file created automatically
optionD: On the screen
correctAnswerText: On the screen
explanation: Only the ordinary output channel was redirected. The error channel still points at the screen.

prompt: A scheduled job runs with its output redirected to a log and nobody watching the screen. It fails with an error. Where does the error go?
optionA: To wherever the error channel points, which is not the log
optionB: Into the log, alongside the output
optionC: To the person who scheduled the job
optionD: Nowhere; scheduled jobs produce no errors
correctAnswerText: To wherever the error channel points, which is not the log
explanation: The redirection covered one channel and the job has no screen. Capturing the error channel as well is what makes a scheduled job diagnosable.

prompt: A team investigates a failure and finds their log file contains the output up to the point of failure and no explanation of it. Only the ordinary output channel was redirected into the log, and the explanation was produced on the error channel. Why is the explanation missing?
optionA: The command failed before it could write the explanation
optionB: The log file was truncated at the point of failure
optionC: It went to the error channel, which was never redirected into the log
optionD: The command produced no explanation at all
correctAnswerText: It went to the error channel, which was never redirected into the log
explanation: The log is complete for what it was told to capture. Directing the error channel to the same file is what would have included the reason.

prompt: The lines "apple", "banana", "apricot" and "cherry" pass through a stage that keeps only lines beginning with the letter a, and then through a stage that converts to upper case. What emerges?
optionA: apple and apricot
optionB: APPLE and APRICOT
optionC: APPLE, BANANA, APRICOT and CHERRY
optionD: APPLE only
correctAnswerText: APPLE and APRICOT
explanation: Two lines survive the filter and both are then converted. The order of the two stages gives filtered-then-converted rather than the reverse.

prompt: The lines "10", "3", "7" and "22" pass through a stage that keeps only lines of exactly one character, and then through a stage that sorts. What emerges?
optionA: 3, 7, 10 and 22 in order
optionB: 10, 3, 7 and 22 unchanged
optionC: 7 and 3, in that order
optionD: 3 and 7, in that order
correctAnswerText: 3 and 7, in that order
explanation: Only the two single-character lines survive, and sorting them puts 3 before 7. The two-digit lines never reach the sorting stage.

prompt: Six lines pass through a stage that removes duplicates, leaving four, and then through a stage that keeps only lines containing the letter x, of which three of the original six qualified and two survived the deduplication. Each stage acts on what the previous stage produced rather than on the original six. What emerges?
optionA: Two lines
optionB: Three lines
optionC: Four lines
optionD: Six lines
correctAnswerText: Two lines
explanation: The filter sees the deduplicated four rather than the original six, so two qualify. Applying the filter to the original set would have given three.

prompt: A file of one hundred lines is filtered to those containing the word failed, and the result is counted. The count reads twelve. What does twelve refer to?
optionA: The lines in the file
optionB: The lines not containing the word
optionC: The lines containing the word failed
optionD: The number of times the word appears
correctAnswerText: The lines containing the word failed
explanation: The counting stage counts what reached it, which is what the filter passed. The size of the original file is no longer visible at that point.

prompt: A line contains the word failed three times. A pipeline filters for that word and counts lines. How much does that line contribute to the count?
optionA: Three, once for each occurrence
optionB: One, since the stage counts lines rather than occurrences
optionC: Nothing, since duplicates within a line are ignored
optionD: It cannot be determined
correctAnswerText: One, since the stage counts lines rather than occurrences
explanation: Filtering keeps the line once and counting counts lines. Counting occurrences would need a different stage.

prompt: A pipeline filters a log for errors, removes duplicate lines, and counts what remains, giving four. A team reports that four errors occurred. Duplicate lines were removed before the count, so identical errors occurring many times contribute one each. What does four actually count?
optionA: Four error occurrences in total
optionB: Four lines in the original log
optionC: Four different files containing errors
optionD: Four distinct error lines, however many times each occurred
correctAnswerText: Four distinct error lines, however many times each occurred
explanation: The deduplication stage is what separates the two readings. One error repeated a thousand times contributes one to this figure.

prompt: A stage in the middle of a pipeline receives lines. Can it tell which file they came from?
optionA: No; it receives the lines and nothing about their origin
optionB: Yes; the file name travels with the lines
optionC: Yes, if the first stage read a file
optionD: Only if the pipeline has exactly two stages
correctAnswerText: No; it receives the lines and nothing about their origin
explanation: A stage sees the content arriving on its incoming channel and nothing else. Including the file name in the content is what makes it available.

prompt: The same filtering stage is used once with its output going to the screen and once with its output going to a file. Does it behave differently?
optionA: Yes; it produces less output when writing to a file
optionB: Yes; it formats differently for a file
optionC: No; it produces the same output either way
optionD: Only if the file already exists
correctAnswerText: No; it produces the same output either way
explanation: A stage does not know where its output is going, so it cannot behave differently. Some tools do adjust their formatting when writing to a screen, and that is a deliberate feature rather than the general rule.

prompt: A team wants a middle stage in a pipeline to behave differently when it is the last stage. A stage receives its input and produces its output without any information about what comes after it. What follows?
optionA: It can, by checking whether its output goes to a screen
optionB: It cannot, since nothing tells a stage what follows it
optionC: It can, by counting the stages in the pipeline
optionD: It can, by asking the previous stage
correctAnswerText: It cannot, since nothing tells a stage what follows it
explanation: Independence from context is what makes stages composable at all. Passing the intention in as a setting is how the requirement actually gets met.

prompt: A command can be given a file as a named target, or the same file can be supplied on its incoming channel. What is the difference from the command point of view?
optionA: There is no difference at all
optionB: In one case the content arrives faster
optionC: In one case the content is read-only
optionD: In one case it knows the file name and in the other it receives only the contents
correctAnswerText: In one case it knows the file name and in the other it receives only the contents
explanation: The contents are identical and the knowledge of where they came from is not. That is why one form can report a file name in its output and the other cannot.

prompt: A command that normally prints the file name alongside each matching line is given its input on the incoming channel instead of as a named file. What happens to the file names in its output?
optionA: They are absent, since the command was never told a name
optionB: They appear as before
optionC: They appear as the word input
optionD: The command refuses to run
correctAnswerText: They are absent, since the command was never told a name
explanation: The command cannot report what it was not given. Supplying the file as a named target is what restores the names.

prompt: A script searches several files and reports which file each match came from. A colleague rewrites it to feed the files in on the incoming channel instead. The rewritten form supplies only the contents, so the command is never told which file a line came from. What is lost?
optionA: Nothing; the same matches are found either way
optionB: The matches themselves, since the search cannot work this way
optionC: The file names, since the command receives contents with no indication of their source
optionD: The order of the results
correctAnswerText: The file names, since the command receives contents with no indication of their source
explanation: The same lines are found and their provenance is not. Naming the files as targets is what keeps the report usable.

prompt: A pipeline of four stages produces nothing. How should the responsible stage be found?
optionA: Rewrite the pipeline from scratch
optionB: Run the first stage alone, then the first two, and so on until the output disappears
optionC: Assume the last stage is at fault, since it produced the empty result
optionD: Check whether the input file exists and stop there
correctAnswerText: Run the first stage alone, then the first two, and so on until the output disappears
explanation: Stopping at each point shows where the content is lost. The last stage produced the visible empty result and need not be the stage that emptied it.

prompt: A pipeline produces nothing. Running the first two stages alone produces forty lines, and running the first three produces nothing. The output survives two stages and disappears after the third. Which stage is responsible?
optionA: The fourth, since the pipeline ends with no output
optionB: The first, since it read the input
optionC: The second, since it passed forty lines
optionD: The third, since the content was present before it and absent after
correctAnswerText: The third, since the content was present before it and absent after
explanation: Bisecting the pipeline locates the loss precisely. The fourth stage received nothing and had nothing to lose.

prompt: A user saw an error on screen while a command output was being written to a file. The file does not contain the error. Why not?
optionA: The error travelled on a channel that was not being written to the file
optionB: The file was written before the error occurred
optionC: The error was too long to fit
optionD: The command removed the error from the file
correctAnswerText: The error travelled on a channel that was not being written to the file
explanation: What went to the file is what was redirected there. The screen showed the other channel, which nothing captured.

prompt: A pipeline captures its final output to a file. A stage in the middle produces an error, which appears on the screen. The team expected it in the file. A pipe carries only the ordinary output channel, so a middle stage error never enters the pipeline. Why is it not in the file?
optionA: The error was overwritten by later output
optionB: The final stage discarded it
optionC: The error never entered the pipeline, so it could not reach the file at the end of it
optionD: The file captured only the last stage output and the error came from an earlier one
correctAnswerText: The error never entered the pipeline, so it could not reach the file at the end of it
explanation: Each stage error channel goes to the screen independently of the pipe. Redirecting each stage error channel, or the whole pipeline, is what captures them.

prompt: A pipeline filters lines containing a word and then counts them. The two stages are swapped so that counting comes first. What changes?
optionA: Nothing; the same number is produced
optionB: The result becomes the count of all lines rather than of the matching ones
optionC: The result becomes zero
optionD: The filter stops working
correctAnswerText: The result becomes the count of all lines rather than of the matching ones
explanation: Counting first produces a single number, which the filter then examines. The filter is looking at a count rather than at the lines.

prompt: A pipeline sorts lines and then removes duplicates. A colleague swaps the two so that duplicates are removed first. Removing duplicates does not depend on the order lines arrive in, and sorting does not depend on whether duplicates are present. Does the result change?
optionA: Yes; duplicates can only be removed from sorted input
optionB: Yes; the output will be unsorted
optionC: Yes; some duplicates will survive
optionD: No; the two stages commute here and the final set of lines is the same
correctAnswerText: No; the two stages commute here and the final set of lines is the same
explanation: Neither stage needs what the other provides, so the order is free. Some tools remove only adjacent duplicates, which would make sorting a prerequisite, and this stem describes one that does not.

prompt: A pipeline takes the first ten lines and then filters for a word, producing two results. Swapping the two stages produces ten results. Taking the first ten before filtering limits the filter to those ten, while filtering first lets the whole input be searched. Which order answers the question "what are the first ten matching lines"?
optionA: Filtering first, then taking ten, since the ten must be chosen from the matches
optionB: Taking ten first, then filtering, since ten is the limit
optionC: Either; both produce the first ten matching lines
optionD: Neither; the question needs a different pipeline
correctAnswerText: Filtering first, then taking ten, since the ten must be chosen from the matches
explanation: The two orders answer different questions, and only one of them is the question asked. Taking ten first answers "how many of the first ten match".

prompt: A pipeline processes a very large file. One stage filters out ninety per cent of the lines and one stage is slow and expensive per line. The expensive stage costs the same per line wherever it sits, and the filter reduces the number of lines reaching whatever follows it. Where should the expensive stage go?
optionA: Before the filter, so that no line is missed
optionB: Either; the total work is the same
optionC: After the filter, so that it processes a tenth as many lines
optionD: Before the filter, so that the filter sees processed lines
correctAnswerText: After the filter, so that it processes a tenth as many lines
explanation: Both orders give the same result here and not the same cost. Where the expensive stage changes what the filter would match, the orders stop being interchangeable and the cost argument no longer applies.

prompt: A team moves a filtering stage earlier in a pipeline for speed, and the results change. The stage that used to run before the filter altered the lines in a way that affected whether the filter matched them. Why did the results change?
optionA: Moving a stage earlier always changes the results
optionB: The filter now sees the unaltered lines, and it matches them differently
optionC: The pipeline became too fast for the filter
optionD: The filter was damaged by the move
correctAnswerText: The filter now sees the unaltered lines, and it matches them differently
explanation: Reordering is free only when neither stage affects what the other does. Here one stage was changing the very text the filter examines.

prompt: A team needs the number of distinct users appearing in a log. Each line names one user and a user may appear many times. Users repeat across lines and the requirement is a count of distinct users rather than of lines. Which pipeline fits?
optionA: Extract the user from each line, then count
optionB: Count the lines, then remove duplicates
optionC: Remove duplicate lines, then count
optionD: Extract the user from each line, remove duplicates, then count
correctAnswerText: Extract the user from each line, remove duplicates, then count
explanation: Deduplication has to come between extraction and counting. Removing duplicate whole lines leaves a user appearing under different remaining text more than once.

prompt: A team wants a log file both captured to disk and visible on screen as it runs. Redirecting sends the output to one destination instead of the other rather than to both. Which approach fits?
optionA: A stage that writes to a file and passes the same content onward
optionB: Redirect to the file, since it can be read afterwards
optionC: Leave it on the screen, since it can be copied out
optionD: Run the command twice, once for each destination
correctAnswerText: A stage that writes to a file and passes the same content onward
explanation: Redirecting is a move rather than a copy, so neither single destination meets the requirement. Running twice would produce two separate runs that need not agree.

prompt: A scheduled job must leave a record of everything that happened, including why it failed. Errors travel on a separate channel and are not captured by redirecting the ordinary output alone. What must the arrangement do?
optionA: Capture the ordinary output channel, which contains everything
optionB: Capture the error channel only, since failures are what matter
optionC: Capture both channels, since the reason for a failure travels on the error channel
optionD: Capture neither, and rely on the reported result value
correctAnswerText: Capture both channels, since the reason for a failure travels on the error channel
explanation: Capturing one channel leaves half the record missing, and which half depends on how the job went. The reported result value says that it failed and never why.

prompt: A team can build a report as one long pipeline of eight stages, or as a script with named intermediate steps. The pipeline is shorter to write and must be understood and modified by people joining the team throughout the year. The report will be modified repeatedly by people who did not write it. Which fits?
optionA: The pipeline, since it is shorter
optionB: The named steps, since the work is maintenance by people who did not write it
optionC: The pipeline, since fewer intermediate files are created
optionD: Either, since the two produce the same report
correctAnswerText: The named steps, since the work is maintenance by people who did not write it
explanation: Both produce the same report, so correctness cannot decide it. Eight anonymous stages have to be reconstructed from scratch by every reader.

prompt: A team must process a file too large to fit in memory. One approach reads the whole file into memory and sorts it; another passes it through a chain of stages, each handling a line at a time. The file is larger than the memory available and a chain of stages holds only what it is currently processing. Which fits?
optionA: The in-memory sort, since sorting is faster in memory
optionB: Either, since both process the same file
optionC: The in-memory sort, with the file split into pieces first
optionD: The chain of stages, since it never holds the whole file at once
correctAnswerText: The chain of stages, since it never holds the whole file at once
explanation: The constraint is what has to be held simultaneously rather than what is processed in total. Splitting first is a real technique and reintroduces the work the chain avoids.

prompt: A data platform lets steps be chained, each consuming what the previous produced. A step in the middle needs a value that was present in the original input and removed by an earlier step. Each step sees only what its predecessor produced, and the value was removed before this step. What follows?
optionA: The value is unavailable to it, and an earlier step must carry it forward
optionB: The step can request the original input
optionC: The step can ask the platform for the missing value
optionD: The value is restored automatically when needed
correctAnswerText: The value is unavailable to it, and an earlier step must carry it forward
explanation: The described chain has the same isolation as a pipeline, and the same consequence. Anything a later step needs has to survive every step before it.

prompt: A processing framework reports success for a chain when the final step succeeds. A middle step fails, produces nothing, and the final step succeeds on the empty input. The final step succeeded on an empty input and the chain is judged by the final step alone. What does the reported success mean?
optionA: That every step in the chain succeeded
optionB: That the chain produced correct output
optionC: Only that the last step ran without error, which an empty input allowed it to do
optionD: That the middle step recovered from its failure
correctAnswerText: Only that the last step ran without error, which an empty input allowed it to do
explanation: Judging a chain by its last step hides failures upstream, exactly as a pipeline can. Checking each step, or checking that the output is non-empty, is what closes the gap.

prompt: A build system chains tasks so that each consumes the previous output. A team adds a task that writes a report to the screen and passes nothing onward. Each task consumes what the previous produced, and this one produces nothing. What happens to the tasks after it?
optionA: They receive the report that was written to the screen
optionB: They receive nothing, so the chain effectively ends there
optionC: They receive the output of the task before it
optionD: They fail with an error about the missing input
correctAnswerText: They receive nothing, so the chain effectively ends there
explanation: Writing to the screen is not the same as passing something on, and the chain carries only what is passed. A task meant to observe without interrupting has to pass its input through unchanged.

prompt: A team must decide whether to build a transformation as one large step or as five small ones chained together. The five would each be independently testable and would pass data between them; the one large step would hold everything internally. Five chained steps can each be tested on their own, while one large step can only be tested end to end. Which fits a system that must be verified in detail?
optionA: The one large step, since it has fewer moving parts
optionB: The one large step, since passing data between steps is expensive
optionC: Either, since both produce the same transformation
optionD: The five chained steps, since each can be checked independently
correctAnswerText: The five chained steps, since each can be checked independently
explanation: Composability buys exactly what the requirement asks for, which is the ability to check the parts. Where verification did not matter, the single step and its lower overhead would be a reasonable choice.

prompt: A form must collect exactly one answer from a fixed list of four. Which kind of control fits?
optionA: A set of independent tick boxes
optionB: A set of options where choosing one clears the others
optionC: A free text field
optionD: A field that accepts a number
correctAnswerText: A set of options where choosing one clears the others
explanation: Exactly one from a fixed set is what a mutually exclusive group expresses. Independent tick boxes would let a visitor choose all four.

prompt: A form must collect any number of answers from a fixed list of six, including none. Which kind of control fits?
optionA: A set of options where choosing one clears the others
optionB: A free text field
optionC: A drop-down allowing one selection
optionD: A set of independent tick boxes
correctAnswerText: A set of independent tick boxes
explanation: Independent boxes permit none, some or all, which is what the requirement allows. A mutually exclusive group would cap it at one.

prompt: A form must collect a comment of a paragraph or two. Which kind of control fits?
optionA: A multi-line text field
optionB: A single-line text field
optionC: A set of tick boxes
optionD: A field that accepts a number
correctAnswerText: A multi-line text field
explanation: A paragraph needs room and line breaks, which a single-line field does not offer. The choice follows from the shape of the answer.

prompt: What decides which kind of control a form should use for a question?
optionA: How the control looks on the page
optionB: How much space is available
optionC: The shape of the answer being collected
optionD: Which control is easiest to style
correctAnswerText: The shape of the answer being collected
explanation: The control encodes what kind of answer is permitted. Appearance can be adjusted afterwards and cannot change how many answers are possible.

prompt: A designer uses independent tick boxes for a question that must have exactly one answer, planning to check afterwards that only one was ticked. What is the weakness?
optionA: Nothing; the check is equivalent to using the right control
optionB: The form permits an invalid answer, so the check has to catch what the control should have prevented
optionC: Tick boxes cannot be checked afterwards
optionD: The form will refuse to submit
correctAnswerText: The form permits an invalid answer, so the check has to catch what the control should have prevented
