explanation: The right control makes the invalid state unreachable. Permitting it and rejecting it afterwards means a visitor can complete the form and be told they were wrong.

prompt: Text reading "Email address" sits immediately to the left of a text field, and nothing in the markup connects the two. Is the field labelled?
optionA: Yes; the text is clearly its label
optionB: Yes, because the text is close enough
optionC: It depends on how far apart they are
optionD: No; the text is adjacent and not associated with it
correctAnswerText: No; the text is adjacent and not associated with it
explanation: A label is a relationship recorded in the markup rather than a position on screen. Proximity is what a sighted reader uses and is not available to anything else.

prompt: What makes text a control label rather than nearby text?
optionA: An association recorded between the two in the markup
optionB: Its position immediately before the control
optionC: Its being written in bold
optionD: Its ending in a colon
correctAnswerText: An association recorded between the two in the markup
explanation: The association is the whole of it. Position, styling and punctuation are conventions that help sighted readers and record nothing.

prompt: Two forms look identical on screen. In one, every label is associated with its control; in the other, none is. What differs?
optionA: Nothing at all
optionB: The visual layout
optionC: What anything other than a sighted reader can determine about the fields
optionD: The speed at which the page loads
correctAnswerText: What anything other than a sighted reader can determine about the fields
explanation: The appearance is the same and the recorded structure is not. Clicking a label to focus its field also stops working, which is the visible symptom.

prompt: A developer replaces every label with placeholder text inside the field, saying the form now looks cleaner and still tells the user what to enter. What is lost?
optionA: Nothing; placeholder text serves the same purpose
optionB: The description disappears as soon as the user types, and nothing records what the field is for
optionC: The ability to style the text
optionD: The ability to make the field required
correctAnswerText: The description disappears as soon as the user types, and nothing records what the field is for
explanation: Placeholder text vanishes exactly when the user might want to check what they were asked for. It is a hint rather than a name for the field.

prompt: A form is submitted. How does the receiving side tell which value came from which control?
optionA: By the label text shown beside it
optionB: By the order the controls appear on the page
optionC: By the text the user typed
optionD: By the name given to each control
correctAnswerText: By the name given to each control
explanation: Each value travels under the control name. The label is for the person filling the form and never reaches the other end.

prompt: A control has no name. What does it contribute when the form is submitted?
optionA: Nothing at all
optionB: An empty value under a default name
optionC: Its value, identified by its label
optionD: Its value, identified by its position
correctAnswerText: Nothing at all
explanation: Without a name there is nothing to send the value under, so it is omitted entirely. Nothing stands in for the missing name.

prompt: Two controls in one form are given the same name and both hold a value. What arrives?
optionA: One value, with the second discarded
optionB: One value, being the two joined together
optionC: Two values under the same name
optionD: Nothing, since the names clash
correctAnswerText: Two values under the same name
explanation: Nothing forbids a repeated name, and the receiving side gets both. This is what makes a group of tick boxes under one name workable.

prompt: A developer changes a field label from "Phone" to "Contact number" and the receiving code stops finding the value. What does that indicate?
optionA: Nothing unusual; changing a label changes the submitted name
optionB: The code was matching on something the change affected, which the label alone should not have been
optionC: The form is now invalid
optionD: The field lost its value when the label changed
correctAnswerText: The code was matching on something the change affected, which the label alone should not have been
explanation: A label change should be invisible to the receiving side. That it was not means the name was changed at the same time, or something is keying off the wrong thing.

prompt: A field collects a postcode that may begin with a zero. Should it be declared as a numeric field?
optionA: Yes; postcodes are made of digits
optionB: Yes, so that a numeric keyboard appears
optionC: It makes no difference either way
optionD: No; a numeric field may discard a leading zero, and a postcode is not a quantity
correctAnswerText: No; a numeric field may discard a leading zero, and a postcode is not a quantity
explanation: Being written in digits is not being a number. Nothing arithmetic is ever done to a postcode and its leading zero is significant.

prompt: A field collects a quantity ordered, between one and ninety-nine. Which declaration fits?
optionA: A numeric field with a stated minimum and maximum
optionB: A plain text field, checked afterwards
optionC: A numeric field with no limits
optionD: A set of ninety-nine tick boxes
correctAnswerText: A numeric field with a stated minimum and maximum
explanation: The value genuinely is a quantity and the range is known, so both can be declared. Checking afterwards leaves the visitor able to enter something the form should never have accepted.

prompt: Four mutually exclusive options share one name. How many can be chosen at once?
optionA: All four
optionB: Any number, including none
optionC: One
optionD: Two
correctAnswerText: One
explanation: Sharing a name is what makes them one group, and choosing one clears the rest. Without the shared name they would behave independently.

prompt: Four mutually exclusive options are placed together in a bordered box on the page, and each is given a different name. How many can be chosen at once?
optionA: One, since they are visually grouped
optionB: All four, since they are not one group
optionC: One, since they are that kind of control
optionD: None, since the names conflict
correctAnswerText: All four, since they are not one group
explanation: Grouping is established by the shared name rather than by the border. Each option with its own name is a group of one and can be chosen independently.

prompt: A tick box is left unticked when a form is submitted. What arrives for it?
optionA: An empty value under its name
optionB: The value "false" under its name
optionC: The value "off" under its name
optionD: Nothing; the name does not appear at all
correctAnswerText: Nothing; the name does not appear at all
explanation: An unticked box contributes nothing, so the receiving side sees the name missing entirely. That is different from a name arriving with an empty value.

prompt: A text field is left empty when a form is submitted. What arrives for it?
optionA: Its name, with an empty value
optionB: Nothing; the name does not appear
optionC: Its name, with the placeholder text as the value
optionD: Its name, with the word empty as the value
correctAnswerText: Its name, with an empty value
explanation: A text field always contributes, so the name arrives carrying nothing. This is the opposite of the unticked box and the pair is what code on the receiving side has to distinguish.

prompt: Receiving code reads a tick box value and treats a missing name as an error, since it expects every field to arrive. An unticked box sends no name at all, while an empty text field sends its name with nothing in it. What happens when a visitor leaves the box unticked?
optionA: The code receives an empty value and handles it
optionB: The code receives the value false and handles it
optionC: The code reports an error, when the visitor simply answered no
optionD: The form refuses to submit
correctAnswerText: The code reports an error, when the visitor simply answered no
explanation: Absent and empty are two different arrivals and the code recognises only one. Treating a missing tick box as a no is what the receiving side has to do deliberately.

prompt: A button sits inside a form and has not been declared to do anything in particular. What does pressing it do?
optionA: Nothing
optionB: Submits the form
optionC: Clears the form
optionD: Depends on the button text
correctAnswerText: Submits the form
explanation: Submitting is the default behaviour for a button inside a form. Anything else has to be declared.

prompt: A developer adds a button labelled "Add another row" inside a form and attaches code to it. The button has not been declared as anything other than a plain button. What happens when it is pressed?
optionA: Only the code runs
optionB: Only the form is submitted
optionC: Nothing, since two behaviours conflict
optionD: The code runs and the form is also submitted
correctAnswerText: The code runs and the form is also submitted
explanation: Attaching code does not remove the default behaviour. The page appears to reload in the middle of adding a row, which is a confusing symptom with a simple cause.

prompt: A form has three buttons: one to submit, one to add a row and one to remove a row. All three submit the form when pressed. None of the three has been declared as anything other than a plain button inside the form. What is the fault?
optionA: All three carry the default submitting behaviour, which only one of them wants
optionB: The two extra buttons are outside the form
optionC: The form has too many buttons
optionD: The buttons are missing their labels
correctAnswerText: All three carry the default submitting behaviour, which only one of them wants
explanation: The default applies to every button in the form regardless of its text. Declaring the two helpers as non-submitting is the fix.

prompt: A numeric field declares a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 10. Which entry is refused?
explanation: Both stated limits are included, so the value 0 is the only one of the four falling outside the permitted range. A declared minimum admits the number it names.

prompt: A field declares a maximum length of eight characters. A visitor enters nine. What happens?
optionA: The field accepts it and the form is refused on submission
optionB: The ninth character is not accepted into the field
optionC: The field accepts it and truncates it on submission
optionD: The whole entry is cleared
correctAnswerText: The ninth character is not accepted into the field
explanation: A length limit of this kind stops the typing rather than rejecting afterwards. The visitor sees the field stop accepting input, which needs explaining if the limit is not obvious.

prompt: A numeric field declares a minimum of 18 and is intended to accept adults only. A visitor enters 18. The declared minimum is 18 and a declared minimum includes the value itself. Is the entry accepted?
optionA: No; the minimum sets the first refused value
optionB: No; the field requires more than 18
optionC: It depends on how the field is styled
optionD: Yes; a declared minimum includes the stated value
correctAnswerText: Yes; a declared minimum includes the stated value
explanation: Boundary values are included, which is what makes 18 acceptable here. A requirement of over 18 would need a minimum of 19.

prompt: A field is marked as required. What does that stop?
optionA: Submitting the form with the field left empty
optionB: Submitting the form with a nonsense value in the field
optionC: Submitting the form at all
optionD: Typing into the field
correctAnswerText: Submitting the form with the field left empty
explanation: Required means not empty and nothing more. Whether what was typed makes sense is a separate question the mark does not address.

prompt: A required field is filled with a single space. Is the form accepted?
optionA: No, since a space counts as empty
optionB: No, since required fields reject whitespace
optionC: Generally yes, since a space is not nothing
optionD: Only if the field has a minimum length
correctAnswerText: Generally yes, since a space is not nothing
explanation: A space is a character and the field is no longer empty. Rejecting whitespace-only entries is something the receiving side has to do.

prompt: A required field collecting an email address is filled with the word "no". A required mark stops the field being empty and says nothing about the form of what is entered. Is the form accepted?
optionA: No; the field is declared as collecting an email address
optionB: Yes; the field is not empty, which is all the mark requires
optionC: No; required fields are checked for sense
optionD: Only if the receiving side accepts it
correctAnswerText: Yes; the field is not empty, which is all the mark requires
explanation: The mark and any format check are separate declarations. Declaring the field as an email address is what would add a shape check on top of the emptiness check.

prompt: A field shows greyed text reading "e.g. 07700 900000" before anything is typed. It is a hint rather than a value. What is submitted if the field is left alone?
optionA: The hint text
optionB: Nothing at all
optionC: The word placeholder
optionD: An empty value
correctAnswerText: An empty value
explanation: A hint disappears on typing and is never sent. The field is empty as far as the submission is concerned.

prompt: A field is pre-filled with a real starting value of "United Kingdom". What is submitted if the field is left alone?
optionA: "United Kingdom", since it is a real value
optionB: An empty value
optionC: Nothing at all
optionD: The word default
correctAnswerText: "United Kingdom", since it is a real value
explanation: A starting value is a value like any other and travels with the submission. It looks the same as a hint before anybody types.

prompt: A required field shows greyed text before anything is typed, and a visitor submits the form without touching it. The greyed text is a hint rather than a value, and the field is marked required. What happens?
optionA: The form is accepted, since the field shows text
optionB: The form is accepted and the hint is submitted
optionC: The form is refused, since the field counts as empty despite showing text
optionD: The form is accepted and an empty value is submitted
correctAnswerText: The form is refused, since the field counts as empty despite showing text
explanation: Text being visible is not the field having a value. The visitor sees a field that looks filled in being rejected as empty, which is why hints are poor substitutes for labels.

prompt: A field is visible, the visitor typed into it, and its name does not appear in the submission at all. Which cause fits?
optionA: The visitor left it empty
optionB: The control has no name
optionC: The field failed its format check
optionD: The field is a tick box that was not ticked
correctAnswerText: The control has no name
explanation: Typing into it rules out emptiness, and an empty field would still send its name. A control with no name is the one case where the name is absent despite a value being present.

prompt: A field appears on the page, has a name, and never arrives in the submission whatever the visitor does. The field is shown greyed out and cannot be typed into. A control that is disabled contributes nothing to a submission whatever it displays. What is the cause?
optionA: It has no name
optionB: The visitor is leaving it empty
optionC: The field is outside the form
optionD: It is disabled, and a disabled control submits nothing
correctAnswerText: It is disabled, and a disabled control submits nothing
explanation: Having a name is stated, which rules that out, and the greyed appearance is the clue. A disabled control is excluded from the submission entirely, even when it displays a value.

prompt: A set of mutually exclusive options lets a visitor select two at once. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The options do not all share one name
optionB: The options are the wrong kind of control
optionC: The options are laid out incorrectly
optionD: The form is missing a submit button
correctAnswerText: The options do not all share one name
explanation: The shared name is what makes them exclusive. Without it each behaves as its own group of one.

prompt: A visitor selects an option in one question and an option in an unrelated question below it clears itself. The two questions use different wording and their options were given the same name. Options sharing a name form a single group whatever question they appear under. What is the cause?
optionA: The two questions are too close together on the page
optionB: The second question is missing its own submit button
optionC: The two questions share one name, so their options form a single group
optionD: The options are the wrong kind of control
correctAnswerText: The two questions share one name, so their options form a single group
explanation: Grouping follows the name and ignores the visual arrangement entirely. Two questions sharing a name behave as one question with more options.

prompt: A form declares a field as required and as accepting only digits. What can the receiving side assume about what arrives?
optionA: That the field is present and contains only digits
optionB: Nothing; the checks help the visitor and do not constrain what is sent
optionC: That the field is present, though its contents may vary
optionD: That the field contains only digits, though it may be absent
correctAnswerText: Nothing; the checks help the visitor and do not constrain what is sent
explanation: The checks run in the visitor browser and a submission can be constructed without one. What arrives has to be checked again where it arrives.

prompt: A developer concludes that browser checks are pointless and removes them, planning to check everything on the receiving side. The checks tell a visitor about a mistake before they submit, and the receiving side can only tell them afterwards. What is lost?
optionA: Nothing; the receiving side does the same job
optionB: The ability to check the data at all
optionC: The ability to mark fields as required
optionD: Immediate feedback, which is what the browser checks were actually for
correctAnswerText: Immediate feedback, which is what the browser checks were actually for
explanation: The conclusion that they guarantee nothing is correct and the conclusion that they are pointless does not follow. They are for the person filling the form rather than for the system.

prompt: A team argues that since ordinary visitors use a browser, browser checks are sufficient for a form with no security implications. A submission can be constructed without a browser by anyone who chooses to, whatever the form is for. What is the position?
optionA: The receiving side will eventually see values the checks would have refused, whether sent deliberately or by a faulty client
optionB: The team is right; without security implications the checks suffice
optionC: The team is right, provided the form is only linked internally
optionD: The checks are worthless and should be removed
correctAnswerText: The receiving side will eventually see values the checks would have refused, whether sent deliberately or by a faulty client
explanation: Security is not the only reason values arrive malformed: an old browser, a retried request or a script written by a colleague will all do it. What the data feeds decides how much the malformed values cost.

prompt: A form marks a field as required and the receiving code assumes it is always present, reading it directly. A required mark constrains what a browser will submit and not what arrives at the receiving side. What is the consequence?
optionA: Nothing; the required mark guarantees presence
optionB: The submission will be rejected before reaching the code
optionC: A submission without the field will make the code fail on something it never expected to be absent
optionD: The code will receive an empty value and continue
correctAnswerText: A submission without the field will make the code fail on something it never expected to be absent
explanation: The failure is not a rejected form but a crash in code that had no branch for absence. Checking presence at the receiving end is what turns it into a handled case.

prompt: A team validates on both sides and the two disagree: the browser accepts a value the receiving side refuses. The visitor sees the form accepted and then an error. The two checks encode the same rule and were written separately, so they have drifted apart. What is the underlying problem?
optionA: Validating on both sides is unnecessary duplication
optionB: One rule is expressed twice, so the two can drift and the visitor experiences the gap
optionC: The browser check is too permissive and should be tightened once
optionD: The receiving side should accept whatever the browser accepted
correctAnswerText: One rule is expressed twice, so the two can drift and the visitor experiences the gap
explanation: Both checks are needed and expressing the rule twice is what allows them to disagree. Generating one from the other, or deriving both from a shared definition, is the repair.

prompt: A question must be answered, must have exactly one answer, and the answer must come from five fixed choices. Exactly one answer is required and the five choices are fixed in advance. Which arrangement fits?
optionA: Five independent tick boxes, with a check afterwards that one was ticked
optionB: A free text field marked as required
optionC: A mutually exclusive group with one option pre-selected
optionD: A mutually exclusive group of five sharing one name, with the group marked as required
correctAnswerText: A mutually exclusive group of five sharing one name, with the group marked as required
explanation: The exclusive group makes two answers impossible and the required mark makes zero impossible. Pre-selecting an option would make it impossible to tell a deliberate answer from an untouched form.

prompt: A form must record whether a visitor consents, and must distinguish a deliberate refusal from not having answered. A single tick box left unticked is indistinguishable from a form the visitor never reached. What arrangement fits?
optionA: A mutually exclusive pair of yes and no, marked as required
optionB: A single tick box, marked as required
optionC: A single tick box, left optional
optionD: A single tick box, pre-ticked
correctAnswerText: A mutually exclusive pair of yes and no, marked as required
explanation: One box has two states and the requirement needs three distinguished. An explicit pair with a required mark forces an answer and records which one it was.

prompt: A form collects a date of birth. A team proposes three separate numeric fields for day, month and year, with each field range-limited. Three separate fields permit 31 February, since each field is within its own range. What is the weakness?
optionA: Nothing; three fields are easier to fill in
optionB: Numeric fields cannot hold a year
optionC: Impossible dates pass, since no field constrains the others
optionD: The fields will be submitted in the wrong order
correctAnswerText: Impossible dates pass, since no field constrains the others
explanation: Each field is individually valid and the combination is not. A date control, or a check across the three, is what closes it.

prompt: A form can present twenty questions on one page or across five pages of four. Visitors frequently abandon it partway, and the team wants to keep whatever was answered before they left. Answers are only sent when a page is submitted, and visitors abandon the form partway. Which fits?
optionA: The single page, since it is quicker to complete
optionB: The five pages, since each submission preserves what was answered up to that point
optionC: The single page, since fewer submissions means fewer failures
optionD: Either, since the same twenty answers are collected
correctAnswerText: The five pages, since each submission preserves what was answered up to that point
explanation: A single page loses everything when abandoned, because nothing was sent. The five-page form costs extra steps and keeps four answers at a time.

prompt: A form marks nine of its ten fields as required. Analysis shows most abandonment happens at a field that is rarely needed downstream. The field is required and the data it collects is rarely used, while abandonment loses every answer on the page. What should be reconsidered?
optionA: Nothing; required fields ensure complete data
optionB: The other eight required fields, which may also be unnecessary
optionC: The page layout, which must be causing the abandonment
optionD: Whether that field needs to be required, since it is costing complete submissions for data that is rarely used
correctAnswerText: Whether that field needs to be required, since it is costing complete submissions for data that is rarely used
explanation: Requiring a field trades completed forms for complete records, and here the record is rarely consulted. The other eight have not been shown to cost anything.

prompt: A form-building toolkit is documented as omitting any control whose identifier is blank, and as sending a blank value for any text control the user did not fill in. A text control with an identifier is left untouched. The toolkit omits controls with a blank identifier and sends a blank value for unfilled text controls. What arrives?
optionA: Its identifier, carrying a blank value
optionB: Nothing at all
optionC: Its identifier, carrying the hint text
optionD: Its identifier, carrying the word blank
correctAnswerText: Its identifier, carrying a blank value
explanation: The documented behaviour settles it without any knowledge of the toolkit. Having an identifier means it is included and being unfilled means the value is blank.

prompt: A survey tool groups options by a question identifier and permits one answer per group. A designer copies a question to create a second and forgets to change the identifier. Options sharing a question identifier form one group permitting one answer between them. What happens?
optionA: The two questions behave independently
optionB: The tool refuses to save the duplicated question
optionC: The two questions behave as one, so answering the second clears the answer to the first
optionD: The second question is ignored entirely
correctAnswerText: The two questions behave as one, so answering the second clears the answer to the first
explanation: This is the shared-name fault under other names. Copying a question is exactly how the duplicate identifier gets created.

prompt: An application programming interface accepts a submission and treats an absent field as "leave unchanged" and a field present with no value as "clear this". A client always sends every field, using an empty value for anything the user did not fill in. Absent means leave alone and present-but-empty means clear, and the client always sends every field. What happens to fields the user did not fill in?
optionA: They are left unchanged, since the user did not fill them in
optionB: They are cleared, since the client sends them present and empty
optionC: They are rejected as invalid
optionD: They are filled with a default value
correctAnswerText: They are cleared, since the client sends them present and empty
explanation: The client and the interface disagree about what an empty value means, and the interface definition wins. Omitting untouched fields is what the client would have to do instead.

prompt: A team must decide whether their interface should distinguish an absent field from a field present with no value. Some updates need to clear a field and others need to leave it untouched, and one representation cannot express both. What follows?
optionA: The two should be treated identically, since both mean no value
optionB: Absent should be rejected, so that every field is always sent
optionC: Present-but-empty should be rejected, so that clearing is done another way
optionD: The distinction has to be kept, since collapsing it makes one of the two operations unexpressible
correctAnswerText: The distinction has to be kept, since collapsing it makes one of the two operations unexpressible
explanation: This is the unticked box and the empty text field again, at a different layer. Collapsing them is simpler right up until something needs to clear a value.

prompt: A developer wants to know where a function was written. Which kind of feature answers that?
optionA: One that lists every place the name is used
optionB: One that jumps to where a name is defined
optionC: One that searches the project for matching text
optionD: One that renames the name everywhere
correctAnswerText: One that jumps to where a name is defined
explanation: Finding the definition and finding the uses are opposite questions. A text search would find both and force the developer to sort them out by eye.

prompt: A developer wants to know everywhere a function is called before changing it. Which kind of feature answers that?
optionA: One that jumps to where the name is defined
optionB: One that renames the name everywhere
optionC: One that reformats the file
optionD: One that reports every place the name is used
correctAnswerText: One that reports every place the name is used
explanation: The question is about uses rather than the definition. Renaming would change them rather than reporting them.

prompt: A developer wants to find every place a particular phrase appears in comments. Which kind of feature answers that?
optionA: One that searches for matching text
optionB: One that jumps to where a name is defined
optionC: One that reports where a name is used
optionD: One that renames a name everywhere
correctAnswerText: One that searches for matching text
explanation: Comments carry no meaning the tool understands, so a text search is the right instrument. The meaning-aware features would ignore them entirely.

prompt: What distinguishes a text search from a search that understands the code?
optionA: One is faster than the other
optionB: One works on saved files and the other on open ones
optionC: One matches characters and the other matches the thing a name refers to
optionD: One is case sensitive and the other is not
correctAnswerText: One matches characters and the other matches the thing a name refers to
explanation: A text search finds a name inside a comment and inside a longer word. A meaning-aware search finds the specific thing and skips coincidental matches.

prompt: A developer uses a text search to find every call to a function named "run" and receives hundreds of results. What accounts for that?
optionA: The function really is called hundreds of times
optionB: The text appears inside longer words, comments and unrelated names
optionC: The search covered too many directories
optionD: The search was case insensitive
correctAnswerText: The text appears inside longer words, comments and unrelated names
explanation: A short common name matches a great deal of text that has nothing to do with it. A meaning-aware usage report would have found only the calls.

prompt: A project-wide search returns no results for a name. What does that establish?
optionA: That the name does not appear in the project
optionB: That the name has been deleted
optionC: That the name was never used
optionD: That the name was not found in what the search covered
correctAnswerText: That the name was not found in what the search covered
explanation: A search reports on what it looked at. What it looked at is a separate question with its own answer.

prompt: A project excludes a directory of generated files from searching. A name used only there is searched for. What is reported?
optionA: No results, because the excluded directory was not examined
optionB: The uses in the excluded directory
optionC: A warning that a directory was skipped
optionD: An error, since the name exists
correctAnswerText: No results, because the excluded directory was not examined
explanation: Exclusions are silent by design, so the search simply reports nothing. Knowing what is excluded is what makes an empty result interpretable.

prompt: Which question does an empty search result answer?
optionA: Whether the text exists anywhere in the project
optionB: Whether the text was ever used
optionC: Whether the text was found in the searched files
optionD: Whether the code compiles
correctAnswerText: Whether the text was found in the searched files
explanation: The result is about the files examined and nothing beyond them. Widening the claim is where the mistake gets made.

prompt: A developer searches for a function name, finds no results, and deletes the function as unused. It breaks the build. What did the search fail to cover?
optionA: The definition of the function itself
optionB: Somewhere the name is used that the search did not examine
optionC: The comments in the project
optionD: The most recently edited files
correctAnswerText: Somewhere the name is used that the search did not examine
explanation: Something used the function and the search did not look there — an excluded directory, a configuration file, or a name assembled at run time. The empty result was accurate and narrower than it appeared.

prompt: A line is underlined in an editor with a note suggesting a shorter way to write it. What kind of claim is that?
optionA: A statement that the code will fail
optionB: A statement that the code will not compile
optionC: A statement that the code has been tested
optionD: A style suggestion, not a statement that the code is wrong
correctAnswerText: A style suggestion, not a statement that the code is wrong
explanation: Suggestions about how something is written are separate from claims that it is broken. Both appear as underlines and mean different things.

prompt: A marker reports that a name cannot be found. What kind of claim is that?
optionA: That the tool could not resolve the name, which usually means the code will not build
optionB: That the code is badly written
optionC: That the code is slow
optionD: That the code has not been saved
correctAnswerText: That the tool could not resolve the name, which usually means the code will not build
explanation: An unresolvable name is a claim about correctness rather than style. It is the kind of marker worth acting on immediately.

prompt: Two editors show different markers on the same file. What does that indicate?
optionA: That one of the two is faulty
optionB: That the file changed between the two
optionC: That the two are checking for different things
optionD: That one editor is a newer version
correctAnswerText: That the two are checking for different things
explanation: A marker is one tool opinion, and different tools hold different opinions. Neither is a property of the code itself.

prompt: A developer treats every underline in their editor as something that must be removed before committing. What is the weakness?
optionA: Nothing; a clean file is always better
optionB: Style suggestions and genuine faults are being treated as one thing
optionC: Underlines cannot be removed
optionD: The editor will re-add them anyway
correctAnswerText: Style suggestions and genuine faults are being treated as one thing
explanation: Some markers report code that will not build and others express a preference. Treating them alike either wastes time or lets a real fault through in the noise.

prompt: A developer follows a function name to its definition and arrives somewhere. What has the tool done?
optionA: Searched the project for matching text
optionB: Guessed based on the file currently open
optionC: Taken them to the first definition alphabetically
optionD: Taken them to where it worked out the name is defined
correctAnswerText: Taken them to where it worked out the name is defined
explanation: The jump rests on the tool understanding of the code. That understanding can be wrong, which is why the destination is worth glancing at.

prompt: Two different modules each define a function with the same name, and a developer follows one call. What determines where they land?
optionA: Which definition the tool has worked out this call refers to
optionB: Which definition appears first in the project
optionC: Which file was most recently edited
optionD: Which module has the shorter name
correctAnswerText: Which definition the tool has worked out this call refers to
explanation: The tool resolves the call the way the language would, and lands on that one. Where two definitions genuinely could apply, some tools offer a choice instead.

prompt: A usage report lists eight places a function is called. What does it establish?
optionA: That the function is called exactly eight times
optionB: That the function is called from eight files
optionC: That the tool found eight; whether there are others depends on what it could see
optionD: That the function is safe to change
correctAnswerText: That the tool found eight; whether there are others depends on what it could see
explanation: The report covers what the tool understood. Calls constructed at run time or made from configuration are outside what it can resolve.

prompt: A project calls some functions by name assembled from a string at run time. A usage report for one such function shows no results. What follows?
optionA: The function is genuinely unused
optionB: The report cannot see calls of that kind, so the absence proves nothing
optionC: The report has failed and should be run again
optionD: The function is called from a different project
correctAnswerText: The report cannot see calls of that kind, so the absence proves nothing
explanation: A name that only exists as text at run time is invisible to a meaning-aware search. A plain text search would find the string.

prompt: A developer renames a function through the editor. What is changed?
optionA: Every occurrence of that text in the project
optionB: The definition only
optionC: The definition and the uses in the open file only
optionD: The definition and every use the tool recognised
correctAnswerText: The definition and every use the tool recognised
explanation: The rename follows the tool understanding of what refers to what. A text-based replacement would change every occurrence including coincidental ones.

prompt: A function name also appears in a comment and in a configuration file. A rename is performed through the editor. What happens to those two?
optionA: Both are left unchanged, since neither is a use the tool recognises
optionB: Both are updated along with the code
optionC: The comment is updated and the configuration file is not
optionD: The configuration file is updated and the comment is not
correctAnswerText: Both are left unchanged, since neither is a use the tool recognises
explanation: Neither a comment nor a configuration entry is code the tool resolves. Both have to be found and changed separately.

prompt: A developer renames a class through the editor, the project builds cleanly, and the application fails at start-up. The class name appears in a configuration file that is read at run time, and a rename changes only what the tool recognises as code. What happened?
optionA: The rename missed some of the code
optionB: The build succeeded incorrectly
optionC: The configuration still names the old class, and nothing checked it at build time
optionD: The new name conflicts with an existing one
correctAnswerText: The configuration still names the old class, and nothing checked it at build time
explanation: Building cleanly is exactly what makes this hard to anticipate. The configuration is read at run time and nothing connects it to the rename.

prompt: A terminal is opened inside an editor. Which directory does it usually start in?
optionA: The directory of the file currently open
optionB: The root of the project being edited
optionC: The user home directory
optionD: The directory where the editor is installed
correctAnswerText: The root of the project being edited
explanation: The project root is the common convention, and it need not match the open file. Which one a given tool uses is worth checking rather than assuming.

prompt: A file is open at a path several directories below the project root, and a terminal is opened inside the editor. A relative path that works when running from the file own directory is typed in. What happens?
optionA: It resolves from the file directory as intended
optionB: The terminal refuses the path
optionC: The terminal moves to the file directory automatically
optionD: It resolves from the project root instead and does not reach the intended file
correctAnswerText: It resolves from the project root instead and does not reach the intended file
explanation: The terminal location and the open file location are independent. A relative path is resolved from wherever the terminal actually is.

prompt: A command works when typed into the editor terminal and fails when a colleague runs the identical command from their own shell. The command contains a relative path and the two terminals were started in different directories. What is the cause?
optionA: The relative path resolves from a different directory in each case
optionB: The colleague lacks permission on the file
optionC: The editor modifies the command before running it
optionD: The command depends on the editor being open
correctAnswerText: The relative path resolves from a different directory in each case
explanation: The command line is identical and what it names is not. Using a path from the project root, or moving to a known directory first, removes the dependence.

prompt: A developer presses run in an editor. What executes the code?
optionA: The editor itself
optionB: The operating system directly
optionC: An interpreter or compiler installed separately, chosen by a setting
optionD: Whichever tool was used to write the code
correctAnswerText: An interpreter or compiler installed separately, chosen by a setting
explanation: The editor hands the work to something else and displays the result. Which something is a configuration choice.

prompt: Three versions of a language are installed on a machine. Which one runs the code when the developer presses run?
optionA: The newest installed version
optionB: Whichever the project or editor setting names
optionC: The oldest installed version
optionD: Whichever was installed most recently
correctAnswerText: Whichever the project or editor setting names
explanation: A setting decides, and it may name a version quite unlike what the developer expects. Nothing about being newest gives a version priority.

prompt: A developer installs a library and the editor still reports that it cannot be found when the code runs. The library was installed into one environment and the editor is configured to run the code with a different one. What is the cause?
optionA: The library failed to install
optionB: The editor needs restarting to see new libraries
optionC: The library is incompatible with the code
optionD: The library and the run configuration point at different environments
correctAnswerText: The library and the run configuration point at different environments
explanation: The install succeeded and put the library somewhere the running code never looks. Pointing the run configuration at the same environment resolves it.

prompt: A file shows no markers of any kind. What does that establish about running it?
optionA: Nothing; the tool found nothing it checks for
optionB: That it will run correctly
optionC: That it will compile and run without error
optionD: That it has been tested
correctAnswerText: Nothing; the tool found nothing it checks for
explanation: A clean file means the checks the tool performs found nothing. Whether the code does the right thing is not among those checks.

prompt: A file shows several markers and the program runs correctly. Is that contradictory?
optionA: Yes; a marked file cannot run correctly
optionB: Yes; the program must be failing silently
optionC: No; markers may report style preferences or checks the running code does not depend on
optionD: No, but only because the markers are stale
correctAnswerText: No; markers may report style preferences or checks the running code does not depend on
explanation: Plenty of markers report things that are not errors. The program running says nothing about whether the suggestions were worth taking.

prompt: A program fails when run, and the developer looks for a marked line to explain it. The file shows no markers at all. The tool reports nothing and the program failed at run time on something the tool does not check. What follows?
optionA: The tool has failed to update its markers
optionB: The fault is of a kind the tool does not examine, so the markers cannot help here
optionC: The program failure must be unrelated to the code
optionD: The file must be reopened for the markers to appear
correctAnswerText: The fault is of a kind the tool does not examine, so the markers cannot help here
explanation: Most run-time faults — a wrong value, a missing file, a bad assumption — are invisible to a tool reading the code. Looking to the markers for them is looking in the wrong place.

prompt: A developer installs an extension giving their editor knowledge of a language. What has become possible?
optionA: The language is now installed and can run code
optionB: Code in that language will now compile
optionC: The editor can run the code without anything else
optionD: The editor can understand and check code in that language
correctAnswerText: The editor can understand and check code in that language
explanation: The extension teaches the editor about the language. Running the code needs the language itself, installed separately.

prompt: A developer installs a language extension, writes code, and finds the editor understands it perfectly while pressing run produces an error saying the command is not found. What is missing?
optionA: The language itself, which the extension does not install
optionB: A second extension for running code
optionC: A restart of the editor
optionD: A project configuration file
correctAnswerText: The language itself, which the extension does not install
explanation: The two capabilities come from different places and are easy to conflate. Understanding the code and being able to execute it are separate installations.

prompt: A developer opens a file in a language for which no extension is installed. No markers appear anywhere in the file. Without an extension the editor has no knowledge of the language, so it has nothing to check the file against. What does the absence of markers establish?
optionA: That the file is free of errors
optionB: That the file is empty
optionC: Nothing at all; the editor has nothing to check the file against
optionD: That the file will run correctly
correctAnswerText: Nothing at all; the editor has nothing to check the file against
explanation: This is the strongest form of the trap: a clean file that has not been examined. Installing the extension often produces a page of markers on the same unchanged file.

prompt: A marker reports that a name cannot be found. The developer has just created that name in another file. What is the likely explanation?
optionA: The name was created incorrectly
optionB: The tool has not re-examined the project since the name was created
optionC: The name must be created in the same file
optionD: The tool has found a second name with the same spelling
correctAnswerText: The tool has not re-examined the project since the name was created
explanation: The tool reports what was true when it last looked. Prompting it to re-examine the project is the usual remedy.

prompt: A developer changes correct code to remove a marker, and the program stops working. The marker described the code as it had been several edits earlier and no longer applied. What went wrong?
optionA: The marker was accurate and the change was made incorrectly
optionB: The program failure is unrelated to the change
optionC: The marker should have been reported as an error rather than a warning
optionD: The marker was out of date and the code it described had already been corrected
correctAnswerText: The marker was out of date and the code it described had already been corrected
explanation: Editing working code to satisfy a stale claim is the expensive direction of this fault. Confirming that the marker still applies before acting on it is what prevents it.

prompt: Code runs correctly from a terminal and fails in the editor with an error about a missing library. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The editor is running the code with a different environment from the terminal
optionB: The library was never installed
optionC: The editor cannot run code with libraries
optionD: The code is different in the two cases
correctAnswerText: The editor is running the code with a different environment from the terminal
explanation: The same code succeeding in one place and failing in another points at what is running it. The library exists somewhere, or the terminal run would have failed too.

prompt: A developer follows an installation instruction, sees it report success, and the editor still cannot find the library. The install ran in one environment and the editor is configured to use another, and both are present on the machine. What should they check?
optionA: Whether the install genuinely succeeded
optionB: Whether the library supports their operating system
optionC: Which environment the editor is configured to use, and whether the install went to that one
optionD: Whether the editor needs reinstalling
correctAnswerText: Which environment the editor is configured to use, and whether the install went to that one
explanation: Both reports are accurate about different environments. Making the install and the run configuration agree is the whole of the fix.

prompt: A tool that checks for unused variables reports nothing on a file. What has been established?
optionA: That the file has no problems
optionB: That it found no unused variables
optionC: That every variable is used correctly
optionD: That the file is well written
correctAnswerText: That it found no unused variables
explanation: The claim is exactly as wide as what the tool checks. Everything outside that remains unexamined.

prompt: A team runs three tools over a file and all report nothing. They conclude the file is correct. The three tools between them check formatting, unused names and type consistency, and none examines whether the logic is right. What has been established?
optionA: That the file is correct
optionB: That the file has no faults of any kind
optionC: Nothing, since automated tools are unreliable
optionD: That the file passes those three kinds of check, which do not include whether it does the right thing
correctAnswerText: That the file passes those three kinds of check, which do not include whether it does the right thing
explanation: Three narrow checks passing is genuinely worth something and is not a verdict on behaviour. Tests are what examine whether the code does what was wanted.

prompt: A developer relies on the absence of markers as their only check before committing. Their editor has no extension installed for one of the languages in the project. Files in that language are never examined, and their cleanliness is indistinguishable from a file that has passed every check. What is the position?
optionA: Files in that language pass unchecked, and nothing in the editor distinguishes them from checked ones
optionB: All files are checked equally
optionC: Files in that language will show an error about the missing extension
optionD: The editor will refuse to open files it cannot check
correctAnswerText: Files in that language pass unchecked, and nothing in the editor distinguishes them from checked ones
explanation: The absence of a marker means the same thing visually whether the file passed or was never looked at. A check that runs outside the editor removes the ambiguity.

prompt: A team adds a rule that no code may be committed while any marker is showing. Some markers report genuine faults and others express style preferences that the team disagrees with. The rule treats a preference the team rejects and a genuine fault as equally blocking. What will happen?
optionA: Every genuine fault will be fixed before committing
optionB: The style preferences will gradually be adopted
optionC: People will silence the preferences they disagree with, and the habit will extend to genuine faults
optionD: Nothing; the rule is unambiguous and workable
correctAnswerText: People will silence the preferences they disagree with, and the habit will extend to genuine faults
explanation: A rule that blocks on things the team considers wrong teaches people to suppress markers. Configuring the tool to stop reporting the unwanted preferences keeps the rule meaningful.

prompt: A developer notices that a tool stops reporting a particular kind of problem after a configuration change somebody made months ago. The tool has been silent on that check since the change, and silence looks identical whether a check is passing or disabled. What follows about the intervening months?
optionA: The problems were fixed, which is why reporting stopped
optionB: Nothing was being checked, and every clean report since then said less than it appeared to
optionC: The tool has been failing and should be reinstalled
optionD: The check was reporting nothing because there was nothing to report
correctAnswerText: Nothing was being checked, and every clean report since then said less than it appeared to
explanation: A disabled check and a passing check produce the same silence. Reviewing what is enabled is the only way to tell one from the other.

prompt: A developer must find every place a method is called before changing its signature. The method has a common name that also appears in comments and inside longer words. The question is about calls to one specific method rather than about occurrences of the text. Which approach fits?
optionA: A text search for the method name
optionB: A text search restricted to one directory
optionC: Reading each file in the project
optionD: A usage report, which resolves the name rather than matching the text
correctAnswerText: A usage report, which resolves the name rather than matching the text
explanation: The text search would return a great deal that has nothing to do with the method. Reading every file would work and is the slowest route available.

prompt: A developer must find every place a configuration key is referenced. The key is named as a string in code and in several configuration files. The key exists only as text and is never a name the tool resolves. Which approach fits?
optionA: A text search, since the key is text everywhere it appears
optionB: A usage report, which understands the code
optionC: Following the key to its definition
optionD: Renaming the key and seeing what breaks
correctAnswerText: A text search, since the key is text everywhere it appears
explanation: Meaning-aware features resolve names in code and a string is not one. Renaming to see what breaks would work and destroys the running system to answer a question.

prompt: A developer must rename something referenced both as code and as a string in configuration. The name appears both as code the tool resolves and as text in files it does not. What approach fits?
optionA: The rename feature alone, which handles both
optionB: A text replacement alone, which handles both
optionC: The rename feature for the code, followed by a text search for the remaining occurrences
optionD: Neither; the name should not be changed
correctAnswerText: The rename feature for the code, followed by a text search for the remaining occurrences
explanation: Each instrument covers one half and neither covers both. A text replacement alone would also change coincidental matches inside longer words.

prompt: A developer can spend ten minutes learning a feature that would answer this question in seconds, or twenty minutes answering it by hand. They will face this question several times a week. The question recurs several times a week and the feature answers it in seconds. What follows?
optionA: Answer it by hand, since twenty minutes is not long
optionB: Learn the feature, since the cost is paid once and the saving recurs
optionC: Answer it by hand this time and learn the feature later
optionD: Neither; the question should be avoided
correctAnswerText: Learn the feature, since the cost is paid once and the saving recurs
explanation: A one-off cost against a recurring saving is settled by the recurrence. For a question asked once, doing it by hand would be the right answer.

prompt: A developer needs to know what a program actually does at a particular point. They can read the code carefully or run it and observe. The code is short and calls into several libraries whose behaviour they do not know. Reading the code would require understanding libraries they have never used. Which fits?
optionA: Reading it carefully, since reading is always more reliable
optionB: Reading it carefully, since the code is short
optionC: Neither; they should ask a colleague
optionD: Running it and observing, since reading requires knowledge they do not have
correctAnswerText: Running it and observing, since reading requires knowledge they do not have
explanation: Reading is the better route when the code is self-contained, and here it is not. The length of the code is not what makes it readable.

prompt: An unfamiliar tool advertises a check that reports every function never called from anywhere in the project. It reports three functions. The check examines calls it can resolve within the project and cannot see calls made from outside it. What has it established?
optionA: That three functions have no resolvable call within the project, which is narrower than being unused
optionB: That three functions are unused and can be deleted
optionC: That the project contains only three unnecessary functions
optionD: Nothing; such checks are unreliable
correctAnswerText: That three functions have no resolvable call within the project, which is narrower than being unused
explanation: Functions called from another project, from configuration or by name at run time are outside what it can see. The report is genuinely useful as a list of candidates to investigate.

prompt: An unfamiliar tool offers to apply a fix automatically wherever it finds a particular pattern. A developer applies it across a large project. The tool applies its change wherever the pattern matches, without regard to whether each match was intended to be that way. What should they do before accepting?
optionA: Accept it, since the tool found genuine matches
optionB: Accept it, since automatic fixes are tested by their authors
optionC: Review what it changed, since a matching pattern is not always a mistake
optionD: Reject it, since automatic fixes are never safe
correctAnswerText: Review what it changed, since a matching pattern is not always a mistake
explanation: The tool is right about the pattern and cannot know which occurrences were deliberate. Reviewing the change is the step that separates the two.

prompt: A developer moves to an unfamiliar editor and finds that a search returns far fewer results than the same search in their previous one. The new editor excludes files listed as ignored by the project, and the previous one did not. Which is right?
optionA: The previous editor, since more results is more complete
optionB: Neither; the two are answering different questions and the developer has to know which they want
optionC: The new editor, since ignored files should not be searched
optionD: The new editor, since fewer results are easier to read
correctAnswerText: Neither; the two are answering different questions and the developer has to know which they want
explanation: Searching generated files is sometimes exactly what is wanted and sometimes noise. Knowing which behaviour a tool has is what makes an empty result interpretable.

prompt: A team must decide whether their agreed checks should run in the editor, in a step everyone runs before committing, or both. Editor checks give immediate feedback and can be configured away individually, while a shared step runs the same way for everyone. Immediate feedback is per-developer and configurable, and the shared step is identical for everyone. Which fits a team that needs the checks actually applied?
optionA: The editor alone, since feedback is most useful while writing
optionB: The shared step alone, since it is the one that counts
optionC: Either, since the checks are the same
optionD: Both, with the shared step as the one that decides and the editor as the one that gives feedback early
correctAnswerText: Both, with the shared step as the one that decides and the editor as the one that gives feedback early
explanation: Each covers what the other cannot: the editor is fast and optional, the shared step is authoritative and late. Choosing one gives up either the speed or the guarantee.

prompt: Text can be written between single quotes or between double quotes. How do the two differ?
optionA: Single quotes hold text and double quotes hold formatted text
optionB: Only in which quote character they can contain without escaping
optionC: Double quotes allow longer text
optionD: Single quotes are faster to process
correctAnswerText: Only in which quote character they can contain without escaping
explanation: The two produce identical text. Which one is chosen matters only when the text itself contains a quote.

prompt: Which of these is a valid way to write text?
optionA: Opening with a single quote and closing with a double
optionB: Opening with a double quote and closing with a single
optionC: Opening and closing with no quote at all
optionD: Opening and closing with the same quote character
correctAnswerText: Opening and closing with the same quote character
explanation: The closing quote has to match the opening one. Mismatched quotes leave the literal unterminated.

prompt: Two pieces of text are written identically except that one uses single quotes and the other double. Are the resulting values the same?
optionA: Yes; the quote form is not part of the text
optionB: No; the quote characters are included in the value
optionC: No; one is longer than the other
optionD: Only if the text contains no letters
correctAnswerText: Yes; the quote form is not part of the text
explanation: Quotes mark where the text begins and ends and do not become part of it. The two values compare equal.

prompt: What decides which quote form to use for a piece of text?
optionA: The length of the text
optionB: Whether the text contains numbers
optionC: What quote characters the text itself contains
optionD: Personal preference alone, in every case
correctAnswerText: What quote characters the text itself contains
explanation: Choosing the form the text does not contain avoids escaping altogether. Where the text contains neither, preference genuinely does decide.

prompt: A piece of text contains both a single quote and a double quote. What follows about writing it with ordinary quotes?
optionA: It cannot be written at all
optionB: Whichever form is chosen, one of the two characters will need escaping
optionC: It must be split into two separate pieces
optionD: Single quotes will work without escaping
correctAnswerText: Whichever form is chosen, one of the two characters will need escaping
explanation: Containing both removes the option of picking the form the text avoids. A triple-quoted form is the other way out.

prompt: A backslash followed by the letter n appears inside a piece of text. What does that pair produce?
optionA: The two characters, a backslash and an n
optionB: A backslash only
optionC: An instruction that is removed with no character produced
optionD: A single line break character
correctAnswerText: A single line break character
explanation: The pair stands together for one character that is neither of the two written. That is the whole purpose of an escape.

prompt: How many characters does an escape sequence of a backslash and one letter produce?
optionA: One
optionB: Two
optionC: None
optionD: It depends on the letter
correctAnswerText: One
explanation: One character results, though two were written: the written form and the value differ in length.

prompt: How is a literal backslash written inside ordinary text?
optionA: As one backslash
optionB: As a backslash followed by a space
optionC: As two backslashes
optionD: A backslash cannot appear in text
correctAnswerText: As two backslashes
explanation: A single backslash begins an escape, so producing one requires escaping the backslash itself. The written form is twice the length of the result.

prompt: A student writes text containing a backslash and one letter, expecting to see both characters, and something else appears. What has happened?
optionA: The backslash was removed and the letter kept
optionB: The pair was read as an escape sequence and produced a different single character
optionC: The text was truncated at the backslash
optionD: The letter was removed and the backslash kept
correctAnswerText: The pair was read as an escape sequence and produced a different single character
explanation: Only some letters form an escape, which is why this surprises people unevenly. Doubling the backslash produces the two characters intended.

prompt: Two literals are written identically except that one carries a marker before its opening quote indicating interpolation. Both contain braces around a name. What differs?
optionA: Nothing; braces always interpolate
optionB: The unmarked one produces an error
optionC: The marked one is longer
optionD: The marked one replaces the braced section with a value; the unmarked one contains the braces as text
correctAnswerText: The marked one replaces the braced section with a value; the unmarked one contains the braces as text
explanation: Interpolation happens only when the literal is marked for it. Without the marker the braces are ordinary characters.

prompt: An unmarked literal contains braces around the word total. What does it produce?
optionA: The braces and the word total, as written
optionB: The value of a variable called total
optionC: An error, since total is not defined
optionD: An empty piece of text
correctAnswerText: The braces and the word total, as written
explanation: Without the interpolation marker nothing is substituted. The braces are characters like any others.

prompt: What makes a literal interpolate the values named inside it?
optionA: The presence of braces
optionB: The names inside being defined
optionC: A marker on the literal itself
optionD: The literal being assigned to a variable
correctAnswerText: A marker on the literal itself
explanation: The marker is what turns braces into substitution points. Defined names and braces alone change nothing.

prompt: A developer builds a message by joining two literals together with an operator, and the second literal is marked for interpolation while the first is not. What happens to braces in the first?
optionA: They interpolate, since the two are joined
optionB: They remain as literal braces, since the marker applies to one literal only
optionC: The join fails because the two forms differ
optionD: They are removed from the result
correctAnswerText: They remain as literal braces, since the marker applies to one literal only
explanation: Marking is a property of each literal rather than of the expression. Joining them does not spread the marker.

prompt: A name holds the value 7. An interpolating literal reads: Total: followed by braces around that name. What text is produced?
optionA: Total: name
optionB: Total: {7}
optionC: Total: "7"
optionD: Total: 7
correctAnswerText: Total: 7
explanation: The braced section is replaced by the value written out, and the surrounding text is kept. No quotes are added around a number.

prompt: A name holds a piece of text that was written between quotes in the source. When that name is substituted into an interpolating literal, does the output show the quotes?
optionA: No; the quotes marked where the text began and ended and were never part of it
optionB: Yes; text values are always written out with their quotes
optionC: Yes, but single quotes only
optionD: Only when the text contains a space
correctAnswerText: No; the quotes marked where the text began and ended and were never part of it
explanation: Quotes delimit a literal in the source and do not survive into the value. Substitution writes out what the value holds, which never included them.

prompt: A literal is marked raw. What does that change?
optionA: The text is displayed differently
optionB: The text cannot be changed afterwards
optionC: Backslashes are kept as backslashes rather than beginning escape sequences
optionD: Interpolation is disabled
correctAnswerText: Backslashes are kept as backslashes rather than beginning escape sequences
explanation: A raw literal changes what the written characters mean and not how the result is used. Every backslash stands for itself.

prompt: A Windows-style path with single backslashes is written as an ordinary literal and again as a raw one. How do the two results differ?
optionA: They are identical, since paths contain no escapes
optionB: The ordinary one has some backslash pairs converted to other characters; the raw one is as written
optionC: The raw one has its backslashes doubled
optionD: The ordinary one removes the backslashes entirely
correctAnswerText: The ordinary one has some backslash pairs converted to other characters; the raw one is as written
explanation: Only the pairs that form escapes are converted, so the ordinary literal is right in some places and wrong in others. That unevenness is what makes the fault confusing.

prompt: A triple-quoted literal spans three lines of text. What does it contain?
optionA: The three lines joined with spaces
optionB: The first line only
optionC: The three lines with the breaks removed
optionD: The three lines including the line breaks between them
correctAnswerText: The three lines including the line breaks between them
explanation: Line breaks inside a triple-quoted literal are part of the text. That is the reason for using the form.

prompt: A triple-quoted literal opens, then a line break, then the word Hello. What does the value begin with?
optionA: A line break, before the word Hello
optionB: The word Hello, with the break discarded
optionC: A space, then the word Hello
optionD: Nothing; the literal is empty until the second line
correctAnswerText: A line break, before the word Hello
explanation: The break immediately after the opening quotes is inside the literal like any other. Ending the first line with a backslash is the usual way to suppress it.

prompt: A triple-quoted literal is written inside an indented function, so every line after the first begins with eight spaces of indentation. A triple-quoted literal keeps every character between its quotes, including leading spaces. What does the value contain?
optionA: No leading spaces, since indentation is stripped
optionB: Eight spaces on the first line only
optionC: Eight spaces at the start of each of those lines
optionD: A single space at the start of each line
correctAnswerText: Eight spaces at the start of each of those lines
explanation: The indentation that makes the code readable becomes part of the text. Output that is mysteriously shifted to the right is the usual symptom.

prompt: A value of 3.14159 is placed into a literal with a format asking for two decimal places. What text appears?
explanation: The format controls how many decimal places are written out. The remaining digits are not shown.

prompt: Two values, 2.567 and 2.561, are each written out with a format asking for two decimal places. What do the two produce?
explanation: A precision rounds rather than cutting digits off, so the two go in different directions and give 2.57 and 2.56. Truncating both would have produced the same pair of digits twice.

prompt: A value of 12 is placed into a literal with a format asking for a width of five. A width pads a value that is shorter than the width and does not shorten one that is longer. What text appears?
optionA: The digits 12 padded out to five characters
optionB: The digits 12, unchanged
optionC: The digits 12 truncated to fit
optionD: Five copies of the digits 12
correctAnswerText: The digits 12 padded out to five characters
explanation: A width states a minimum rather than a maximum. A value longer than the width is written out in full.

prompt: The text "ab" is added to the text "cd". What is produced?
optionA: ab cd
optionB: The two kept separate
optionC: abcd
optionD: An error
correctAnswerText: abcd
explanation: Adding text joins the two with nothing between them. No separator is inserted.

prompt: The text "12" is added to the text "3". What is produced?
optionC: "12" and "3" as separate values
optionD: An error
explanation: Both operands are text, so they are joined rather than summed. Looking like numbers changes nothing about what they are.

prompt: A program reads two values typed by a user and adds them, producing 57 where 12 was expected. Values read from a user arrive as text, and adding text joins it rather than summing it. What were the two values?
optionA: 50 and 7, summed correctly
optionB: 5 and 7, summed incorrectly by the language
optionC: 57 and 0, entered as one value
optionD: 5 and 7, arriving as text and joined rather than summed
correctAnswerText: 5 and 7, arriving as text and joined rather than summed
explanation: Joining "5" and "7" gives "57", which is exactly what was seen. Converting each to a number before adding is the fix.

prompt: Two quoted pieces of text are written next to each other with nothing between them. What results?
optionA: One piece of text, being the two joined
optionB: Two separate pieces of text
optionC: An error, since no operator was given
optionD: The first piece only
correctAnswerText: One piece of text, being the two joined
explanation: Adjacent literals join automatically with no operator needed. This is deliberate and useful for splitting a long piece of text across lines.

prompt: A long message is written across three lines as three adjacent quoted pieces, each ending in a space. What results?
optionA: Three separate messages
optionB: One message with no spaces between the parts
optionC: One message with a space between each part
optionD: One message with a line break between the parts
correctAnswerText: One message with a space between each part
explanation: The pieces join exactly as written, so the trailing spaces survive and the line breaks in the source do not. Forgetting those spaces is how words run together.

prompt: A list is written with four quoted items and a comma is accidentally omitted between the second and third. Two quoted pieces with nothing between them join into one, and no comma separates the second and third items. How many items does the list hold?
optionA: Four, since all four are still written
optionB: Three, with the second and third joined into one
optionC: Two, since the missing comma splits the list
optionD: None; the list is invalid
correctAnswerText: Three, with the second and third joined into one
explanation: The join is silent and produces a perfectly valid list one item shorter than intended. Nothing reports an error, which is what makes this hard to spot.

prompt: A name holds a list of three numbers. It is placed into an interpolating literal. What appears?
optionA: The three numbers with spaces between them
optionB: The number of items in the list
optionC: An error, since a list is not text
optionD: The list written out, including its brackets and separators
correctAnswerText: The list written out, including its brackets and separators
explanation: Any value is written out in its usual form when substituted. The brackets are part of how a list is written.

prompt: A name holds the value representing absence of a value. It is placed into an interpolating literal. What appears?
optionA: The word that names that absence, written out as text
optionB: Nothing, leaving a gap
optionC: An empty pair of braces
optionD: An error, since there is no value to write
correctAnswerText: The word that names that absence, written out as text
explanation: The absence is itself a value with a written form, so it appears as a word in the output. A report reading "Owner: None" is the usual and confusing symptom.

prompt: A report is generated for every record and one field is sometimes unset. The output for those records reads oddly, with a word appearing where a name should be. Substituting an unset value writes out the word naming that absence rather than producing nothing. What is happening?
optionA: The field is being read from the wrong record
optionB: The literal is missing its interpolation marker
optionC: The unset value is being written out as a word rather than leaving a blank
optionD: The report is truncating the field
correctAnswerText: The unset value is being written out as a word rather than leaving a blank
explanation: Nothing fails, so every record generates a report and some of them contain a word no reader expects. Checking for the unset case and substituting a blank is the fix.

prompt: A literal is opened with a single quote and contains an apostrophe partway through. Where does the literal end?
optionA: At the closing quote at the end of the line
optionB: At the apostrophe, since it matches the opening quote
optionC: At the end of the line, wherever that falls
optionD: It does not end, and the file is truncated
correctAnswerText: At the apostrophe, since it matches the opening quote
explanation: The apostrophe is indistinguishable from a closing quote, so the literal ends there. Everything after it is read as something else entirely.

prompt: A developer writes a sentence containing an apostrophe inside single quotes and the file will not run. The apostrophe matches the opening quote and ends the literal early. What are the two ways to fix it?
optionA: Remove the apostrophe, or shorten the sentence
optionB: Use double quotes, or move the sentence to its own line
optionC: Escape the apostrophe, or remove the surrounding quotes
optionD: Use double quotes around the whole sentence, or escape the apostrophe
correctAnswerText: Use double quotes around the whole sentence, or escape the apostrophe
explanation: Either choosing a quote form the text does not contain, or escaping the offending character, resolves it. Removing the apostrophe changes the text rather than fixing the code.

prompt: A path written with single backslashes behaves wrongly, and inspecting it shows a line break where a backslash and the letter n were written. What happened?
optionA: That pair formed an escape sequence and became a line break
optionB: The path was truncated at the backslash
optionC: The backslash was removed entirely
optionD: The whole path was converted to a different form
correctAnswerText: That pair formed an escape sequence and became a line break
explanation: Only that pair was converted; the rest of the path is as written. A raw literal or doubled backslashes would have kept it intact.

prompt: Two paths written the same way behave differently: one works and one does not. Only some backslash-and-letter pairs form an escape sequence, and the two paths use different letters after their backslashes. Why do they differ?
optionA: One path is longer than the other
optionB: One path points at a file that does not exist
