optionC: One path happens to contain a pair that forms an escape and the other does not
optionD: The two were written with different quote forms
correctAnswerText: One path happens to contain a pair that forms an escape and the other does not
explanation: The behaviour depends on which letters follow the backslashes, which varies from path to path. That unevenness is why the fault appears to come and go.

prompt: A value is displayed rounded to two decimal places and then used in a later calculation. Which value does the calculation use?
optionA: The rounded value that was displayed
optionB: The original unrounded value
optionC: Whichever was used most recently
optionD: An average of the two
correctAnswerText: The original unrounded value
explanation: Formatting produces text and leaves the value untouched. Rounding the value itself is a separate operation.

prompt: Three amounts are each displayed rounded to two decimal places, and their total is computed from the unrounded values and displayed the same way. A reader adds the three displayed figures and gets a different answer. The three displayed figures are rounded individually while the total is computed from the unrounded values. Why do they disagree?
optionA: One of the three figures was displayed incorrectly
optionB: The total was computed from the wrong values
optionC: The rounding was applied twice to the total
optionD: The rounding of each figure is lost from the total, which was computed before any rounding
correctAnswerText: The rounding of each figure is lost from the total, which was computed before any rounding
explanation: Everything here is correct and the displayed figures cannot be expected to add up. Rounding each value before summing is what makes the report internally consistent.

prompt: A team fixes a report that did not add up by rounding each value before summing. An auditor objects that the total is now wrong. Rounding before summing makes the report add up and moves the total away from the exact figure. Who is right?
optionA: Both; the report is now internally consistent and its total no longer matches the exact figure
optionB: The team; a report that adds up is correct
optionC: The auditor; the total must always be exact
optionD: Neither; the two totals are identical
correctAnswerText: Both; the report is now internally consistent and its total no longer matches the exact figure
explanation: The two requirements genuinely conflict and only one can be satisfied. Which matters depends on whether the report is read by people adding columns or fed into something needing the exact figure.

prompt: A value is stored, displayed rounded, read back from the display by another system, and stored again. The value stored the second time came from the rounded text rather than from the original value. What has happened to the precision?
optionA: Nothing; formatting never changes a value
optionB: It is recoverable from the original store
optionC: It has been lost permanently, since the rounding became the stored value
optionD: It is halved with each round trip
correctAnswerText: It has been lost permanently, since the rounding became the stored value
explanation: Formatting leaves the value alone right up until the formatted text is read back as data. That round trip is where display rounding becomes real.

prompt: A developer displays a value with no format at all and finds it shows many more decimal places than expected. Displaying without a format writes out the value as it is actually held rather than as it was typed. What does that reveal?
optionA: A fault in the display
optionB: What the value actually holds, which differs from what was typed in
optionC: That the value has been corrupted
optionD: That a format is required for every value
correctAnswerText: What the value actually holds, which differs from what was typed in
explanation: The unformatted display is the honest one and the surprise is about how such values are stored. A format hides the difference rather than removing it.

prompt: A piece of text contains several single quotes and no double quotes. The text contains single quotes and no double quotes, and choosing the form the text avoids removes the need to escape anything. Which form fits?
optionA: Single quotes, with each internal quote escaped
optionB: Single quotes, with the internal quotes removed
optionC: Triple single quotes, with each internal quote escaped
optionD: Double quotes, with nothing escaped
correctAnswerText: Double quotes, with nothing escaped
explanation: Choosing the form the text does not contain is the simplest route and needs no escaping. Escaping works and produces a harder literal to read.

prompt: A piece of text is a Windows path ending in a backslash. A developer proposes a raw literal to avoid escaping. A raw literal cannot end in a single backslash, because that backslash would escape the closing quote. What follows?
optionA: A raw literal will not work here, so the backslashes must be doubled in an ordinary literal
optionB: A raw literal works and is the right choice
optionC: The path cannot be written in any form
optionD: A triple-quoted raw literal solves it
correctAnswerText: A raw literal will not work here, so the backslashes must be doubled in an ordinary literal
explanation: This is the one thing a raw literal cannot express, and it is exactly the case paths run into. Doubling the backslashes in an ordinary literal is the way out.

prompt: A message spans four lines and must preserve the line breaks. A developer proposes a triple-quoted literal placed inside a deeply indented block. A triple-quoted literal keeps the indentation of the lines it contains, and the block is deeply indented. What should they consider?
optionA: Nothing; indentation is stripped automatically
optionB: That triple quotes cannot be used inside an indented block
optionC: That the indentation will become part of the text and has to be removed or avoided
optionD: That the line breaks will be lost
correctAnswerText: That the indentation will become part of the text and has to be removed or avoided
explanation: The form is right for the requirement and brings the indentation with it. Dedenting afterwards, or writing the literal unindented, both address it.

prompt: A message is built from a fixed sentence and one value. A developer can use interpolation or join the parts with an operator. The value is a number and joining with an operator requires converting it to text first, while interpolation writes it out directly. Which fits?
optionA: Joining, since it is more explicit
optionB: Interpolation, since it writes the value out without a separate conversion
optionC: Joining, since interpolation is slower
optionD: Either; the two require the same amount of code
correctAnswerText: Interpolation, since it writes the value out without a separate conversion
explanation: Joining a number to text without converting it is an error, so the operator route carries an extra step. Both produce identical text once that step is taken.

prompt: A long piece of text must be written across several source lines without introducing line breaks into the value. Adjacent quoted pieces join with nothing between them, and a triple-quoted literal keeps every line break. Which form fits?
optionA: A triple-quoted literal spanning the lines
optionB: A triple-quoted raw literal spanning the lines
optionC: One very long line, since no other form works
optionD: Several adjacent quoted pieces, one per source line
correctAnswerText: Several adjacent quoted pieces, one per source line
explanation: Adjacency joins the pieces and the source line breaks are not part of any literal. A triple-quoted form would put every one of those breaks into the value.

prompt: A language is documented as follows: text is written between backticks; a backslash before any character produces that character literally; there is no interpolation. A literal is written containing a backslash followed by the letter n. The rules state that a backslash produces the following character literally, and there is no special meaning for any letter. What does the literal contain?
optionA: The letter n
optionB: A line break
optionC: A backslash and the letter n
optionD: Nothing; the escape is invalid
correctAnswerText: The letter n
explanation: These rules differ from the ones this skill has been using, and the stated rules are what govern. Assuming a line break would be importing a convention the description rules out.

prompt: A configuration format is documented as treating every value as literal text with no escape processing whatsoever. A developer writes a path containing backslashes into it. No escape processing occurs, so every character stands for itself. What does the value contain?
optionA: The path with escape sequences converted
optionB: The path with backslashes doubled
optionC: Exactly the characters written, backslashes included
optionD: An error, since backslashes must be escaped
correctAnswerText: Exactly the characters written, backslashes included
explanation: A format with no escape processing behaves like a raw literal everywhere. That also means there is no way to write a character the format uses structurally.

prompt: A template system is documented as substituting anything between double braces and leaving single braces alone. A developer writes a message containing a literal double brace they do not want substituted. Double braces are always substituted and the documentation describes no way to escape them. What follows?
optionA: Single braces should be used instead, which produce the same output
optionB: The message cannot express a literal double brace, so the format has to be extended or avoided
optionC: The double brace will be left alone since no name follows it
optionD: The system will report an error and leave the text unchanged
correctAnswerText: The message cannot express a literal double brace, so the format has to be extended or avoided
explanation: A format that reserves a sequence and offers no escape cannot express that sequence. Recognising the gap is the point; working around it is a separate decision.

prompt: A team must choose between a message format that substitutes values automatically and one that requires every value to be inserted explicitly. Messages sometimes contain characters the substituting format treats as structural. A format that substitutes automatically will act on those characters wherever they appear in the message. Which fits messages containing arbitrary user text?
optionA: The substituting form, since it is more convenient
optionB: The substituting form, since users rarely type such characters
optionC: Either, since both produce the same messages
optionD: The explicit form, since arbitrary text will otherwise collide with the structural characters
correctAnswerText: The explicit form, since arbitrary text will otherwise collide with the structural characters
explanation: Automatic substitution is convenient right up until the content contains what the format reserves. Arbitrary user text is precisely the case where that stops being rare.

prompt: A page control can only be operated by clicking it with a mouse. Who is prevented from using it?
optionA: Anyone using a screen reader only
optionB: Anyone navigating by keyboard
optionC: Anyone with a small screen
optionD: Anyone on a slow connection
correctAnswerText: Anyone navigating by keyboard
explanation: The barrier is about how the control is operated rather than how it is perceived. People navigate by keyboard for many reasons, including motor difficulties and simple preference.

prompt: A status is shown only by making a row red or green. Who is prevented from reading it?
optionA: Anyone navigating by keyboard
optionB: Anyone using a large screen
optionC: Nobody; colour is universally understood
optionD: Anyone who cannot distinguish those colours, and anyone hearing the page read aloud
correctAnswerText: Anyone who cannot distinguish those colours, and anyone hearing the page read aloud
explanation: Two separate groups are affected by the same fault. Colour vision and non-visual reading are different situations with the same consequence here.

prompt: An image conveys information and carries no description. Who is prevented from getting that information?
optionA: Anyone who cannot see the image
optionB: Anyone navigating by keyboard
optionC: Anyone who cannot distinguish colours
optionD: Anyone using an old browser
correctAnswerText: Anyone who cannot see the image
explanation: A missing description affects people who do not receive the image itself. Keyboard use and colour vision are unrelated to it.

prompt: What identifies something as an accessibility barrier?
optionA: That the page looks unpolished
optionB: That the page is slow to load
optionC: That a described person cannot do or learn something others can
optionD: That the page has not been tested
correctAnswerText: That a described person cannot do or learn something others can
explanation: A barrier is stated as who is prevented from what. Whether a page looks acceptable is a separate judgement entirely.

prompt: A team fixes every missing image description and declares the page accessible. What is wrong with the conclusion?
optionA: Nothing; image descriptions are the whole of accessibility
optionB: One barrier has been removed and others — keyboard reach, focus order, colour alone — were never examined
optionC: The descriptions should have been checked by a specialist
optionD: The page cannot be accessible until it is retested for speed
correctAnswerText: One barrier has been removed and others — keyboard reach, focus order, colour alone — were never examined
explanation: Image descriptions address people who cannot see images and nobody else. A page can have perfect descriptions and be entirely unusable by keyboard.

prompt: A chart shows the sales figures being discussed, and the figures appear nowhere else on the page. Should it be described?
optionA: No; charts are decorative
optionB: No; the surrounding text is enough
optionC: Only if the page has no other images
optionD: Yes; it carries information available nowhere else
correctAnswerText: Yes; it carries information available nowhere else
explanation: The chart is the only source of those figures, so a reader who cannot see it loses them. That is what makes an image meaningful rather than decorative.

prompt: A decorative swirl separates two sections and carries no information. Should it be described?
optionA: No; it should be passed over silently
optionB: Yes; every image should be described
optionC: Yes; it should be described as a swirl
optionD: Yes; it should be described as decorative
correctAnswerText: No; it should be passed over silently
explanation: Describing it inserts noise into the reading of the page. Being passed over is the correct treatment for an image that says nothing.

prompt: What decides whether an image needs describing?
optionA: How large the image is
optionB: How many images the page contains
optionC: Whether it carries information the reader would otherwise lose
optionD: Whether the image loads quickly
correctAnswerText: Whether it carries information the reader would otherwise lose
explanation: The test is what would be missing without it. Size and quantity have nothing to do with it.

prompt: A team adds a description to every image on the page, including forty decorative dividers. What is the consequence for someone hearing the page read aloud?
optionA: Nothing; more description is always better
optionB: Forty meaningless announcements interrupt the content
optionC: The page becomes faster to navigate
optionD: The decorative images are skipped automatically
correctAnswerText: Forty meaningless announcements interrupt the content
explanation: Every description is read out, so describing nothing-in-particular forty times buries the content. Conscientiousness applied without judgement makes the page worse.

prompt: A page uses a genuine button element for an action. Can a keyboard user reach and operate it?
optionA: No; buttons require a mouse
optionB: Only if extra code is added
optionC: Only if the button carries a description
optionD: Yes; a button is reachable and operable by keyboard as it stands
correctAnswerText: Yes; a button is reachable and operable by keyboard as it stands
explanation: Elements that exist to be operated come with keyboard behaviour already. That is the main practical reason to use them.

prompt: A page makes a plain area of the layout clickable by attaching code to it. Can a keyboard user reach it?
optionA: No; a plain area is not something the keyboard stops at
optionB: Yes; anything clickable is keyboard reachable
optionC: Yes, if it is styled to look like a button
optionD: Only on a page with no other controls
correctAnswerText: No; a plain area is not something the keyboard stops at
explanation: Attaching a click handler adds mouse behaviour and nothing else. The element remains ordinary layout as far as the keyboard is concerned.

prompt: What makes a control reachable by keyboard?
optionA: Being visible on the page
optionB: Being styled to look interactive
optionC: Being the kind of element the keyboard stops at, or being explicitly made one
optionD: Having a click handler attached
correctAnswerText: Being the kind of element the keyboard stops at, or being explicitly made one
explanation: Reachability follows from what the element is rather than how it looks or what code it carries. Styling and handlers are both invisible to keyboard navigation.

prompt: A developer styles a plain area to look exactly like the page other buttons and attaches a click handler. A reviewer using a mouse finds no difference between it and the real buttons. What has the review missed?
optionA: That it is styled differently from the real buttons
optionB: That the keyboard never stops at it, which a mouse review cannot reveal
optionC: That the click handler is slower than a real button
optionD: Nothing; it is equivalent to a real button
correctAnswerText: That the keyboard never stops at it, which a mouse review cannot reveal
explanation: A mouse review exercises the one route that works. The fault is invisible until somebody tries to reach the control another way.

prompt: A page uses heading levels one, two, two, three, two. What does that sequence describe?
optionA: Five sections of equal importance
optionB: A section with four subsections
optionC: Nothing; the sequence is invalid
optionD: A top-level section with three subsections, the first of which has a subsection of its own
correctAnswerText: A top-level section with three subsections, the first of which has a subsection of its own
explanation: Levels state nesting, so each level two opens a subsection of the level one and the level three sits inside the first of them. The sequence is entirely well formed.

prompt: A page uses heading levels one, four, two. What is the problem with jumping from one to four?
optionA: It claims two intervening levels of nesting that do not exist, so the structure is misleading
optionB: Nothing; heading levels may be used in any order
optionC: The page will not display correctly
optionD: Level four headings are not permitted on a page
correctAnswerText: It claims two intervening levels of nesting that do not exist, so the structure is misleading
explanation: Someone navigating by structure is told there are two enclosing levels between them. The page displays perfectly and describes itself wrongly.

prompt: A button shows only a pencil icon and carries no text of any kind. What is announced to somebody hearing the page?
optionA: That there is a pencil icon
optionB: That there is an edit button
optionC: That there is a button, with nothing to say what it does
optionD: Nothing; the button is skipped
correctAnswerText: That there is a button, with nothing to say what it does
explanation: The icon is a picture and conveys nothing to a non-visual reader. The control is reachable and unidentifiable, which is worse than being absent.

prompt: A row of five icon-only buttons carries no text. What does somebody hearing the page encounter?
optionA: Five buttons, distinguishable by their position
optionB: Five buttons, none of which can be told apart
optionC: One button, since the five are identical
optionD: Nothing, since the buttons carry no text
correctAnswerText: Five buttons, none of which can be told apart
explanation: Each is announced as a button and nothing distinguishes them. Guessing which is which by counting positions is not something the page has offered.

prompt: A page contains three controls, appearing in the markup in the order A, B, C, and displayed on screen in that same order. In what order does keyboard focus visit them?
optionA: C, then B, then A
optionB: Whichever is visually closest to the top
optionC: In a random order
optionD: A, then B, then C
correctAnswerText: A, then B, then C
explanation: Focus follows the order in the markup, which here matches the visual order. The two agreeing is what makes ordinary pages behave predictably.

prompt: Three controls appear in the markup in the order A, B, C. Styling places them on screen in the order C, A, B. In what order does keyboard focus visit them?
optionA: A, then B, then C, following the markup rather than the screen
optionB: C, then A, then B, following the screen
optionC: In whichever order they were styled
optionD: Focus visits only the first of the three
correctAnswerText: A, then B, then C, following the markup rather than the screen
explanation: Focus follows the markup and the eye follows the screen, so the two disagree here. A sighted keyboard user watches the focus jump around the page.

prompt: A form is laid out in two visual columns. In the markup, every field of the left column comes first, followed by every field of the right. Focus follows the markup, in which the whole left column precedes the whole right column. A visitor tabbing through expects to move across each row. What do they experience?
optionA: Focus travels across each row as expected
optionB: Focus visits the left column only
optionC: Focus travels down the whole left column before returning to the top of the right
optionD: Focus travels down the right column first
correctAnswerText: Focus travels down the whole left column before returning to the top of the right
explanation: The visual arrangement suggests rows and the markup describes columns. Reordering the markup, rather than restyling, is what aligns the two.

prompt: A table marks overdue rows in red and current rows in green, with no other difference between them. What information is lost to someone who cannot distinguish those colours?
optionA: The contents of the rows
optionB: Which rows are overdue
optionC: The order of the rows
optionD: Nothing at all
correctAnswerText: Which rows are overdue
explanation: The colour is the only carrier of the status, so the status is what disappears. Everything else in the row is still readable.

prompt: A table marks overdue rows in red and also labels each one "Overdue" in a status column. Is this a fault?
optionA: Yes; colour should never be used to convey status
optionB: Yes; the label duplicates the colour unnecessarily
optionC: Only if the red is too pale
optionD: No; the colour is redundant and the information is carried in text as well
correctAnswerText: No; the colour is redundant and the information is carried in text as well
explanation: Colour used alongside another signal is a help rather than a barrier. Removing it would make the table harder for sighted readers and easier for nobody.

prompt: A form marks fields with errors by turning their borders red, and adds no other indication. A visitor reports submitting repeatedly without knowing what was wrong. The red border is the only indication of which fields are at fault and it is a purely visual one. What is the fault?
optionA: The error is conveyed by colour alone, so anyone not perceiving it has nothing to go on
optionB: The red is not bright enough to notice
optionC: The form should not have refused the submission
optionD: The fields should have been marked before submission
correctAnswerText: The error is conveyed by colour alone, so anyone not perceiving it has nothing to go on
explanation: The visitor is told something is wrong and never which field or why. A message associated with each faulty field carries the information regardless of colour.

prompt: A page contains six links, each reading "click here". Read out on their own, what do they convey?
optionA: Their destinations, from the surrounding sentences
optionB: That they are all the same link
optionC: Nothing about where any of them goes
optionD: That the page has six sections
correctAnswerText: Nothing about where any of them goes
explanation: Listing links is a common way of navigating, and six identical entries distinguish nothing. The surrounding sentence is not part of the link.

prompt: Which link text works when read on its own, away from its sentence?
optionA: "Read more"
optionB: "Download the 2024 annual report"
optionC: "Here"
optionD: "This document"
correctAnswerText: "Download the 2024 annual report"
explanation: Only the first names its destination without help. The other three depend entirely on text that does not travel with them.

prompt: A results table gives every row a link reading "View". A team argues the row makes the destination obvious. A list of the links on the page shows the link text without the row it sat in. What is the difficulty?
optionA: The word View is too short to be a link
optionB: The links should open in a new window
optionC: Nothing; the row supplies the context
optionD: Listed on their own, every link reads identically and none can be told from another
correctAnswerText: Listed on their own, every link reads identically and none can be told from another
explanation: Within the row the meaning is clear and the row is exactly what is lost. Naming the subject in each link, visibly or otherwise, is what makes the list usable.

prompt: A form shows an error message in small text at the top of the page after a failed submission. A visitor hearing the page is left at the submit button. What is the difficulty?
optionA: Nothing draws their attention to the message, which is now far from where they are
optionB: The message is too small to read
optionC: The message should be at the bottom instead
optionD: Nothing; the message is on the page
correctAnswerText: Nothing draws their attention to the message, which is now far from where they are
explanation: Being present on the page and being noticed are different things. Somebody reading sequentially has no reason to go back up.

prompt: A form marks a faulty field with a message placed immediately beside it, associated with the field. What does a visitor hearing the page get when they reach that field?
optionA: The field and its name only
optionB: The message only
optionC: The field, its name and the message describing what is wrong
optionD: Nothing, since messages are visual
correctAnswerText: The field, its name and the message describing what is wrong
explanation: Associating the message with the field makes it part of what the field announces. Placement beside it is what helps a sighted reader.

prompt: A form reports errors by scrolling to the first faulty field and turning its border red, without moving keyboard focus or announcing anything. A visitor hearing the page and navigating by keyboard is not moved and is told nothing. What do they experience?
optionA: A clear indication of which field is wrong
optionB: A submission that appears to do nothing at all
optionC: A message read out automatically
optionD: The form being submitted successfully
correctAnswerText: A submission that appears to do nothing at all
explanation: The page changed in ways that reach only a sighted mouse user. Moving focus to the faulty field would carry both the location and its message.

prompt: A company logo appears in the page header as decoration beside the company name in text. How should it be treated?
optionA: Described as the company logo
optionB: Described with the company name
optionC: Described as a decorative image
optionD: Passed over silently, since the name is already present as text
correctAnswerText: Passed over silently, since the name is already present as text
explanation: Describing it would announce the company name twice in succession. The text beside it already carries the information.

prompt: The same company logo is the entire content of a link to the home page, with no text beside it. How should it be treated now?
optionA: Described by where the link goes, since it is the only content the link has
optionB: Passed over silently, as before
optionC: Described as the company logo
optionD: Described as a decorative image
correctAnswerText: Described by where the link goes, since it is the only content the link has
explanation: The image is now carrying the name of a control rather than decorating one. A silently passed over image would leave the link announcing nothing.

prompt: A magnifying-glass icon is the whole content of a button that runs a search. A team describes it as "magnifying glass". The icon is the only content of the button, and what a user needs to know is what pressing it does. What should it be described as?
optionA: A magnifying glass, since that is what the image shows
optionB: A search icon, since that names the image accurately
optionC: What the button does, since the description is naming a control rather than a picture
optionD: Nothing, since icons are decorative
correctAnswerText: What the button does, since the description is naming a control rather than a picture
explanation: Describing the picture tells the user what they cannot see and not what they can do. When an image is a control, its description is the control name.

prompt: A control works perfectly with a mouse and cannot be reached by keyboard at all. It is built from a plain layout element with a click handler. What is the cause?
optionA: The click handler is written incorrectly
optionB: The element is not a kind the keyboard stops at
optionC: The control is styled to hide it from the keyboard
optionD: The browser does not support keyboard navigation
correctAnswerText: The element is not a kind the keyboard stops at
explanation: A click handler adds one route and creates none for the keyboard. Using a real button, or explicitly making the element focusable and operable, is the repair.

prompt: A menu opens on hover and closes as soon as the pointer leaves it. A keyboard user cannot open it at all. The menu opens only in response to a pointer hovering, and a keyboard produces no hover. What is the cause?
optionA: The menu items are not focusable
optionB: The menu closes too quickly to use
optionC: The menu is positioned outside the page
optionD: Opening is tied to an interaction the keyboard cannot produce
correctAnswerText: Opening is tied to an interaction the keyboard cannot produce
explanation: Even perfectly focusable items are unreachable inside a menu that never opens. Opening on focus as well as on hover is what makes both routes work.

prompt: A developer uses a heading element for a line of bold text that is not a heading, because it produced the right size. What does the page now claim?
optionA: That a new section begins there, which is untrue
optionB: Nothing; the size is all that changed
optionC: That the text is important
optionD: That the text should be read first
correctAnswerText: That a new section begins there, which is untrue
explanation: Choosing an element for its appearance puts a false statement into the structure. Anyone navigating by heading is offered a section that does not exist.

prompt: A page lays out a set of related items using a table, because the columns line up neatly. The items have no row-and-column relationship. A table states that its cells are related by row and column, and these items have no such relationship. What does the page claim?
optionA: Nothing; a table is a layout choice
optionB: That the items are in a particular order
optionC: That the items stand in a row-and-column relationship they do not have
optionD: That the items are of equal importance
correctAnswerText: That the items stand in a row-and-column relationship they do not have
explanation: Somebody navigating a table is told which column and row each cell belongs to, and the answers are meaningless here. Layout that carries no relationship should not use an element that asserts one.

prompt: A page presents a chart visually and the same figures in a table below it. Is a reader who cannot see the chart at a disadvantage in what they can learn?
optionA: Yes; they cannot see the chart
optionB: No; the figures are available to both, though the experience differs
optionC: Yes; a table is harder to read than a chart
optionD: No; the two experiences are identical
correctAnswerText: No; the figures are available to both, though the experience differs
explanation: Equivalence is about what can be learned rather than about having the same experience. Both readers can obtain every figure.

prompt: A page offers a phone number for anyone who cannot use its booking form. A team calls this equivalent access. Using the phone route requires another person to act, and the form does not. Is it equivalent?
optionA: Yes; both routes result in a booking
optionB: Yes, provided the phone line is always staffed
optionC: No; a phone number is never an acceptable alternative
optionD: No; one route requires another person and the other does not
correctAnswerText: No; one route requires another person and the other does not
explanation: A route that depends on somebody else answering is not the same as one the person completes themselves. It is a genuine fallback and not equivalence.

prompt: A team builds a separate simplified version of the site for people using screen readers. It carries the same content and is updated less often than the main site. The two versions carry the same content today, and only one of them is updated regularly. What is the difficulty?
optionA: The two will diverge, and the people on the simplified version will silently get older information
optionB: Nothing; a separate version is a reasonable solution
optionC: The simplified version will be too slow
optionD: Screen reader users prefer the main site
correctAnswerText: The two will diverge, and the people on the simplified version will silently get older information
explanation: Equivalence today is not equivalence next month, and the divergence is invisible to the people affected by it. One site that works for everybody has no such drift.

prompt: A video carries captions and no transcript. A team asks whether that is sufficient. Captions appear synchronised with the video and cannot be searched or read at the reader own pace. Who is still not served?
optionA: Nobody; captions cover the requirement
optionB: Only people who cannot hear
optionC: Anyone who cannot hear and cannot see, and anyone wanting to search or skim the content
optionD: Only people on slow connections
correctAnswerText: Anyone who cannot hear and cannot see, and anyone wanting to search or skim the content
explanation: Captions serve people who can see and not hear, which is a real and partial win. A transcript reaches people using braille output and everyone who would rather read than watch.

prompt: A page is fully operable by keyboard, and reaching the main content requires tabbing through sixty navigation links on every page. A keyboard user passes sixty controls before reaching the content, and a mouse user passes none. Is the page equivalent?
optionA: Yes; everything is reachable by keyboard
optionB: Not in practice; the same information is reachable at a cost nobody else pays
optionC: Yes, since sixty links is not many
optionD: No; the page is not operable by keyboard at all
correctAnswerText: Not in practice; the same information is reachable at a cost nobody else pays
explanation: Reachability is satisfied and the cost is not shared. A link that jumps straight to the main content removes the difference at almost no expense.

prompt: A control cannot be reached by keyboard because it is built from a plain layout element. Four changes are proposed. The barrier is that the keyboard never stops at the element, and only a change to what the element is can alter that. Which removes the barrier?
optionA: Increasing its contrast against the background
optionB: Adding a description to it
optionC: Making it larger and easier to click
optionD: Replacing it with a real button element
correctAnswerText: Replacing it with a real button element
explanation: All four are genuine improvements and three of them address different barriers. Only changing what the element is affects whether the keyboard stops there.

prompt: Status is conveyed by row colour alone. A team proposes darkening the colours so they are easier to distinguish. Darkening changes which colours are used and leaves colour as the only carrier of the status. Does that remove the barrier?
optionA: No; the information is still carried by colour alone
optionB: Yes; the colours will now be distinguishable
optionC: Yes, provided the contrast is checked
optionD: No; the rows should be reordered instead
correctAnswerText: No; the information is still carried by colour alone
explanation: Improving contrast helps people with low vision and is worth doing. It does nothing for somebody who cannot distinguish hues, or for anyone hearing the page.

prompt: A page has a barrier for keyboard users. A team proposes hiding the affected control from screen readers so that it is not announced. Hiding the control removes the announcement and leaves the control unreachable by keyboard. What does that achieve?
optionA: It removes the barrier for both groups
optionB: It removes the barrier for screen reader users only
optionC: It hides the symptom from one group and removes the function from another
optionD: Nothing at all; the page is unchanged
correctAnswerText: It hides the symptom from one group and removes the function from another
explanation: Hiding something that does not work is a way of removing the evidence rather than the fault. Keyboard users are still unable to reach it and now nobody is told it exists.

prompt: A team can fix a barrier affecting a small number of users at significant cost, or fix three smaller barriers affecting many users at the same cost. The single barrier prevents its users from completing the task at all, while the three make the task slower. One group cannot complete the task and the other is merely slowed. What should decide?
optionA: The number of users affected, which favours the three
optionB: That one group cannot complete the task at all, which outranks inconvenience to a larger group
optionC: The cost, which is the same either way
optionD: Neither; both should be deferred until cheaper
correctAnswerText: That one group cannot complete the task at all, which outranks inconvenience to a larger group
explanation: Counting affected users treats prevention and inconvenience as the same quantity. Being unable to complete a task is a different kind of harm from taking longer over it.

prompt: An automated checker reports no problems on a page. A team concludes the page is accessible. The checker examines what can be determined from the markup and cannot judge whether a description is meaningful or an order is sensible. What has been established?
optionA: That the page is accessible
optionB: That the page has no barriers for screen reader users
optionC: Nothing; automated checkers are useless
optionD: That the page passes the checks the tool performs, which are a subset of what matters
correctAnswerText: That the page passes the checks the tool performs, which are a subset of what matters
explanation: Automated checking genuinely catches missing descriptions and unlabelled controls, which is worth having. Whether a description says anything useful is not something a tool can decide.

prompt: A ticket machine presents every option on a touchscreen and has no physical buttons. The screen requires the user to see where to touch, and the machine offers no other way to select an option. Who is prevented from using it?
optionA: Anyone who cannot see the screen
optionB: Anyone unfamiliar with ticket machines
optionC: Anyone in a hurry
optionD: Nobody; touchscreens are universally usable
correctAnswerText: Anyone who cannot see the screen
explanation: The barrier is the same as an unlabelled control on a page, in a machine with no markup at all. A physical keypad or audio guidance is the equivalent remedy.

prompt: A telephone menu system announces its options and requires a response within three seconds. A caller who needs longer to process the options is cut off before choosing. The options are announced once and the response window is fixed at three seconds. What is the barrier?
optionA: The menu has too many options
optionB: The announcements are too quiet
optionC: A fixed time limit that some callers cannot meet, with no way to repeat the options
optionD: Nothing; three seconds is a reasonable time
correctAnswerText: A fixed time limit that some callers cannot meet, with no way to repeat the options
explanation: This is a time limit with no extension, which is a recognised barrier on a page as well. Allowing the options to be repeated, or removing the limit, is the remedy.

prompt: A printed form asks respondents to tick a box in one of two coloured columns, with no other label distinguishing them. A team argues that a printed form is outside the scope of accessibility work. The two columns are distinguished by colour alone and carry no other label. Is the argument sound?
optionA: Yes; accessibility applies to digital products
optionB: No; the barrier is the same one, and being printed does not change who it excludes
optionC: Yes, provided a digital version is also offered
optionD: No; printed forms should not use colour at all
correctAnswerText: No; the barrier is the same one, and being printed does not change who it excludes
explanation: The medium changes the remedy and not the reasoning. A heading on each column removes the barrier as surely as a text label removes it on a page.

prompt: A team must decide whether to build accessibility into a new product from the start or to audit and remedy it before release. Retrofitting has previously required changing the structure of pages rather than their styling. Barriers of this kind live in the structure, and changing structure late is far more expensive than choosing it early. Which fits?
optionA: Auditing before release, since it can be done once for the whole product
optionB: Auditing before release, since the product may change during development
optionC: Either, since the resulting product is the same
optionD: Building it in from the start, since the barriers live in decisions made early
correctAnswerText: Building it in from the start, since the barriers live in decisions made early
explanation: The resulting product can indeed be the same, which is why cost is what decides. Element choices and focus order are structural, and structure is what a late remedy has to unpick.

prompt: Two programs are running at the same time. Which of these is the operating system's job?
optionA: Checking the spelling of text typed into one of them
optionB: Deciding which of them uses the processor next
optionC: Working out the answer to a calculation one of them performs
optionD: Deciding which of them matters more to the person's work
correctAnswerText: Deciding which of them uses the processor next
explanation: Sharing the processor between programs is the operating system's decision. Spell-checking belongs to the application, the arithmetic is carried out by the processor itself, and how much a program matters to someone is a judgement the operating system has no basis for.

prompt: A program is closed. Which of these does the operating system do?
optionA: Deletes the files the program created
optionB: Removes the program from the machine
optionC: Saves whatever the person had not yet saved
optionD: Reclaims the memory the program was using
correctAnswerText: Reclaims the memory the program was using
explanation: Memory handed to a program is taken back when it ends, so another program can use it. Closing a program does not delete its files, uninstall it, or save work on the person's behalf — each of those is a separate action somebody has to ask for.

prompt: A program asks to save a file. Which part decides where on the storage device the data is actually placed?
optionA: The operating system
optionB: The program that asked to save it
optionC: The person, through the name they gave the file
optionD: The storage device itself, with no software involved
correctAnswerText: The operating system
explanation: The program says what to save and under what name; where those bytes physically land is the operating system's decision, because it is the part that keeps track of what the device already holds. The name the person chose is a label, not a location.

prompt: Which of these is an operating system?
optionA: Firefox
optionB: Microsoft Word
optionC: Linux
optionD: File Explorer
correctAnswerText: Linux
explanation: Linux manages the machine and everything else runs on top of it. A browser and a word processor are plainly applications; a file manager is the harder case, because it arrives with the system and looks like part of it, but it is an application that asks the operating system to do the work.

prompt: Three of these are operating systems. Which one is not?
optionA: Android
optionB: File Explorer
optionC: Windows
optionD: macOS
correctAnswerText: File Explorer
explanation: File Explorer is a program for browsing files; the operating system underneath it is what actually reads the disk. Android, Windows and macOS each manage a machine's resources for every other program on it.

prompt: A phone runs Android and a laptop runs Windows. What kind of software are both of these?
optionA: Applications the owner chose to install
optionB: Web browsers
optionC: Device drivers
optionD: Operating systems
correctAnswerText: Operating systems
explanation: Both manage their machine's processor, memory, storage and devices on behalf of everything else running there, which is what makes something an operating system. A driver is a much smaller piece of software that handles one device, under the operating system.

prompt: A machine already has Windows installed. Linux is then installed alongside it, and the person chooses between the two each time the machine starts. Which statement is correct?
optionA: Both are operating systems, and only one manages the machine at a time
optionB: Linux becomes an application running inside Windows
optionC: The machine now has two file managers but still one operating system
optionD: Windows must be removed before Linux can manage the machine
correctAnswerText: Both are operating systems, and only one manages the machine at a time
explanation: An operating system takes charge of the whole machine, so two of them cannot be in charge at once — but both can be installed, with the choice made at startup. Neither is running inside the other, and neither has to be removed for the other to work.

prompt: A text editor is installed on a machine, but nobody has opened it. What is the correct term for the editor as it sits on the disk?
optionA: A process
optionB: A driver
optionC: A program
optionD: A directory
correctAnswerText: A program
explanation: On disk it is a program: a stored set of instructions, doing nothing. It only becomes a process once it is loaded and running.

prompt: Someone opens that text editor and it appears on screen. What is the correct term for the copy now running in memory?
optionA: A program
optionB: A process
optionC: A file
optionD: An operating system
correctAnswerText: A process
explanation: The running copy is a process — the program in execution, with memory of its own. The program is still on the disk, unchanged, and could be started again as a second process.

prompt: Which statement uses the terms "program" and "process" correctly?
optionA: A process is stored on disk; a program is that process running in memory
optionB: A program and a process are two names for the same thing
optionC: A process is a program that has finished running
optionD: A program is stored on disk; a process is that program running in memory
correctAnswerText: A program is stored on disk; a process is that program running in memory
explanation: The distinction is between the stored instructions and a running copy of them. Swapping the terms, treating them as synonyms, or attaching "process" to something that has ended all lose the one difference the words exist to mark.

prompt: What does a directory actually contain?
optionA: Entries naming the files and directories inside it
optionB: The data of every file inside it, joined together
optionC: Only files, never other directories
optionD: A copy of each file inside it
correctAnswerText: Entries naming the files and directories inside it
explanation: A directory holds names and references, not the data itself — which is why moving a file between directories does not touch its contents. Directories can also contain other directories, which is what makes the structure a tree.

prompt: Which of these reliably tells you that something is a file rather than a directory?
optionA: Its name ends with a dot and an extension
optionB: Its name is longer than a directory's would be
optionC: Nothing in the name does; the system records which it is
optionD: It appears lower down in a listing
correctAnswerText: Nothing in the name does; the system records which it is
explanation: An extension is part of a name and nothing more — a directory may be named with one and a file may have none. Which of the two something is, is recorded by the system, not inferred from how the name looks.

prompt: A machine is switched on and someone immediately tries to open a spreadsheet application. Why can it not start yet?
optionA: The application loads the operating system, and that takes time
optionB: The operating system it depends on is not running yet
optionC: The application's own files have not been read from the disk yet
optionD: The processor has not finished its first calculation
correctAnswerText: The operating system it depends on is not running yet
explanation: An application needs the operating system for everything it does — memory, files, the screen — so it cannot run before the operating system does. The dependency runs one way: the operating system does not wait for the application, and the application does not load it.

prompt: A file can be renamed by typing a command, or by clicking it and typing a new name. What is happening in the two cases?
optionA: The typed command changes the file directly, while the click asks the operating system to
optionB: Each interface keeps its own separate record of the files
optionC: The typed command does something the graphical interface is unable to do
optionD: The same operating system service is asked to do the same thing, in two different ways
correctAnswerText: The same operating system service is asked to do the same thing, in two different ways
explanation: Both are ways of asking the operating system to rename a file, and it is the operating system that does it either way. What differs is how the request is expressed, not what happens underneath or who carries it out.

prompt: Someone is told that a particular task "can only be done from the command line". What is the most accurate reading of that claim?
optionA: The graphical tools installed happen not to offer it, though the system itself can do it
optionB: The operating system refuses to perform that task when a graphical program asks
optionC: The task needs privileges that only the command line is granted
optionD: The task changes files, and graphical programs cannot change files
correctAnswerText: The graphical tools installed happen not to offer it, though the system itself can do it
explanation: Both interfaces ask the same operating system for the same services, so a claim like this is about which tools expose the task, not about what the system permits. Nothing about arriving through a graphical program changes what is allowed or what is possible.

prompt: A machine with one processor core appears to run a browser, a music player and an editor at the same time. What is actually happening?
optionA: All three run at the same instant, because one core can handle three things at once
optionB: Each program has been given a processor core of its own
optionC: The operating system switches between them fast enough that the switching is not noticed
optionD: Two are paused entirely until the third is closed
correctAnswerText: The operating system switches between them fast enough that the switching is not noticed
explanation: One core executes one thing at a time, so simultaneity is an appearance produced by switching quickly. If any of the other options were true there would be nothing for a scheduler to decide.

prompt: On a single-core machine, more and more programs are opened. Every one of them keeps responding, but everything feels slower. What accounts for this?
optionA: The processor runs more slowly as the number of programs grows
optionB: The same processor time is now divided among more programs, so each waits longer for its turn
optionC: Each new program takes a share of the speed of the machine's memory
optionD: The operating system adds a delay deliberately, to keep the machine stable
correctAnswerText: The same processor time is now divided among more programs, so each waits longer for its turn
explanation: The amount of processor time per second is fixed; opening more programs does not create more of it, it only divides it further, so each program's turn comes round less often. The processor itself has not changed speed, and nothing is being slowed on purpose.

prompt: Two programs both ask to use the printer at the same moment. What happens?
optionA: Both print at once, and the pages come out interleaved
optionB: The second program's request fails and it reports an error
optionC: The two programs agree between themselves which goes first
optionD: The operating system lets one use it and makes the other wait
correctAnswerText: The operating system lets one use it and makes the other wait
explanation: Arbitrating between competing requests is the operating system's job, and waiting is the normal outcome — not failure, not interleaved output, and not a negotiation, since the two programs have no way to reach each other.

prompt: Two programs are both reading large amounts of data from the same disk. Neither fails, but each is slower than it would be alone. What explains this?
optionA: The operating system is giving each of them turns at a device that serves one request at a time
optionB: The disk halves its own speed whenever two programs use it
optionC: Each program is waiting for the other to finish before it begins
optionD: The operating system has lowered the priority of both programs
correctAnswerText: The operating system is giving each of them turns at a device that serves one request at a time
explanation: The device can serve one request at a time, so two streams of requests are interleaved and each program spends part of its time waiting. Neither is blocked outright — that is why both still finish — and the disk has not changed speed.

prompt: Two programs request the same device. In one case the second program waits and then succeeds; in another the second program is refused straight away. What decides which of these happens?
optionA: Whether the second program was written to cope with waiting
optionB: Which of the two programs the person started first
optionC: Whether the operating system queues requests for that device or grants one program exclusive use
optionD: Whether the two programs belong to the same application
correctAnswerText: Whether the operating system queues requests for that device or grants one program exclusive use
explanation: Both outcomes are the operating system arbitrating; they differ in the policy it applies to that resource. Some resources are shared by taking turns, others are handed to one holder until released, and it is that choice — not the program, its author or its start time — that produces waiting rather than refusal.

prompt: The same text editor is started twice, so two editor windows are open, each holding a different document. How many processes are running?
optionA: One, because only one editor is installed
optionB: Two, each with memory of its own
optionC: One, because both windows show the same program
optionD: Two, sharing a single block of memory between them
correctAnswerText: Two, each with memory of its own
explanation: Each start produces a separate process with its own memory, whatever the windows look like. One installed program can be running as many independent processes at once.

prompt: Two copies of the same editor are running. The zoom level is changed in one of them, and the other is unaffected. Why?
optionA: The setting is written to disk only when the program closes
optionB: The two copies take turns, and the change has not reached the second one yet
optionC: Zoom affects only the display and is not part of a program's state
optionD: Each running copy holds its own memory, so a value set in one does not exist in the other
correctAnswerText: Each running copy holds its own memory, so a value set in one does not exist in the other
explanation: The two processes came from one program but do not share memory, so a value one holds is invisible to the other. There is no delay involved and nothing is waiting to be written — the second copy simply never had that value.

prompt: The same editor is opened twice. Changing a preference in one copy leaves the other unchanged. Both are then closed, the editor is opened again, and the preference has changed. What accounts for both observations together?
optionA: The preference was written to a file that a copy reads when it starts, while the running copies each kept their own value in memory
optionB: Once the first copy closed, the second was able to read its memory
optionC: Closing a process passes its memory on to the next process that starts
optionD: The operating system merges the memory of processes from the same program when they end
correctAnswerText: The preference was written to a file that a copy reads when it starts, while the running copies each kept their own value in memory
explanation: Two facts have to hold at once: the running copies were isolated, and something outlived both of them. Memory explains the first, a file on disk explains the second. The other options all require one process to reach another's memory, which is exactly what the operating system prevents.

prompt: A program holds a password in memory while it runs. Another program running at the same time tries to read that memory. What happens?
optionA: It succeeds, because running programs share the machine's memory
optionB: It succeeds, provided both programs were started by the same person
optionC: The operating system does not allow it; each process reaches only its own memory
optionD: It succeeds, but the value that comes back is scrambled
correctAnswerText: The operating system does not allow it; each process reaches only its own memory
explanation: Keeping processes out of one another's memory is one of the operating system's core jobs, and it does not depend on who started them. The attempt is refused outright rather than allowed and obscured.

prompt: A program that had been using a large amount of memory is closed. What becomes of that memory?
optionA: It stays reserved for that program in case it is started again
optionB: The operating system reclaims it and can hand it to another program
optionC: It is cleared only when the machine is restarted
optionD: It goes to the next program that asks, with the previous contents still in it
correctAnswerText: The operating system reclaims it and can hand it to another program
explanation: Memory is lent for as long as a process exists and taken back when it ends, which is what lets a machine run far more programs over a day than would fit at once. It is not held in reserve, and it is not passed on still carrying the last process's data.

prompt: One program crashes. Every other program keeps running normally and the machine stays up. What does that tell you about how memory was arranged?
optionA: The crash happened before the program had been given any memory
optionB: The operating system copied the other programs' memory to disk in time
optionC: The other programs had already finished using their memory
optionD: Each process had memory of its own, so damage inside one could not reach the others
correctAnswerText: Each process had memory of its own, so damage inside one could not reach the others
explanation: The survival of everything else is the evidence: a fault confined to one process is a fault that could not touch memory belonging to another. Had memory been shared, one program writing wrongly could have corrupted the rest.

prompt: A machine holds /home/work/report.txt and /home/archive/report.txt. Which statement is correct?
optionA: They are two different files that happen to share a name
optionB: They are one file, reachable by two different paths
optionC: Only one of them can exist at a time
optionD: The second one is a shortcut to the first
correctAnswerText: They are two different files that happen to share a name
explanation: A name only has to be unique within its own directory, so the same name in two directories names two unrelated files. Editing one leaves the other exactly as it was.

prompt: The current directory is /home/work. A program is asked to open notes.txt. Which file does it open?
optionA: /notes.txt
optionB: /home/notes.txt
optionC: /home/work/notes.txt
optionD: Whichever notes.txt was opened most recently
correctAnswerText: /home/work/notes.txt
explanation: A name given without a leading slash is resolved against the current directory, so it means notes.txt inside /home/work. Nothing about the resolution depends on history — the same name from a different current directory would mean a different file.

prompt: A script finds data.txt when it is run from /home/work, and fails to find it when the very same script is run from /home. The file has not been moved or altered. What explains this?
optionA: The file's contents changed when the working directory changed
optionB: The script names the file relatively, so it is looked for in whatever directory the script is run from
optionC: Running from /home gives the script fewer permissions
optionD: A file can only be opened from the directory that contains it
correctAnswerText: The script names the file relatively, so it is looked for in whatever directory the script is run from
explanation: The script is unchanged and the file is unchanged, so what changed is the starting point the name is measured from — the signature of a relative path. Naming the file from the root instead would make the script behave the same wherever it is run.

prompt: A word processor prints a document. Which describes the route the request takes?
optionA: The application reaches the printer directly
optionB: The printer's driver is part of the application and reaches the printer from there
optionC: The printer needs no software; the application sends it the page
optionD: The application asks the operating system, which uses the printer's driver to reach the printer
correctAnswerText: The application asks the operating system, which uses the printer's driver to reach the printer
explanation: Applications do not address hardware themselves. The operating system stands in between, and the driver is the piece that knows how this particular printer expects to be spoken to.

prompt: Two different printers are attached to a machine. The same application prints to both, and nothing about the application was changed to make that work. Which part knows how each printer expects to be addressed?
optionA: Each printer's own driver
optionB: The application, which identifies the model when it starts
optionC: The operating system, which contains instructions for every printer ever made
optionD: The printer itself, which converts whatever it is sent
correctAnswerText: Each printer's own driver
explanation: The application being identical for both is the evidence: whatever differs between the printers must be held somewhere the application is not. That is the driver — one per device, so a new printer means a new driver rather than a new version of every application.

prompt: Three programs are open. One is waiting for the person to type something, one has finished and exited, and one has calculations still to do. Which can the scheduler run next?
optionA: The one waiting for typing, as it has waited longest
optionB: The one that has exited, so that it releases its resources
optionC: The one with calculations still to do
optionD: Any of them; the choice is made at random
correctAnswerText: The one with calculations still to do
explanation: Only a process that is ready can be given the processor. Waiting for input is not ready — running it would achieve nothing, because the thing it needs has not arrived — and a process that has exited no longer exists to be run.

prompt: A program shows no sign of activity, yet the processor is mostly idle. Which explanation fits what is observed?
optionA: The scheduler has given all the processor time to other programs
optionB: It is waiting for something outside the processor, so processor time would not help it
optionC: The program has been given too little memory to run
optionD: The processor is too slow for this program
correctAnswerText: It is waiting for something outside the processor, so processor time would not help it
explanation: An idle processor is the clue that settles it: if time were available and the program were ready, it would be running. Both the competition explanation and the too-slow explanation require a busy processor, and neither survives the evidence.

prompt: A machine runs one program that must react to typing without noticeable delay, and another that performs a long calculation nobody is waiting on. If the scheduler gave both equal turns of the same long length, what would go wrong and what would fix it?
optionA: The calculation would never finish; giving it longer turns would fix it
optionB: Both would fail, and only a second processor would fix it
optionC: Nothing would go wrong; turn length does not affect how responsive a program feels
optionD: Typing would feel unresponsive during the calculation's turns; shorter turns would fix it
correctAnswerText: Typing would feel unresponsive during the calculation's turns; shorter turns would fix it
explanation: How long a turn lasts sets how long a ready program may have to wait for its next one, and that wait is exactly what a person notices while typing. Shortening turns costs a little efficiency in switching but buys responsiveness; the calculation still finishes either way, just later.

prompt: Every program on a machine is waiting for something — one for a key press, one for data from the network, one for a disk read. Nothing is ready to run. What does the scheduler do?
optionA: Nothing runs until one of them stops waiting, and the processor sits idle
optionB: It picks whichever has waited longest and runs it anyway
optionC: It reports an error, because a processor must always be executing something
optionD: It divides the time equally among the three waiting programs
correctAnswerText: Nothing runs until one of them stops waiting, and the processor sits idle
explanation: A scheduler chooses among ready processes, and here there are none, so there is nothing to choose. Running or sharing time between waiting processes would accomplish nothing, since what each needs has not arrived. An idle processor is a normal state, not a fault.

prompt: A single-processor machine must run two tasks: one continually checks that a robot arm will not collide with anything, and one produces a report needing several hours of processor time. Which arrangement is defensible, and what does it cost?
optionA: Give the two equal turns of equal length — neither is affected
optionB: Finish the report first and then start the collision check — both get what they need
optionC: Run the collision check whenever it is ready and let the report use what is left — the report takes longer to finish
optionD: Run the collision check only while the report is waiting for the disk — nothing is delayed
correctAnswerText: Run the collision check whenever it is ready and let the report use what is left — the report takes longer to finish
explanation: One processor cannot give both tasks everything, so the question is what to give up. A late collision check is dangerous and a late report is not, so the check takes priority and the report pays in elapsed time. The other arrangements each claim the choice is free, and on a single processor it never is.

prompt: A user may read a file but not change it. They open it, edit the text on screen, and try to save. What happens?
optionA: Opening is refused, because editing requires permission to change the file
optionB: Opening and editing on screen succeed; the save is refused
optionC: The save succeeds, because the file was opened successfully
optionD: The save succeeds, but the change is discarded when the file is closed
correctAnswerText: Opening and editing on screen succeed; the save is refused
explanation: Permissions govern what reaches the file, not what happens in the editor's own memory. Reading it in is allowed and changing the copy on screen touches nothing on disk; the refusal comes at the moment the change would be written back.

prompt: A user may read and change a particular file. They try to delete it and are refused. The file's own permissions have not changed. What explains the refusal?
optionA: A file cannot be deleted while the user is still able to read it
optionB: Deletion always requires ownership of the file
optionC: The file must be emptied of its contents before it can be deleted
optionD: Deleting removes the file's entry from its directory, and they may not change that directory
correctAnswerText: Deleting removes the file's entry from its directory, and they may not change that directory
explanation: Deleting is not an operation on the file's contents but on the directory that names it, so the permission that decides it sits on the directory. That is why full access to a file can still leave it undeletable.

prompt: On a shared machine, a user may add files to a directory but may not list what it contains. What can that user do?
optionA: Add a file, and open one whose exact name they already know, but not discover what else is there
optionB: Nothing at all, since they cannot see the directory
optionC: Everything, since being able to add files implies being able to see them
optionD: Only add files; anything they add becomes unreachable to them
correctAnswerText: Add a file, and open one whose exact name they already know, but not discover what else is there
explanation: The two permissions are independent, so a directory can accept new entries while refusing to reveal the ones it holds. Reaching a file by its exact name does not require listing, which is what makes a drop-off directory possible at all.

prompt: The owner of a file removes their own permission to change it, then tries to edit it. What happens, and why?
optionA: The edit succeeds; an owner is never restricted by permissions
optionB: The edit is refused permanently, as the owner cannot restore the permission
optionC: The edit is refused; ownership decides who may set the permissions, not what the current ones allow
optionD: The edit succeeds, and the permission is restored automatically
correctAnswerText: The edit is refused; ownership decides who may set the permissions, not what the current ones allow
explanation: Permissions are checked as they stand, so an owner who has removed a permission is refused like anyone else. What ownership still gives them is the ability to grant it back — the refusal is real but not permanent.

prompt: A user is allowed to run a program but not to read its contents. Is that a meaningful combination?
optionA: No; running a program requires reading its instructions, so the two amount to one permission
optionB: Yes; they can use the program without being able to inspect or copy how it works
optionC: Yes, but only for programs that need no input
optionD: No; a program that cannot be read cannot be loaded into memory at all
correctAnswerText: Yes; they can use the program without being able to inspect or copy how it works
explanation: Loading the program is done by the operating system on the user's behalf, and permission to run it is a separate decision from permission to open and read it as a file. That separation is precisely what allows a program to be offered for use without being handed over.

prompt: An ordinary program needs to write data to a disk. What must it do?
optionA: Write to the disk hardware directly
optionB: Wait until no other program is using the disk, then write directly
optionC: Ask the person to grant it access to the hardware
optionD: Ask the kernel, which performs the access on its behalf
correctAnswerText: Ask the kernel, which performs the access on its behalf
explanation: Ordinary programs run with limited privilege and cannot touch hardware at all, whether or not anything else is using it. Every such action is a request to the kernel, which decides whether to carry it out.

prompt: A program started by an administrator still cannot write to the disk hardware directly; it goes through the kernel like any other program. Why?
optionA: The boundary is a property of how a program runs, not of which account started it
optionB: The administrator account had not been granted all of its rights
optionC: The program was not written to make use of its administrator rights
optionD: Administrators can reach hardware only after the machine is restarted
correctAnswerText: The boundary is a property of how a program runs, not of which account started it
explanation: Two different things are being confused. An administrator account may be permitted more — more files, more settings — but it is still an ordinary program that runs, and ordinary programs ask the kernel. Wider permissions do not move the boundary.

prompt: A machine stays usable when an ordinary program contains a serious fault, but can stop altogether when a driver running with kernel privilege contains one. What accounts for the difference?
optionA: Drivers are larger, so faults in them are more serious
optionB: Ordinary programs are checked for faults before they are allowed to run
optionC: The ordinary program is confined by the boundary and can damage only its own state; kernel-privileged code is not confined
optionD: The operating system restarts ordinary programs automatically but cannot restart drivers
correctAnswerText: The ordinary program is confined by the boundary and can damage only its own state; kernel-privileged code is not confined
explanation: What matters is not the size or quality of the code but which side of the boundary it runs on. Inside the confinement a fault reaches one process; outside it, the same kind of fault can reach anything.

prompt: Some systems take a driver out of the kernel and run it as an ordinary program instead. What does that buy, and what does it cost?
optionA: It buys speed, because ordinary programs run with fewer checks
optionB: A fault in it can no longer bring the whole system down, but every device request must now cross the boundary, which takes longer
optionC: It costs nothing, since the driver behaves identically wherever it runs
optionD: It buys nothing, because a driver has kernel privilege wherever it runs
correctAnswerText: A fault in it can no longer bring the whole system down, but every device request must now cross the boundary, which takes longer
explanation: Moving code outside the boundary confines its faults, which is the gain. The price is paid on every single request, because what used to be an ordinary call now has to cross into the kernel and back. Whether that trade is worth taking depends on how often the device is used.

prompt: A machine slows badly whenever several large programs are open, and the disk is active almost constantly. Closing one program restores normal speed. Which resource has run short?
optionA: Disk space, since the disk is so busy
optionB: Processor time, since the programs are running slowly
optionC: Network capacity
optionD: Memory — with too little, data is moved between memory and disk continually
correctAnswerText: Memory — with too little, data is moved between memory and disk continually
explanation: Constant disk activity that appears only when many programs are open, and stops when one is closed, points at memory rather than the disk itself: what is not fitting in memory has to be shuttled to and from the disk. A shortage of disk space would not be relieved by closing a program.

prompt: A machine refuses to save new files, and programs report failures when they try to write. It responds normally in every other way, and closing programs does not help. Which resource has run short, and what would relieve it?
optionA: Storage space; deleting or moving files would relieve it
optionB: Memory; closing more programs would relieve it
optionC: Processor time; waiting for other work to finish would relieve it
optionD: Memory; restarting the machine would relieve it
correctAnswerText: Storage space; deleting or moving files would relieve it
explanation: Closing programs frees memory, and it made no difference, which rules memory out. Writes failing while everything else is normal points at somewhere to put the data, so the remedy is to free space rather than to free memory.

prompt: A machine stays responsive to typing and window switching, files save normally, but one calculation takes far longer than usual. A monitoring tool reports the processor fully used, with ample free memory and disk. Which resource is the limit?
optionA: Memory, in spite of what the tool reports
optionB: Storage space
optionC: Processor time
optionD: The driver for the disk
correctAnswerText: Processor time
explanation: Every other resource has been observed to be fine — saving works, memory and disk are free — and the one thing reported as fully consumed is the processor. The work is arriving faster than it can be executed, so the calculation waits its turn.

prompt: Adding memory to a machine that had been moving data between memory and disk constantly makes it much faster. Adding the same memory to a machine whose processor was already fully used changes almost nothing. Why?
optionA: The second machine's memory must have been installed incorrectly
optionB: Extra memory helps only where a shortage of memory was what caused the extra work
optionC: Memory improves speed only on machines that also have a fast disk
optionD: The second machine needed faster memory rather than more of it
correctAnswerText: Extra memory helps only where a shortage of memory was what caused the extra work
explanation: A remedy relieves the resource that was actually short. On the first machine the shortage of memory was creating disk work that then disappeared; on the second nothing was waiting on memory, so supplying more of it removes no obstacle at all.

prompt: A machine is short of memory. One suggestion is to let it use disk space as overflow. What does that buy, and what does it cost?
optionA: It buys nothing, because a disk cannot hold a program's working data
optionB: It buys speed, because the disk is added to memory and the total is faster
optionC: It costs nothing, as long as there is enough free disk space
optionD: Programs that would not otherwise fit can run, but reaching data held in the overflow is far slower than reaching memory
correctAnswerText: Programs that would not otherwise fit can run, but reaching data held in the overflow is far slower than reaching memory
explanation: The overflow buys capacity and pays for it in time, because disks are far slower than memory. That is why it rescues a machine that is slightly short and cripples one that is badly short: the more traffic goes to the overflow, the more the cost is paid.
